1. From a transversal to a correspondence

Let \(i:N\hookrightarrow V\) be an embedded transversal of dimension \(q\). Put

\[ Z_N=r^{-1}(N)\subset G. \]

The map \(s:Z_N\to V\) is a local diffeomorphism. Its fibres are discrete countable sets: they are the intersections of the holonomy covering of a leaf with \(N\), including the different lifts of an intersection point.

Let \(E\) be a continuous Hermitian Hilbert field on \(N\), given by a countably generated Hilbert \(C_0(N)\)-module. Initially use compact chart sections

\[ \xi\in C_c(Z_N,r^*E\otimes s^*D_F^{1/2}). \]

For a non-Hausdorff arrow space, this means the finite span of sections supported in Hausdorff charts, as in the preceding lesson. For \(\gamma:x\to y\), define

\[ \langle\xi,\eta\rangle_A(\gamma) =\sum_{\substack{z\in Z_N\\s(z)=x}} \left\langle\xi(z\gamma^{-1}),\eta(z)\right\rangle . \tag{1} \]

The two source half-densities give the summand the required endpoint density. On a pair of compact chart supports the sum has finitely many local terms; partitioning supports reduces (1) to ordinary continuous chart kernels. Thus its value is in \(A\).

Right multiplication is convolution. In a density trivialization its formula is

\[ (\xi f)(z) =\int_{s(h)=s(z)}\xi(zh^{-1})f(h). \tag{2} \]

Fubini's theorem gives

\[ \langle\xi f,\eta g\rangle_A =f^**\langle\xi,\eta\rangle_A*g. \tag{3} \]

To check positivity without a coordinate guess, use the fibre

\[ H_x^N=\ell^2(Z_N\cap s^{-1}(x),r^*E). \]

The coefficient kernel in (1), represented on \(L^2(G_x)\), is \(T_\xi(x)T_\xi(x)^*\), where

\[ T_\xi(x):H_x^N\longrightarrow L^2(G_x) \]

is the coefficient map of the equivariant section \(\xi\). The same formula for a finite list of sections proves matrix positivity. Since the regular representations define the norm of \(A\), (3) completes the sections to a right Hilbert \(A\)-module, denoted \(\mathcal E_N(E)\). Chart bump functions and a countable dense family of sections on \(N\) show that it is countably generated.

A bounded adjointable field map \(T:E_1\to E_2\) acts by

\[ (i_!T)_x v(z)=T_{r(z)}v(z),\qquad v\in H_x^N. \tag{4} \]

The action preserves the chart section space and has adjoint \(i_!(T^*)\). It therefore gives an adjointable map of the completed modules. Its norm is at most \(\|T\|\).

The discrete set in \(H_x^N\) must include holonomy lifts. For example, a transversal point on a leaf with twofold holonomy contributes two points on its holonomy covering. Removing one lift changes the equivariant representation.

2. Why compact maps remain compact

The compact operators in this section are compact module operators. They can have infinitely many nonzero diagonal blocks in the Hilbert space of one recurrent leaf.

Theorem 2.1 (transversal compactness). If \(T:E_1\to E_2\) is compact as a Hilbert \(C_0(N)\)-module map, then \(i_!T\) is compact as a Hilbert \(A\)-module map.

Proof. First take \(E_1=E_2=E\) and \(T=\theta_{\sigma,\sigma}\), where \(\sigma\) is a continuous section with compact support in a small transverse coordinate neighbourhood \(U\subset N\). Near the units over \(U\), the map \(s:Z_N\to V\) identifies a neighbourhood with a plaque tube. Choose a compactly supported source half-density \(b\) in that tube, normalized by

\[ \int |b(n,t)|^2\,dt=1 \quad\text{for }n\in\operatorname{supp}\sigma. \tag{5} \]

Such a \(b\) is a fixed normalized plaque bump times a transverse cutoff equal to one on the support. The tube can be chosen so that two arrows in it with the same source have the same range in \(N\) and are the same arrow. This follows from the local diffeomorphism \(s\) near the units; shrink the transverse coordinate neighbourhood before choosing the bump.

Set \(\xi(z)=b(z)\sigma(r(z))\). We claim

\[ \theta_{\xi,\xi}=i_!(\theta_{\sigma,\sigma}). \tag{6} \]

Evaluate the left side on \(H_x^N\). The averaged rank-one formula first sums over \(w\in Z_N\cap s^{-1}(x)\) and then integrates the plaque variable. A mixed term involving distinct \(z,w\) can be nonzero only if both corresponding short arrows lie in the chosen tube. Their quotient has its source and range in \(N\). The uniqueness just established makes that quotient a unit, so \(w=z\). The remaining diagonal term is

\[ v(z)\longmapsto \sigma(r(z))\left\langle\sigma(r(z)),v(z)\right\rangle \int|b(r(z),t)|^2\,dt. \]

By (5) this is exactly (4) for \(T=\theta_{\sigma,\sigma}\). The regular fibre representations are faithful on module endomorphisms, so (6) follows.

For a section with an arbitrary compact support \(K\), take a finite nonnegative partition of unity \(\phi_j\) on \(K\), subordinate to neighbourhoods of the above kind. Pointwise,

\[ \theta_{\sigma,\sigma} =\sum_j\theta_{\sqrt{\phi_j}\sigma,\sqrt{\phi_j}\sigma}. \]

Each term has compact pushforward by (6). Polarization treats \(\theta_{\sigma,\eta}\), and continuous cutoffs approximate sections vanishing at infinity by sections with compact support. Finite sums of rank-one maps are norm dense in the compact module maps. Since (4) is contractive, their pushforwards converge in norm to \(i_!T\). The compact maps form a norm closed space, proving the theorem. \(\square\)

In particular \(C_0(N)\) acts by compact operators on \(\mathcal E_N(\mathbb C)\), through multiplication at \(r(z)\).

For clarity, an even Kasparov cycle from \(B\) to \(A\) consists of a countably generated graded Hilbert \(A\)-module \(\mathcal E\), an even *-representation \(\rho:B\to\mathcal L_A(\mathcal E)\), and an odd adjointable \(F\) such that

\[ [F,\rho(b)],\qquad(F^2-1)\rho(b),\qquad(F-F^*)\rho(b) \]

are compact for every \(b\in B\). Homotopy and the addition of degenerate cycles define \(KK(B,A)\). Section0 constructs its associative product and proves the homotopy and unit conventions. Theorem 0.14 proves its scalar identification \(KK(\mathbb C,A)=K_0(A)\) and the odd version, including general Hilbert-module homotopies.

The correspondence above gives the cycle

\[ i_!=[\mathcal E_N(\mathbb C),\rho,0]\in KK(C_0(N),A). \tag{7} \]

The only nonzero defect in its definition is \(-\rho(h)\), which is compact by Theorem 2.1. Theorem 0.14 and the product in Section 0 give its action

\[ K_c^j(N)\longrightarrow K_j(A),\qquad x\longmapsto x\otimes_{C_0(N)}i_!. \tag{8} \]

The same construction works for an étale map to the leaf space described by local transverse maps and holonomy transition arrows. The local modules glue by those arrows; the proof of compactness is local on the support in the domain, so the partition-of-unity argument remains valid.

3. A compact transversal gives a projection

Assume now that \(N\) is compact. A uniform plaque tube along \(N\) exists: the exponential in a leafwise metric is transverse to \(N\) at its zero section, and compactness permits a tubular neighbourhood on which it is injective. Its corresponding unit neighbourhood in \(Z_N\) has the uniqueness used in Theorem 2.1.

Choose a scalar section \(b\) in this tube satisfying (5) for every \(n\in N\). Then

\[ \theta_{b,b}=1_{\mathcal E_N(\mathbb C)}. \tag{9} \]

Proposition 3.1. The element \(e=\langle b,b\rangle_A\) is a projection in \(A\), and \(\mathcal E_N(\mathbb C)\cong eA\). If \(\Lambda\) is an invariant transverse measure, then

\[ \tau_\Lambda(e)=\Lambda(N). \tag{10} \]

Proof. The element \(e\) is self-adjoint. By (9), \(be=b\), and

\[ e^2=\langle b,be\rangle_A=\langle b,b\rangle_A=e. \]

The map \(eA\to\mathcal E_N(\mathbb C)\), \(a\mapsto ba\), preserves inner products. Every \(\xi\) satisfies \(\xi=b\langle b,\xi\rangle_A\) by (9), so it is onto.

At a unit \(1_x\), the kernel \(e(1_x)\) is the sum of \(|b(z)|^2\) over the short arrows \(z:x\to n\) in the chosen tube. There is at most one such arrow. The diagonal trace formula from the measured-index lesson integrates this function using plaque volume and transverse measure. Integration first in the plaque direction gives one by (5), and the remaining integral is precisely \(\Lambda(N)\). All terms are nonnegative and have compact support, so this order of integration is valid. \(\square\)

This projection is in the algebra itself. A class in \(K_0(A)\) need not have a representative of that form: unitization and matrix stabilization allow differences of projections that are absent from \(A\).

Example 3.2 (a product foliation). For \(V=P\times N\), with \(P\) connected, choose a normalized \(\psi\in L^2(P)\). The construction gives

\[ e(t,t',n)=\psi(t)\overline{\psi(t')}. \]

Under \(A\cong C_0(N)\otimes\mathcal K(L^2(P))\), this is \(1_N\otimes\theta_{\psi,\psi}\) when \(N\) is compact. Formula (10) gives the total transverse mass.

4. A local transverse orientation class

Assume \(V\) is connected and the normal bundle \(\tau=TV/F\) is oriented. A positively oriented transverse embedding of an open \(q\)-disk defines, using (8),

\[ [V/F]^*=\varphi_!(\beta_q)\in K_q(A). \tag{11} \]

Here \(\beta_q\) is the compactly supported Bott generator. The open disk is diffeomorphic to \(\mathbb R^q\); its parity is \(q\bmod2\). A closed disk with its ordinary K-theory would give a different statement.

Proposition 4.1 (independence of the transverse disk). Within each connected component of \(V\), the class (11) does not depend on the centre or the positively oriented transverse embedding.

Proof. The Bott class can be represented with support in any smaller disk about its centre. Extension by zero from that disk gives the same generator; this is the local form of Bott periodicity. Thus only the germ of the embedding matters.

In a foliation chart, shrink that germ and rescale its coordinates. It is isotopic through transverse embeddings to the linear transverse graph given by its derivative: its transverse derivative is invertible, and on a sufficiently small disk it remains so throughout the straight interpolation to that derivative. The positively oriented linear transverse frames are connected. Indeed Gram–Schmidt writes an element of \(\operatorname{GL}^+(q,\mathbb R)\) as an orthogonal matrix of determinant one times an upper triangular matrix with positive diagonal. Straight interpolation contracts the latter to identity without losing its positive diagonal. Elimination by plane rotations writes the former as a product of plane rotations, each contracted through its angle. For rank zero or one there is no rotation step. Therefore two choices at one point are joined through positively oriented frames.

To obtain a correspondence homotopy, apply Sections 1–2 to \(V\times[0,1]\), foliated by \(F\) at fixed parameter, and to the family of transverse disk embeddings. Its algebra is \(A\otimes C([0,1])\). The parameter-family disk is transverse, since its parameter derivative has component one. The same normalized plaque bumps and finite partitions give a module with compact coefficient action; pull its domain representation back along the constant inclusion of \(C_0(D^q)\). Its endpoint cycles are exactly the two disk correspondences. Section 0 homotopy invariance and the fixed coefficient Bott class therefore give their equal K-classes.

Join two centres by a path in \(V\). The oriented normal bundle along this interval is trivial, so choose a continuous positively oriented transverse frame along the path. A small transverse exponential disk varies along it; finitely many intervals suffice if the radius needs to shrink. The preceding support argument permits those shrinkings. Homotopy invariance on the successive intervals proves equality of the endpoint classes. \(\square\)

The component restriction is necessary. For the zero-dimensional foliation of \(V=\{0,1\}\), the two transverse point classes are the two distinct coordinate projections in \(K_0(C(V))=\mathbb Z^2\). There is no path joining their centres.

Orientation establishes this definition, not its nonvanishing. A sufficient test is a class

\[ \zeta\in KK^q(A,\mathbb C) \quad\text{with}\quad [V/F]^*\otimes_A\zeta=1\in\mathbb Z. \tag{12} \]

Indeed a zero class has zero product with every class. For a submersion onto an oriented spin-c manifold \(B\), the Morita equivalence \(A\sim C_0(B)\) turns (11) into the local Bott class on \(B\). To use the geometric spin-c Dirac K-homology class as \(\zeta\), its local Bott–Dirac pairing must be proved with the same orientation. The vector-bundle Dirac comparison required below includes this assertion; the local disk construction does not supply it.

For a general foliation, a holonomy invariant spin-c structure on \(\tau\) does not by itself produce the operator in (12). Transverse ellipticity, compactness of commutators, and an appropriate representation still need to be proved. The construction of a suitable transverse Dirac class is a substantive problem formulated by Connes; the elementary local disk argument does not solve it.

5. Maps to a leaf space retain transition arrows

The geometric-cycle framework originates in the work of Paul Baum and Ronald G. Douglas. For the smooth foliation model used here, see the freely available Connes, Section 9, which credits its collaboration with Baum. The definitions below retain the actual arrow cocycles and full stable orientations; Theorems 6.0ae and 6.1 prove descent for this specified model.

A smooth map \(f:M\to V/F\) is described by an open cover \((U_a)\), smooth maps \(f_a:U_a\to V\), and smooth arrows

\[ g_{ba}(x):f_a(x)\longrightarrow f_b(x) \]

on overlaps, satisfying \(g_{ca}=g_{cb}g_{ba}\). Refining the cover or changing its lifts by compatible arrows gives the same map. Keeping only the assertion that \(f_a(x)\) and \(f_b(x)\) lie on the same leaf would discard holonomy.

The derivatives of the holonomy maps glue the bundles \(f_a^*\tau\) to a rank-\(q\) real bundle \(f^*\tau\) on \(M\). A K-orientation of \(f\) is a stable spin-c orientation of the virtual bundle

\[ f^*\tau-TM. \tag{13} \]

The canonical complex spin-c structure on \(TM\oplus TM\) converts this to full Clifford orientation data on \(TM\oplus f^*\tau\). In positive rank these data are a spin-c structure, as proved in Lemma6.0j. In rank zero a stable orientation can retain an odd graded line; it is interpreted after positive even stabilization and is not identified with the canonical even rank-zero unit. The finite construction in Lemma6.0j retains that grading. This stable convention fixes the full orientation, including its line twist, needed for the Thom map.

There is also a useful principal bundle. Glue \(U_a\times_{f_a,r}G\) using the transition arrows. It is a manifold \(P_f\) of dimension \(\dim M+p\), with projection to \(M\) and a free transitive groupoid action on each fibre. The fibres have dimension \(p\). Local sections recover the cocycle, so the bundle and cocycle descriptions are equivalent.

Geometric cycles are triples \((M,E,f)\), where \(M\) is compact without boundary, \(E\) is a finite-rank complex bundle, and \(f\) has the orientation (13). Their parity is \(\dim M-q\bmod2\). Impose the following relations:

  1. Disjoint union is addition, and replacing \(E_1\oplus E_2\) by the two separate cycles does not change the sum.
  2. The oriented boundary of a compact cycle with boundary is zero.
  3. For an even-rank spin-c real bundle \(W\to M\), replace \(M\) by the sphere bundle \(S(W\oplus\mathbb R)\), replace \(E\) by its pullback tensored with the fibre Bott bundle, and replace \(f\) by its composite with the sphere projection.

The resulting group is denoted \(K_{*,\tau}^{\mathrm{geom}}(BG)\). The symbol \(BG\) records the classifying space of the groupoid and its normal bundle. Identifying this cycle model with other models of groupoid topological K-theory is a theorem that must include its hypotheses.

6. The geometry of a wrong-way map

The global Clifford Thom equivalence

The Clifford Bott and Dirac method is classical; see [Kasparov] and the point-space discussion in [Emerson]. We give the bundle proof with both product operators and their homotopies. The argument works over a noncompact base and retains the Clifford twist until a spin-c structure is specified. Its analytic inputs are the complete-source energy argument of Lemma 8.19, the module-generator proof of Lemma 8.15a and the product criterion of Definition 0.3. No local-to-global KK exactness theorem is needed.

Let \(X\) be a second-countable locally compact manifold and \(E\to X\) a rank-\(r\) real vector bundle with a continuous metric. Write \(\pi:E\to X\) and \[ C_X=C_0(X),\qquad A_E=C_0(E,\pi^*\mathrm{Cl}^+(E)). \tag{128} \] All tensor products and Clifford representations in this subsection are graded. In an orthonormal fibre frame, let \(e_i\) denote exterior multiplication by the corresponding vector and \(\iota_i=e_i^*\) contraction. On \(\Lambda E_{\mathbb C}\), put \[ a_i=e_i+\iota_i,\qquad c_i=e_i-\iota_i, \qquad \{a_i,a_j\}=2\delta_{ij},\quad \{c_i,c_j\}=-2\delta_{ij},\quad \{a_i,c_j\}=0. \tag{129} \] The operators \(a_i\) are odd self-adjoint and the \(c_i\) odd skew-adjoint. These formulas are equivariant under orthogonal frame changes. They therefore define global Clifford actions. Exterior-degree parity is the grading \(\Gamma\).

Lemma 6.0a (the two global cycles). Let \(b_E\) be the standard-module cycle \[ \left(A_E,\phi_X, B(v)=\frac{c^+(v)}{\sqrt{1+\|v\|^2}}\right), \qquad \phi_X(f)(v)=f(\pi(v))1. \tag{130} \] Let \(\mathcal H_E\) be the Hilbert \(C_X\)-module of continuous fibrewise \(L^2\) sections of \(\Lambda E_{\mathbb C}\) whose fibre norms vanish at base infinity. The fibre metric supplies Lebesgue measure. The positive Clifford action in (129) represents \(A_E\) on this module by multiplication. The vertical operator and its bounded transform are \[ D=\sum_i c_i\partial_{v_i},\qquad F_D=D(1+D^2)^{-1/2}. \tag{131} \] They define \(d_E\in KK(A_E,C_X)\); (130) defines \(b_E\in KK(C_X,A_E)\). Neither construction requires an orientation or spin-c structure.

Proof. For (130), \(B\) is an odd self-adjoint multiplier of norm at most one, and its coefficient commutators vanish. Its localized square defect is \(-f(x)/(1+\|v\|^2)\). This vanishes at infinity on the total space: cut off a compact base set using \(f\in C_X\), then a fixed fibre radius. A closed bounded disk bundle over a compact base set is compact, by a finite bundle-chart cover and uniform equivalence of its fibre norms. Thus the defect belongs to \(A_E=\mathcal K(A_E)\). Base approximate identities prove nondegeneracy of \(\phi_X\). A countable chart exhaustion makes \(A_E\) separable and its standard module countably generated.

For (131), the physical transform \(\widehat u(p)=\int e^{-i\langle p,v\rangle}u(v)\,dv\) gives the odd self-adjoint multiplier \(ic(p)\), with square \(|p|^2\). Its inverse shifts are the matrices \((ic(p)\mp i)/(1+|p|^2)\). Acting on compact-parameter Fourier test sections, these are inverse operators with dense ranges. The inverse-domain argument of Lemma 8.15a proves regular self-adjointness on the full module domain. Orthogonal covariance glues the Fourier constructions; local compactly supported test sections form a graph core by Fourier cutoffs and a countable base partition. This is a module-domain argument, not just a list of fibre self-adjoint operators.

Multiplication by a smooth compact fibre cutoff followed by a Dirac resolvent is compact. Indeed a Fourier truncation produces a Hilbert–Schmidt kernel, and its remaining order-\(-1\) Fourier multiplier has norm tending to zero. This is the compact-frequency argument of the index lesson's Lemma 6.1. The same estimates are uniform in a compact base chart, and a base cutoff gives a compact module operator. Hence both-sided coefficient localizations of \(C_0\) functions of \(D\) are compact. Fibre-smooth compact sections of \(A_E\) are dense, by chart smoothing only in the fibre variables. If \(u\) is homogeneous of parity \(k\) in this dense algebra, then \([D,\rho(u)]_{\mathrm{gr}}=\sum_i c_i\rho(\partial_i u)\) is bounded, and multiplication preserves the graph domain by the ordinary first-derivative product estimate.

We state the graded commutator identity used below. For any such regular odd operator \(T\), a homogeneous \(u\), \(\sigma=(-1)^k\), \(C=Tu-\sigma uT\), \(q=\sqrt{1+\tau^2}\), and \(R_\tau=(T^2+q^2)^{-1}\), \[ [TR_\tau,u]_{\mathrm{gr}} =q^2R_\tau C R_\tau-\sigma TR_\tau C TR_\tau, \qquad \|[TR_\tau,u]_{\mathrm{gr}}\| \le\frac{5\|C\|}{4(1+\tau^2)}. \tag{132} \] To justify it without assuming that \(C\) preserves the domain, use the first-order identity \[ (T-z)^{-1}u-\sigma u(T-\sigma z)^{-1}=-\sigma(T-z)^{-1}C(T-\sigma z)^{-1}. \] Sum the two poles \(z=\pm iq\). The bound follows from \(\|R_\tau\|\le q^{-2}\) and \(\|TR_\tau\|\le(2q)^{-1}\). Its terms are compact whenever the coefficient localizations of the resolvents are compact. Integration against \(2/\pi\) over \(\tau\ge0\) gives a norm-convergent compact graded commutator for \(T(1+T^2)^{-1/2}\). The individual transform integrals converge strictly, as proved in Lemma 8.15b. Density treats every coefficient. This proves all the defects for \(d_E\). The module is countably generated by fibre tests in countably many charts. Rank zero gives the identity homomorphism cycle in both cases. \(\square\)

Lemma 6.0b (uniform linear-potential homotopy). On \(\mathcal M=\mathcal H_E\widehat\otimes_{C_X}A_E\), denote the target fibre variable by \(z\), the integration variable by \(v\), and let \(A_i=a_i\widehat\otimes1\), \(B_i=1\widehat\otimes L_{c_i^+}\). In the underlying ordinary tensor product the latter is \(\Gamma\otimes L_{c_i^+}\); the grading sign is inserted exactly once. Here \(L_{c_i^+}\) is left multiplication on the target Clifford algebra. Put \[ T_{t,z}=D+A(tv-z),\qquad A(w)=\sum_i w_iA_i, \quad 0\le t\le1. \tag{133} \] Represent a section \(u(v)\in A_E\) using the positive generators \(B_i\). Then the bounded transforms of (133) define a single Kasparov homotopy over \(C([0,1],A_E)\). In particular, the localized defects are compact and jointly continuous in \(t,z\), and vanish at target infinity after the prescribed coefficient localization.

Proof. It suffices to work in an orthonormal chart with compact base support; all constructions are orthogonally equivariant. The source metric is Euclidean and complete. The potential is Hermitian and linear. The deficiency-cutoff and moving-cutoff energy proofs of Lemma 8.19 apply: \([T_{t,z},\eta]=c(d\eta)\), so the unbounded potential contributes neither to the deficiency estimate nor to propagation speed. Each closure is self-adjoint and its waves have speed at most one.

For compact parameter support and a compact source test, the reachable source set at finite wave time is a fixed compact set. On this set a change in \(t,z\) changes the potential by a bounded coefficient tending uniformly to zero. Duhamel's integral therefore proves strong continuity of the wave group, and of its adjoint, in the parameters. Source derivatives are controlled by the differentiated energy equation on that same set. These waves define a strongly continuous unitary group on the whole parameter Hilbert module. Time smoothing, the two strict Laplace inverses and their dense ranges now give regular self-adjointness on its full domain exactly as in Lemma 8.15a. The assertion has thus been constructed over the parameter algebra before any compactness conclusion is drawn.

Write \(N\) for exterior degree and \(K=2N-r\); \(\|K\|=r\). Directly from (129), \[ T_{t,z}^2=-\Delta_v+|tv-z|^2+tK. \tag{134} \] Let \(R=(T_{t,z}\pm i)^{-1}\), \(w=R\xi\), and \(h=\chi w\), for a fixed smooth cutoff supported in \(|v|\le R_0\). The spectral bounds give \(\|w\|,\|T_{t,z}w\|\le\|\xi\|\). Therefore \(\|T_{t,z}h\|\le C_\chi\|\xi\|\), since its cutoff commutator is independent of the potential. Formula (134) gives \[ \|\nabla h\|^2+\|(tv-z)h\|^2 \le C_\chi^2\|\xi\|^2+r\|h\|^2. \tag{135} \] Thus the localized resolvents have uniformly bounded range in \(H^1\) on a fixed compact source support. Rellich compactness, or the compact-frequency proof in Lemma 6.0a, makes them fibrewise compact. Also \(|tv-z|\ge |z|-R_0\) there, so \(\|\chi R\|\le C/(1+|z|)\), uniformly in \(t\).

We include the norm-continuity step. The waves and their Laplace integrals give strong continuity of \(R\) and \(R^*\). The outputs of \(\chi R\) form a uniformly relatively compact set by (135). If norm continuity failed along a convergent parameter sequence, choose unit input vectors witnessing the failure. A convergent subsequence of the outputs, paired with each fixed vector and strong continuity of the adjoints, has zero limit. This contradiction proves norm continuity of the compact operators. The argument applies to their finite Clifford matrix components in a faithful representation, with the same bounds. With a compact base cutoff and the \(z\)-decay just proved, these are compact operators of the parameter module. Products and uniform approximation give the same coefficient localizations for the entire \(C_0\) calculus.

The \(B_i\) anticommute with both \(c_j\) and \(A_j\). Consequently the graded commutator with a compact fibre-smooth coefficient has only its bounded first-derivative term, uniformly in \(t,z\). Formula (132) gives its compact bounded-transform commutator, with an integrable parameter-independent tail. Strong continuity of bounded spectral factors multiplied by norm-continuous compact localized factors proves continuity of each integrand; the tail then gives continuity of the integral. The square defect is a localized resolvent. Density finishes the parameter-cycle assertions. A locally finite base partition and compact-base approximation globalize them without any geometry bound on all of \(X\). \(\square\)

Theorem 6.0c (both global Clifford Thom inverse products). The actual cycles of Lemma 6.0a satisfy \[ b_Ed_E=1_{C_X},\qquad d_Eb_E=1_{A_E}. \tag{136} \] These are global graded KK identities for the stated possibly noncompact base.

Proof: the first product. Rank zero was handled in Lemma 6.0a, so assume \(r>0\). Its tensor module is \(\mathcal H_E\). Put \[ Q=D+A(v),\qquad Q^2=L+2N-r, \quad L=-\Delta_v+|v|^2, \qquad F_Q=Q(1+Q^2)^{-1/2}. \tag{137} \] The Hermite basis gives the full spectral information needed here. In one variable, the normalized Gaussian \(h_0=\pi^{-1/4}e^{-v^2/2}\), followed by repeated normalized application of \((-\partial_v+v)/\sqrt2\), gives orthonormal eigenvectors \(h_n\) of \(L\) with eigenvalues \(2n+1\). Their completeness can be checked without an oscillator spectral assumption: orthogonality to all of them makes every Taylor coefficient of \(\int f(v)e^{-v^2/2}e^{wv}\,dv\) zero. This integral is entire, by Cauchy–Schwarz and Gaussian domination on compact complex sets. Its values on the imaginary axis vanish, and Fourier uniqueness gives \(f=0\). Tensoring proves completeness in \(r\) variables. On exterior degree \(k\), (137) has eigenvalues \(2(|n|+k)\). Its sole zero space is the even Gaussian times \(\Lambda^0E_{\mathbb C}\); the next eigenvalue is two. Every fixed eigenspace is finite dimensional. The symmetric \(Q\) preserves each fixed \(|n|+k\) space. Its finite self-adjoint matrices define inverse shifts on their algebraic sum. Uniform inverse bounds and dense finite-energy cutoffs give the full regular closure and graph core by the inverse-domain argument. These spaces form finite-rank bundles under the orthogonal transitions, and base-localized resolvents are compact module operators.

We verify the connection condition. For a homogeneous smooth compact \(\xi\in A_E\), let \(\sigma=(-1)^{|\xi|}\). Then \(K_\xi=Q\rho(\xi)-\sigma\rho(\xi)D=[D,\rho(\xi)]_{\rm gr}+A(v)\rho(\xi)\) is bounded and has compact base and fibre support. The mixed first-order resolvent identity gives \[ (Q-z)^{-1}\rho(\xi)-\sigma\rho(\xi)(D-\sigma z)^{-1} =-\sigma(Q-z)^{-1}K_\xi(D-\sigma z)^{-1}. \tag{138} \] Each right side is compact, by the oscillator resolvent with the compact base support, and its norm is at most \(\|K_\xi\|/|\operatorname{Im}z|^2\). Sum the two poles \(z=\pm i\sqrt{1+\tau^2}\), then integrate the bounded-transform formula. It proves that \(F_Q\rho(\xi)-\sigma\rho(\xi)F_D\) is compact; adjoints give the other connection error. Norm approximation treats every creation vector.

Here is a direct positivity check. Put \(b=A(v)/s(v)\), \(s(v)=\sqrt{1+|v|^2}\), \(g=|v|^2/s(v)\), and \(S=(1+L)^{-1/2}\). The bounded constant matrix \(2N-r\) commutes with \(L\). Its spectral bounds imply that \(F_Q-QS\) is compact after a base cutoff: the scalar difference of the two inverse square roots is \(O((1+\lambda)^{-3/2})\), and \(Q(1+L)^{-1/2}\) is bounded. Also \[ \{b,Q\}=2g+K_b,\qquad K_b=\sum_i c_i\partial_i b, \qquad \{b,QS\}=2gS+K_bS+Q[S,b]. \tag{139} \] The first remainder is compact since \(K_b\) is bounded and \(S\) has compact fibre resolvent. To control the second, use \(S=\pi^{-1}\int_0^\infty u^{-1/2}(1+L+u)^{-1}\,du\). The resolvent commutator inserts \([L,b]=-2\sum_i(\partial_i b)\partial_i-\Delta b\). Its coefficients are bounded. Both \(\|Q(1+L+u)^{-1}\|\) and \(\|[L,b](1+L+u)^{-1}\|\) are at most \(C(1+u)^{-1/2}\). Thus the integral for \(Q[S,b]\) has compact integrands and norm bounded by an integrable multiple of \(u^{-1/2}/(1+u)\).

Finally \(gS\) is positive modulo compacts. The function \(g\) has bounded first and second derivatives. The same resolvent argument with exponent \(1/4\) shows that \([g,S^{1/2}]\) is a bounded compact operator: its integrand is bounded by \(Cu^{-1/4}(1+u)^{-3/2}\). For this unbounded multiplier, first replace \(g\) by smooth cutoffs with uniformly bounded first and second derivatives and prove the resolvent identity on the Schwartz core. The derivative coefficients converge strongly, whereas both \((1+L+u)^{-1}\) and \(\partial_i(1+L+u)^{-1}\) are compact by their Hermite spectral bounds. Thus each commutator integrand converges in norm. The displayed integrable bound gives norm convergence of its integral and a compact bounded extension for the limit. Hence \[ gS=S^{1/2}gS^{1/2}+[g,S^{1/2}]S^{1/2}. \tag{140} \] The equality is first on the Schwartz core and extends as bounded operators. To justify the positive middle form, \(1+L\ge1+|v|^2=s^2\) implies \((1+L)^{1/2}\ge s\). Indeed inverse order follows from the quadratic-form variational formula for \((A+u)^{-1}\); integrating \(A(A+u)^{-1}=1-u(A+u)^{-1}\) against \(u^{-1/2}/\pi\) proves this square-root order. Since \(0\le g\le s\), the form \(S^{1/2}gS^{1/2}\) is positive and bounded by one. Also \(gS\) is bounded because \(g\le s\) and \(s(1+L)^{-1/2}\) is bounded. This establishes the extension in (140). All the compact remainders have uniform fibre estimates and are orthogonally equivariant; a \(C_X\) coefficient makes them compact over the base. Equations (139)–(140) therefore give the positivity condition of Definition 0.3. Thus \(F_Q\) is an actual product operator.

Replace \(F_Q\) on the complement of its kernel by its phase. The spectral gap makes this a continuous functional-calculus change whose difference is a base-localized compact. It is a Kasparov homotopy. The complement is then a degenerate cycle. The even kernel is canonically \(C_X\), because the normalized radial Gaussian and exterior vacuum are invariant under every orthogonal change of frame. Its zero operator and usual coefficient representation are the identity homomorphism cycle. This proves the first identity in (136).

Proof: the reverse product. Its tensor module is \(\mathcal M\) of Lemma 6.0b, with left \(A_E\) represented by the positive generators \(A_i\) in the \(v\)-variable. A product operator is \[ F_0=\frac{D+B(z)}{\sqrt{1+D^2+|z|^2}}, \qquad B(z)=\sum_i z_iB_i. \tag{141} \] The numerator's square is \(D^2+|z|^2\). Fibre Fourier transformation constructs its full regular domain and inverse shifts, as in Lemma 6.0a. Localized resolvents are compact by compact-frequency approximation, and their norm tends to zero as \(|z|\to\infty\). Its coefficient graded commutator is only the first derivative term, because \(B_i\) anticommute with all the \(A_j\). Formula (132) proves the cycle defects.

For a homogeneous smooth creation vector \(\xi\in\mathcal H_E\) in \(\operatorname{Dom}D^2\), the connection error with \(B(z)/\sqrt{1+|z|^2}\) is a vector-valued function of \(z\). The derivative part has norm at most \(\|D\xi\|/\sqrt{1+|z|^2}\). The remaining normalizer difference has norm at most \(\|D^2\xi\|/(2(1+|z|^2))\), by the scalar inverse-square-root estimate and \(|z|\le\sqrt{1+|z|^2}\). It is continuous and vanishes at target infinity; a base cutoff and approximation treat all creation vectors. Such vector-valued functions are precisely compact creation maps from the standard target module. The adjoint errors have the same conclusion. Positivity is exact: \[ \{F_D\widehat\otimes1,F_0\} =\frac{2D^2}{\sqrt{1+D^2}\sqrt{1+D^2+|z|^2}}\ge0. \tag{142} \] So (141) represents \(d_Eb_E\).

We give its global homotopy to the identity. The even unitary \[ U_\theta=\exp\left(-\frac\theta2\sum_iA_iB_i\right) \tag{143} \] sends \(A_i\) to \(\cos\theta A_i+\sin\theta B_i\) and \(B_i\) to \(-\sin\theta A_i+\cos\theta B_i\). Different \(A_iB_i\) commute; the identities follow by differentiating conjugation. Also \(D\) commutes with \(U_\theta\). This unitary is orthogonally equivariant, so it exists on the bundle module. At \(\theta=\pi/2\) it sends (141) to the transform of \(D-A(z)\), with left coefficients represented by \(B_i\).

Lemma 6.0b now gives the full parameter homotopy from \(D-A(z)\) to \(D+A(v-z)\), with that coefficient representation fixed. The fibre translation \((W_z\xi)(v)=\xi(v+z)\) is a continuous even module unitary. It sends the endpoint to \(Q=D+A(v)\), and sends the coefficient \(u(v)\) to \(u(v+z)\), still represented by the \(B_i\).

Keep \(Q\) fixed and deform this representation to \(u(z+sv)\), \(1\ge s\ge0\). These are bounded graded representations on a single interval module. They are nondegenerate: on a test with compact base, \(z\)-support and \(v\)-support, the argument \(z+sv\) stays in a common compact disk, where scalar coefficient approximate identities converge uniformly. Such tests are dense. To check the compactness assertion that is sometimes hidden in this step, note that \(f(Q)\) has finite-rank spectral approximations in the fibre for every \(f\in C_0(\mathbb R)\). For a compact fibre-smooth coefficient \(u\), multiplication by \(u(z+sv)\) is strongly continuous in \(s,z\). On any fixed compact \(v\)-set it tends uniformly in \(s\) to zero as \(|z|\to\infty\). Multiplication by each finite-rank spectral approximation consequently is norm continuous and vanishes at target infinity; its uniform spectral tail proves the same for \(u(z+sv)f(Q)\). Compact base approximation globalizes this statement. The graded commutator with \(Q\) has coefficient \(s\partial_i u(z+sv)\), uniformly bounded, and has the identical compact localization property. Formula (132), with its uniform integrable tail, proves the compact and continuous bounded-transform commutator. These are therefore actual Kasparov homotopies, even at \(s=0\).

At the last endpoint the coefficients are \(u(z)\), represented by \(B_i\). Replace the transform of \(Q\) by its phase off the Gaussian kernel, as for the first product. The kernel projection commutes with the endpoint representation: the exterior vacuum is even, and each \(B_i\) restricts there to ordinary left multiplication by the target Clifford generator. Thus the even kernel module is precisely the standard right \(A_E\)-module with its identity representation. The complement is degenerate. This proves the second identity in (136). All rotations, translations, scalings and the vacuum are defined intrinsically in the metric fibre and are orthogonally equivariant; no global frame or compactness of \(X\) was used. \(\square\)

Corollary 6.0d (orientation, naturality and ordered sums). The equivalence in Theorem 6.0c is independent of the metric under the induced section-algebra identification. It is natural for proper base pullbacks. For a specified spin-c structure on \(E\), it gives the positive spin-c Thom class and its two-sided KK inverse. The Thom and inverse classes compose for an ordered direct sum of bundles, including their Clifford twists.

Proof: the metric and spin-c module. Given two metrics, use \(g_s=(1-s)g_0+sg_1\) on the bundle over \(X\times[0,1]\). Write \(g_s(u,v)=g_0(G_su,v)\), and use the positive isometry \(G_s^{-1/2}:(E,g_0)\to(E,g_s)\), with its induced Clifford and exterior isometries. The eigenvalues of \(G_s\) and their inverses are bounded on each compact base set, uniformly in \(s\). This identifies the total-space section algebras and the fibre \(L^2\) modules continuously. The defect and resolvent arguments above work on this compact parameter interval. They give homotopies of both classes under this identification. No uniform bound on a change of metric over all of \(X\) is needed. Transport the chosen spin-c structure by the same positive isometries when one is specified.

For the spin-c structure, construct a right Hilbert \(C_r\)-module bundle with fibre \(C_r\). A principal transition \([s,z]\in\mathrm{Spin}^c(r)\) acts on this fibre by the even left unitary \(zs\). The relation \((s,z)\sim(-s,-z)\) gives the same unitary. It preserves the right \(C_r\) action and inner product. Conjugation by it gives the orthogonal Clifford transition of \(\mathrm{Cl}^+(E)\). Thus its sections vanishing at base infinity form an even bimodule \(\mathcal S_E\) from \(C_0(X,\mathrm{Cl}^+(E))\) to \(C_X\widehat\otimes C_r\).

Locally its compact endomorphisms are all left multiplications by \(C_r\); these glue by precisely the Clifford transitions. Thus \(\mathcal K(\mathcal S_E)=C_0(X,\mathrm{Cl}^+(E))\). Right fullness follows from chart-supported sections and a locally finite partition, followed by compact-base approximation. For clarity, the two Morita evaluation maps are \(\xi\widehat\otimes\overline\eta\mapsto\theta_{\xi,\eta}\) and \(\overline\xi\widehat\otimes\eta\mapsto\langle\xi,\eta\rangle\). Their tensor inner-product formulas show that they are isometries. The compact-endomorphism equality and fullness show that their ranges are dense and hence onto. Both maps are even. These are the actual two Morita inverse products of Section 0.

Pulling this bimodule to the total space gives \[ m_E\in KK(A_E,C_0(E)\widehat\otimes C_r),\qquad \beta_E=b_Em_E,\qquad \alpha_E=m_E^{-1}d_E. \tag{144} \] Their types are respectively \(KK(C_X,C_0(E)\widehat\otimes C_r)\) and \(KK(C_0(E)\widehat\otimes C_r,C_X)\). Associativity and the two proved Morita evaluations give \(\beta_E\alpha_E=b_Ed_E=1_{C_X}\) and \(\alpha_E\beta_E=m_E^{-1}(d_Eb_E)m_E=1_{C_0(E)\widehat\otimes C_r}\). The notation \(KK_r(C_X,C_0(E))\) uses exactly the ordered Clifford contractions specified in Section 0; these computations never permute odd factors.

The product \(b_Em_E\) is represented by the pulled-back spin-c module with the multiplier \(c^+(v)/\sqrt{1+|v|^2}\). To check this assertion by Definition 0.3, the Morita cycle has operator zero. A creation vector \(\xi\in A_E\) acts compactly on that module, so its connection error with the proposed bounded multiplier is compact. The positivity condition is the positive operator \(2B(v)^2\). This proves the representative, rather than merely its K-group action. In even rank \(r=2\ell\), the ordered matrix-Clifford contraction produces the ordinary spinor bundle. With \(c_i=-i\varepsilon_i\), its symbol is \(ic(v)=c^+(v)\), and its grading is \[ i^\ell c_1\cdots c_{2\ell} =(-i)^\ell\varepsilon_1\cdots\varepsilon_{2\ell}. \tag{145} \] This is the chirality of the index lesson's Lemma 6.24. In odd rank retain the final positive Clifford factor. Rank-zero unit normalization uses the canonical trivial spin-c structure. Changing a chosen spin-c structure by a line bundle tensors the above transition module by that line, so twists \(\beta_E\) and its inverse accordingly; the orientation choice is part of the data.

Proof: proper pullbacks. Let \(Y\) also be a second-countable locally compact manifold. If \(h:Y\to X\) is continuous and proper, then the induced total-space map \(\widetilde h:h^*E\to E\) is proper. Indeed the inverse image of a compact total-space set has base in a compact inverse image and bounded fibre norm, and is a closed subset of its compact disk bundle. There are therefore the pullback homomorphisms on both \(C_0\) algebras. On the standard target module, the two cycles representing \[ [h^*]b_{h^*E}=b_E[\widetilde h^*] \tag{146} \] have the identical coefficient action and Clifford multiplier, so the equality holds in KK. Multiplying by the actual inverses on the appropriate sides gives \([\widetilde h^*]d_{h^*E}=d_E[h^*]\). Pulling back the spin-c transition module gives the identical statement for (144). Properness is the precise hypothesis for these \(C_0\) homomorphisms.

Proof: ordered sums. Let \(F\to X\) be another metric bundle. Identify \(E\oplus F\) in that order and use \(\mathrm{Cl}^+(E\oplus F)=\mathrm{Cl}^+(E)\widehat\otimes\mathrm{Cl}^+(F)\). Over the base \(E\), the pulled-back \(F\)-bundle has a coefficient Thom cycle \(b_F^{\mathrm{Cl}E}\in KK(A_E,A_{E\oplus F})\): its standard module is \(A_{E\oplus F}\), its left action evaluates the old \(A_E\) coefficient at \(v\), and its operator is \(c_F^+(w)/\sqrt{1+|w|^2}\). The old Clifford coefficients graded-commute with this operator, and the localized defects vanish in \((v,w)\).

The product operator with \(b_E\) is \[ \frac{c_E^+(v)+c_F^+(w)}{\sqrt{1+|v|^2+|w|^2}},\qquad \left\{\frac{c_E^+(v)}{\sqrt{1+|v|^2}}, \frac{c_E^+(v)+c_F^+(w)}{\sqrt{1+|v|^2+|w|^2}}\right\} =\frac{2|v|^2}{\sqrt{1+|v|^2}\sqrt{1+|v|^2+|w|^2}}\ge0. \tag{147} \] For a compact old creation section \(\xi(v)\), the connection errors are the old-numerator term divided by the joint normalizer and the difference of the joint and \(w\)-only normalizers multiplied by the new numerator. Both vanish when \(|w|\to\infty\) with \(v\) bounded. Outside a compact \(v\)-set their norms are at most a fixed multiple of \(\|\xi(v)\|\), which tends to zero. Base cutoffs and density give the complete connection condition and its adjoint. Positivity is (147). Definition 0.3 thus proves \[ b_Eb_F^{\mathrm{Cl}E}=b_{E\oplus F},\qquad d_{E\oplus F}=d_F^{\mathrm{Cl}E}d_E. \tag{148} \] Here \(d_F^{\mathrm{Cl}E}\in KK(A_{E\oplus F},A_E)\) is the vertical Dirac inverse for the pulled-back \(F\)-bundle with the old Clifford coefficient retained. To verify that coefficient extension, in each old Clifford chart tensor every module in Lemmas 6.0a–b and Theorem 6.0c with that finite-dimensional coefficient algebra, using the graded tensor action. All conjugating unitaries are even, the spectral cutoffs and estimates are unchanged, and the Gaussian evaluations become the identity on the old Clifford coefficient. Old Clifford frame transitions intertwine these formulas. They therefore give both inverse products globally over \(E\), with compact old-base cutoffs as before. It follows that \(d_F^{\mathrm{Cl}E}d_E\) is a two-sided inverse of the first class in (148). Uniqueness of a two-sided inverse gives the displayed equality with the already proved \(d_{E\oplus F}\).

Finally, the spin-c structures on the ordered summands induce the ordered sum structure. Locally the map \(C_r\widehat\otimes C_s\to C_{r+s}\) sends the first block of generators to the first block and the second to the second. It preserves the graded inner products, actions and both Morita evaluations. The transition units \(z_Es_E\) and \(z_Fs_F\) are even and their product is the sum transition unit. Consequently the map glues the tensor of the two spin-c transition modules to the sum module. Transferring (148) through these exact maps proves the spin-c composition and its inverse composition with the same block order. \(\square\)

Figure 6.0. The full global proof of Lemmas 6.0a–b, Theorem 6.0c and Corollary 6.0d, equations (128)–(148). Here \(X\) is second-countable and \(E\) has the fixed rank \(r\); no orientation is needed before the last Morita transfer. In the spectrum formula \(n\) is the Hermite multi-index and \(k\) exterior degree. The plot samples the exact scalar potentials \((tv-2)^2\) on \(-1\le v\le5\) at \(t=0,1/2,1\); the Clifford term \(t(2N-1)\) in the displayed rank-one square is separate. The source cutoff estimate is uniform in the homotopy parameter, and its constant depends on the cutoff and rank. The Gaussian is even and invariant under all orthogonal transitions. Exercises 36–37 check the actual signs, compactness and inverse order. The Clifford Bott–Dirac method is classical [Kasparov; Emerson, Section 11.4]; the complete bundle and parameter-module arguments are supplied above.

Full-size PNG · Editable SVG.

Tubes and composition of compact embeddings

The normal bundle theorem is already proved in the programme: DG-CHAR, Manifold duality, the diagonal and Wu classes, Lemma 3.1 and Theorem 3.2. Its proof constructs a local addition and proves injectivity on a normal disk; Lemma 3.3 supplies the compact Euclidean embedding used below. The smooth metric and complement arguments are DG-CHAR, Vector bundles and their constructions, Theorem 4.2 and Section 5. We use precisely these geometric assertions. Their singular-cohomology conclusions are not premises for the KK argument.

Here manifolds are smooth, Hausdorff, second countable and without boundary. A normalized tube for an embedding \(i:M\hookrightarrow Y\), with normal quotient \(E=i^*TY/TM\), is an open embedding from a neighbourhood of the zero section in \(E\) to \(Y\), equal to \(i\) on that section, whose vertical derivative induces the identity on the normal quotient. The theorem just cited gives one. A whole-bundle tube is obtained by first shrinking to a disk of radius \(\rho(x)>0\) and then using \[ q_\rho(x,v)=\left(x,\frac{v}{\sqrt{1+|v|^2/\rho(x)^2}}\right). \tag{149} \] This diffeomorphism from \(E\) to \(D_\rho E\) has vertical derivative the identity at zero; its inverse is \(w/\sqrt{1-|w|^2/\rho(x)^2}\). Thus the resulting whole-bundle tube remains normalized. For a compact base a constant positive radius suffices after shrinking.

If \(a:U\hookrightarrow V\) is an open embedding, write \(e_a:C_0(U)\to C_0(V)\) for extension by zero after its diffeomorphism onto its image. It is a *-homomorphism: a compactly supported function extends continuously, and approximation by such functions proves the assertion for \(C_0(U)\). This is the covariant map used here. Restriction of a general \(C_0(V)\) function to \(U\) need not vanish at infinity in \(U\).

Lemma 6.0e (compression and tube independence). Let \(E\to M\) be a metric real rank-\(k\) bundle on a compact manifold with a specified spin-c structure. Write \(\beta_E\in KK(C(M),C_0(E)\widehat\otimes C_k)\) for Corollary 6.0d's Thom class, where \(C_k=\mathrm{Cl}^+(\mathbb R^k)\). For a positive constant \(r\), let \(q_r:E\to D_rE\) be (149) and define \(\beta_{D_rE}=\beta_E[e_{q_r}]\), where here \(e_{q_r}\) is the isomorphism onto the disk algebra. Then \[ \beta_{D_rE}[e_{D_rE\hookrightarrow E}]=\beta_E. \tag{150} \] Consequently that disk inclusion, tensored with \(1_{C_k}\), is a KK equivalence. For a compact embedding \(i:M\hookrightarrow Y\), the class \[ i_!=\beta_E[e_\tau]\in KK(C(M),C_0(Y)\widehat\otimes C_k) \tag{151} \] is independent of the normalized whole-bundle tube \(\tau:E\to Y\). It retains the specified normal spin-c structure.

Proof: compression as an actual algebra homotopy. Put \(q_{r,s}(v)=v/\sqrt{1+s|v|^2/r^2}\), for \(0\le s\le1\), and extend its image functions by zero in \(E\). The resulting maps are \[ \Phi_s(f)(x,w)= \begin{cases} f\!\left(x,\dfrac{w}{\sqrt{1-s|w|^2/r^2}}\right), &s|w|^2<r^2,\\ 0,&s|w|^2\ge r^2. \end{cases} \quad \Phi_0(f)=f. \tag{152} \] Each is a *-homomorphism, of norm at most one. For \(f\) of compact support \(K\subset E\), the set \(\{(s,q_{r,s}(v)):s\in[0,1],v\in K\}\) is compact. On the open image of the map \((s,v)\mapsto(s,q_{r,s}(v))\), the formula is continuous by its displayed inverse. At its boundary it is continuous with value zero: any nonzero value of size at least \(\epsilon\) has its preimage in the compact set \(\{|f|\ge\epsilon\}\), whose image is a closed subset inside that open image. Hence \((s,w)\mapsto\Phi_s(f)(w)\) is continuous, has uniformly compact support and lies in \(C([0,1],C_0(E))\). Uniform continuity on a compact neighbourhood of the support proves norm continuity in \(s\). Density and the norm bound prove the same for every \(f\in C_0(E)\). Tensor with the finite-dimensional graded algebra \(C_k\), using its identity map.

We have obtained the genuine homomorphism \(\Phi:C_0(E)\widehat\otimes C_k\to C([0,1],C_0(E)\widehat\otimes C_k)\). Corollary 0.11 represents it by the standard interval module with operator zero; the localized square defect is \(-\Phi(f)\), a compact module endomorphism. No nondegeneracy or complemented range is needed. Its endpoints are the identity and \(e_{q_r}e_{D_rE\hookrightarrow E}\). Homotopy invariance and multiplication by \(\beta_E\) prove (150). Both \(\beta_E\) and \(\beta_{D_rE}\) are invertible by Theorem 6.0c, Corollary 6.0d and the disk isomorphism. Thus \([e_{D_rE\hookrightarrow E}]=\beta_{D_rE}^{-1}\beta_E\) is invertible, with all Clifford factors retained. Smaller disks give the same argument. In particular, if \(0<r<R\), cancellation after extension to \(E\) gives \(\beta_{D_rE}[e_{D_rE\hookrightarrow D_RE}]=\beta_{D_RE}\).

Proof: the comparison of two tubes. Let \(\tau_0,\tau_1\) be normalized whole-bundle tubes. The map \(g=\tau_1^{-1}\tau_0\) is defined on a neighbourhood of the zero section, fixes it and has identity normal derivative. Let \(\lambda_t\) denote fibre multiplication by \(t\). For \(t>0\) set \[ g_t=\lambda_{1/t}g\lambda_t,\qquad g_0=\mathrm{id}. \tag{153} \] This has a smooth extension at zero, even when \(g\) changes the base point. Indeed, in bundle coordinates write \(g(x,v)=(a(x,v),b(x,v))\). Here \(a(x,0)=x\), \(b(x,0)=0\) and \(D_vb(x,0)=I\). The second component of \(g_t\) is \[ \frac{b(x,tv)}t=\int_0^1D_vb(x,utv)v\,du, \] which is smooth in \((t,x,v)\) at zero and equals \(v\) there; the first component tends smoothly to \(x\). These coordinate formulas agree because the expression for positive \(t\) is intrinsic. At the zero section its derivative on tangent and normal coordinates has blocks \(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}I&tA_x\\0&I\end{smallmatrix}\right)\), hence is invertible for every \(t\).

Compactness of \(M\) supplies \(r>0\) on which every \(g_t\), \(0\le t\le1\), is defined and locally invertible. Each is injective: for \(t>0\) it is a composition of injective maps, and for zero it is the identity. By making \(r\) smaller we arrange that all their images are in a fixed disk \(D_RE\). The map \((t,v)\mapsto(t,g_t(v))\) is then an injective local diffeomorphism of \([0,1]\times D_rE\) onto a relatively open subset of \([0,1]\times D_RE\), and its inverse is smooth. For the endpoint parameters apply the inverse lemma to the smooth extension in \(t\); this proves the relative openness there too. The family of extensions by zero consequently defines \[ C_0(D_rE)\widehat\otimes C_k \longrightarrow C([0,1],C_0(D_RE)\widehat\otimes C_k). \tag{154} \] To check the required norm continuity, a compact source support \(K\) has compact image under \((t,v)\mapsto(t,g_t(v))\), inside the relatively open image. The same compact-level-set boundary argument used for (152) proves joint continuity of the zero extension. Uniform continuity and density give norm continuity. Its endpoints are the disk inclusion and \(e_{g_1}\), with the constant Clifford factor unchanged.

Multiplication by \(\beta_{D_rE}\) and (150) show \(\beta_{D_rE}[e_{g_1}]=\beta_{D_RE}\). Since \(\tau_0=\tau_1g_1\) on \(D_rE\), subsequent extension into \(Y\) gives \(\beta_{D_rE}[e_{\tau_0|D_rE}]=\beta_{D_RE}[e_{\tau_1|D_RE}]\). Use (150) and composition of extensions to identify these respectively with \(\beta_E[e_{\tau_0}]\) and \(\beta_E[e_{\tau_1}]\). This proves (151). The proof transports no spin-c structure through a base-changing map: (154) acts on the scalar disk algebra and the fixed target Clifford algebra. The chosen normal spin-c module was already incorporated in \(\beta_{D_rE}\). Changing that structure by a line bundle is a change of orientation data, as in Corollary 6.0d. \(\square\)

For the next statement define an ordered coefficient extension as follows. If \(y\in KK(A,B\widehat\otimes C_\ell)\), let \(y^{[k]}\in KK(A\widehat\otimes C_k,B\widehat\otimes C_k\widehat\otimes C_\ell)\) be its exterior product with \(1_{C_k}\), with the even base algebras moved past \(C_k\). The old \(C_k\) block precedes the new \(C_\ell\) block. In a module representative the new odd operator graded-commutes with the old block. This convention is exactly the coefficient convention of (147)–(148).

Theorem 6.0f (composition of compact spin-c embeddings). Let \(i:M\hookrightarrow N\) and \(j:N\hookrightarrow P\) be smooth embeddings with \(M,N\) compact. Suppose their normal bundles \(E=\nu_i\) and \(F=\nu_j\) have specified spin-c structures of ranks \(k,\ell\). Give the composite's normal bundle the spin-c structure induced from \[ 0\longrightarrow E\longrightarrow\nu_{ji} \longrightarrow i^*F\longrightarrow0, \qquad \nu_{ji}\cong E\oplus i^*F \tag{155} \] in this order, through a splitting of this exact sequence. Then \[ i_!\widehat\otimes_{C(N)\widehat\otimes C_k}j_!^{[k]} =(ji)_! \quad\text{in }KK(C(M),C_0(P)\widehat\otimes C_{k+\ell}). \tag{156} \] The right side uses the block identification \(C_k\widehat\otimes C_\ell\cong C_{k+\ell}\). Auxiliary metrics, connections and splittings do not affect this equality when the specified orientation is transported along their comparison paths.

Proof: a compatible composite tube. Take normalized whole-bundle tubes \(\tau:E\to N\), \(\sigma:F\to P\), and put \(U=\tau(E)\). A principal connection on the spin-c frame bundle of \(F\) exists, and has smooth parallel transport along compact path intervals, by DG-FND, Connections and parallel transport, Theorems 3.1 and 4.1, Corollary 4.2. The complete invariant-equation argument is its local-tools lesson, Theorem 2.1 and Lemma 2.2. Apply it to \(r\mapsto\tau(x,rv)\), \(0\le r\le1\). It gives a smooth spin-c, hence metric, identification \(T_{x,v}:F_{i(x)}\to F_{\tau(x,v)}\), equal to the identity at \(v=0\). Smoothness holds near each finite \((x,v)\); a finite subdivision of the compact path interval suffices in each parameter neighbourhood. No uniform bound for all \(v\) is asserted or needed.

The map \[ \Psi:E\oplus i^*F\longrightarrow F|_U, \qquad (x,v,w)\longmapsto(\tau(x,v),T_{x,v}w) \tag{157} \] is a diffeomorphism. Its inverse first applies \(\tau^{-1}\) to the base, then \(T_{x,v}^{-1}\) to the fibre. Thus \(\Omega=\sigma\Psi\) is a whole-bundle open embedding into \(P\), equal to \(ji\) at the zero section. At zero its derivative on \((v,w)\) is the sum of the \(j\)-image of the normal lift furnished by \(d\tau(v)\) and the normal lift \(d\sigma(w)\). Modulo \(TM\) this is the direct-sum isomorphism in (155); in particular the derivative of \(T_{x,v}\) contributes no term at \(w=0\). Choose this splitting first, and choose on \(\nu_{ji}\) the metric transported from the orthogonal sum. Then \(\Omega\) is a normalized tube for that normal identification. Lemma 6.0e permits its use in (151).

Proof: open restriction of the actual Thom cycle. We need the equality on cycles before using (148). For an arbitrary spin-c bundle \(F\to N\) and an open set \(U\subset N\), the restriction to the ideal \(C_0(U)\subset C(N)\) of the left action on \(\beta_F\) has essential module precisely its spin-c section module over \(F|_U\). To prove this assertion, multiply by approximate identities of \(C_0(U)\). On every compact support in \(F|_U\) they converge uniformly to one; finite local section approximations then give the entire module. Conversely their products are supported over \(U\). The multiplier \(c^+(w)/\sqrt{1+|w|^2}\) preserves this submodule and its adjoint does too. Its localized square defects and graded commutators are compact in that submodule: use compact-support section approximations there and the same fibre decay as Lemma 6.0a. The restriction is an \(F\)-connection on the essential module, since multiplication by an old ideal creation section intertwines the two identical multipliers exactly. Lemma 0.10 and Corollary 0.11 therefore identify the full restricted cycle with the extension of the Thom cycle over \(U\). This does not require an orthogonal complement of the open-ideal module.

Replace \(U\) by \(E\) using \(\tau\), and identify the pulled-back bundle and its spin-c section module by the transport \(T\). Both are actual isomorphisms, and \(\Psi\) is proper as a map between these two total spaces because it is a homeomorphism. The restricted Thom multiplier becomes exactly \(c_{i^*F}^+(w)/\sqrt{1+|w|^2}\), while its left action evaluates an old coefficient at \((x,v)\). Retaining the old constant \(C_k\) block gives the coefficient class \[ \gamma\in KK(C_0(E)\widehat\otimes C_k, C_0(E\oplus i^*F)\widehat\otimes C_k\widehat\otimes C_\ell). \] Writing \(a:F|_U\hookrightarrow F\) for inclusion, the checked restriction of cycles gives \[ [e_\tau]\,\beta_F^{[k]} =\gamma[e_\Psi][e_a]. \tag{158} \] Here \(e_\Psi\) is the total-space algebra isomorphism and the last two maps retain both Clifford blocks. One can also see the module identification explicitly: a section over \(F|_U\) at \((y,w')\) is sent to its value at \((\tau(x,v),T_{x,v}w)\), using the inverse transport on its spin-c fibre. This preserves the right inner product, grading and both coefficient actions, and intertwines the displayed multiplier.

The ordered product calculation of Corollary 6.0d, (147)–(148), now gives \[ \beta_E\gamma=\beta_{E\oplus i^*F}. \tag{159} \] Its hypotheses hold on the noncompact old base \(E\); compact old-coefficient cutoffs, not a pullback along the nonproper projection \(E\to M\), were used in that calculation. The tensor of the spin-c transition modules in (159) is the sum transition module because both transition units are even. The product operator is the joint normalized numerator \(c_E^+(v)+c_{i^*F}^+(w)\); its connection errors vanish at joint infinity and its positivity is precisely (147). Thus (159) is an equality of KK classes, with the full product criterion already checked, rather than only a statement about the induced K-group maps.

Finally use associativity, (158), (159), and composition of open extensions: \[ \begin{aligned} i_!j_!^{[k]} &=\beta_E[e_\tau]\,\beta_F^{[k]}[e_\sigma]\\ &=\beta_E\gamma[e_\Psi][e_a][e_\sigma]\\ &=\beta_{E\oplus i^*F}[e_\Omega]=(ji)_!. \end{aligned} \tag{160} \] The maps compose in their geometric order \(\Omega=\sigma a\Psi\); no odd Clifford blocks have been exchanged.

Proof: the auxiliary choices. Changing a connection changes \(T\) and therefore \(\Omega\), but its value and normal derivative at the zero section remain the same. Lemma 6.0e proves equality for those tubes. Changing a metric is covered by Corollary 6.0d's full metric-interval cycle. Two splittings of (155) differ by a bundle map \(i^*F\to E\); their linear interpolation is a path of splittings. Explicitly, relative to one splitting their isomorphisms are the triangular maps \((v,w)\mapsto(v+sAw,w)\). They are invertible with inverses \((v,w)\mapsto(v-sAw,w)\), for every \(s\in[0,1]\). On the compact base their norms and inverse norms are uniformly bounded. Thus these maps induce a norm-continuous interval family of total-space algebra isomorphisms: compactly supported functions have uniformly compact transported support, and continuity and density give the assertion for all \(C_0\) functions. Transport the ordered sum metric and spin-c transition module through that family. The Clifford multiplier becomes its transported vector with the transported norm, so its localized defects vanish uniformly at fibre infinity. This is a genuine Thom-cycle homotopy over the fixed normal bundle. It identifies the induced normal orientations and their Thom classes. Tube independence then proves equality in (160) for the second splitting as well. No independence of distinct, untransported spin-c orientations is claimed. \(\square\)

The construction of an embedding's push-forward from a Thom class and an open extension is classical; Carey–Wang, Section 4.1 and the embedding-composition lemma in Section 4.3 gives a twisted-K-theory formulation. The complete algebra homotopies and the actual KK product comparison required here are proved in Lemma 6.0e and Theorem 6.0f. These results concern compact ordinary embeddings; Lemma6.0t extends the tube/product argument to a noncompact intermediate base. Lemmas6.0l–n and Theorem6.0o prove the full foliation correspondence and factorization choices, and Theorems6.0s/6.0w prove projection and compact ordinary-map/foliation composition. Theorems 6.0ab–ae below prove bordism, sphere normalization and geometric-cycle descent. The longitudinal analytic-index comparison requires its further argument.

Figure 6.0a. Lemma 6.0e, Theorem 6.0f and equations (149)–(160). The top-left graph samples the exact radius-one compression on \(-3\le v\le3\) at \(s=0,1/2,1\); its compact support bound is for a function supported in \([-3,3]\). The top-right graph samples the exact scalar germ \(g(v)=v+v^2/2\) and its rescaling at \(t=0,1/2,1\) on \([-1/4,1/4]\). Its derivative is at least \(3/4\), and all images lie in \((-0.3,0.3)\); the complete proof also treats base-changing bundle germs. The middle panel uses the unwrapped cylinder chart \(-\pi<\theta<\pi\), rather than a projection of the whole cylinder. Shading indicates only the displayed height window \(|w|\le1\); the tube includes all real heights. The dot is the point \((1,0)\in S^1\times\mathbb R\), whose chart coordinates are \((0,0)\). The lower panel retains the order \(E\) then \(i^*F\), with the positive Clifford convention. Exercises 38–39 verify the support, proper-map and actual product details. Geometric prerequisites are the exact DG-CHAR and DG-FND proofs linked above; the push-forward construction is classical [Carey–Wang, Section 4].
