B1. Actual transverse charts and holonomy arrows

Choose a countable disjoint family of small transverse plaque disks T_i whose associated foliation boxes cover V. Such a family follows from a countable foliation-box basis; a finite family suffices for compact V. Let T be their disjoint union and H=G|_T the groupoid with both endpoints in those disks. The disks are disjoint as labelled components, even if their images in V meet. The arrow charts of the course give H its smooth étale structure. Its object space is Hausdorff, second countable and locally compact. Its arrows can be non-Hausdorff. Restricting a countable G path-chart basis and a countable disk basis gives a countable bisection basis for H: in an étale path chart both endpoint maps are local diffeomorphisms, and a smaller open chart makes both injective. No Hausdorffness of all arrows, no amenability and no quotient by isotropy is used here.

The plaque short arrows give an actual comparison between G-cocycles and H-cocycles over any locally compact Hausdorff second-countable base X. Refine a G-cocycle chart so its lift lies in one foliation box, project to that box's labelled transverse disk, and conjugate its transition arrows by the short plaque arrows. This produces an H-cocycle and an actual G-arrow equivalence. Composing an H-cocycle with T→V is its inverse up to this equivalence. Two choices of projection disks have their short-arrow comparison on a common refinement; the derivatives give exactly the comparison of their pulled normal bundles. Over X×I the identical formulas compare concordances. This proves the equivalence of the actual cocycle/concordance functors on these bases. It does not assert a C*-algebra Morita equivalence, which is not needed for χ: its target analytic algebra remains A=C*r(G).

Fix a countable basis of contractible open coordinate disks in the transverse object manifold T.

B4. A locally compact replacement of any countable CW complex

Let K be a countable CW complex. Enumerate its cells; adjoining their finitely many lower-dimensional faces recursively gives finite subcomplexes K_n whose union is K. Put

\[ X=\operatorname{Tel}(K_1\hookrightarrow K_2\hookrightarrow\cdots), \qquad p:X\longrightarrow K. \tag{396} \]

There is a continuous proper height h:X→[1,∞), with each closed bounded height slab contained in a finite collection of compact mapping cylinders. Local neighbourhoods meet only the two adjacent such cylinders and are locally compact. Closed gluing along the finite subcomplexes makes X Hausdorff. The finite cylinders are compact metrizable; countably many open slab neighbourhoods with their countable bases make X second countable. Its cells from the cylinder subdivisions give a CW structure. Thus X meets every hypothesis of (389)–(394).

For clarity the weak-equivalence proof of p is direct. A compact subset of a CW complex meets only finitely many open cells: otherwise choose one point in each of infinitely many distinct cells. Closure finiteness makes the chosen points, and every subset of them, closed by the weak topology (each closed cell meets only finitely many). They form an infinite closed discrete subspace of the original compact set, a contradiction. Thus a map of a sphere, disk or finite homotopy cylinder into K has image in some K_N. Its lift to the height-N copy of K_N in X proves surjectivity on homotopy groups and components. Any compact image in X has bounded height and lies in finitely many cylinders. That finite telescope deformation retracts onto its last K_M: collapse the first mapping cylinder to its target, then the second, and so on. These standard cylinder contractions commute with p. If a sphere map's projection is null in K, its null disk lies in a further K_L. Retracting its original map to height M, then sliding the constant projected map along the cylinders to height L, gives its null disk in X. This proves injectivity, with the same argument on relative paths proving the components claim. Hence p is a weak homotopy equivalence of CW complexes.

A full homotopy inverse is available with an explicit relative cell argument. Here are its filling step and its application, so the cell-filling input is supplied here rather than assumed. Let j:L→M be an inclusion of CW complexes inducing bijections of components and isomorphisms of every based homotopy group. Suppose a disk d:D^n→M has its boundary in L. For n≥2 the boundary class is zero in M and hence in L, by injectivity on π_(n−1); choose a filling e:D^n→L with the same boundary. The disk d glued to the reversed e is a sphere in M. Surjectivity on π_n lets us change e, by inserting an L-valued sphere in a small interior disk, until this difference sphere is null in M. A null homotopy of that difference sphere gives a homotopy d≃je fixed on the boundary: regard its two hemispheres as the bottom and top of D^n×I, and its equator as ∂D^n×I. The quotient which collapses the constant equatorial intervals is a disk; precomposing the null filling with that quotient gives the required cylinder. Basepoint paths are kept in the same boundary component. For n=1, component injectivity first gives a path e in L between the endpoints. The difference loop can be corrected by a loop in L using surjectivity on π_1, and the same null-loop disk gives the relative path homotopy. For n=0 use component surjectivity to select a point of L and a path from each new vertex to it. These arguments prove the relative disk-filling step in every dimension, with the original boundary map fixed.

It also solves the extension problem with a prescribed boundary homotopy. If a cell's boundary is already being homotoped from its original map into M to an L-valued map, append that boundary cylinder to the original disk. A collar identifies the result with a disk whose final boundary is in L. Apply the preceding filling step, and remove the collar parametrization. This extends the given boundary homotopy over the cell, ending in L; its end map has exactly the already prescribed boundary values.

Start with the identity on L. Induct over the relative cells of (M,L), using this extension problem on each cell. It constructs r:M→L, rj=1_L, and H:jr≃1_M fixed on L. The choices on cells of a given dimension are independent, since they agree on their boundaries. The CW weak topology makes r continuous. It also makes H continuous: the product CW structure with the finite interval has precisely the weak topology tested by the closed cell disks times I. Thus the construction works on the entire CW complex at once, even with infinitely many cells and without passing to an inverse limit of homotopy classes.

Apply this to the mapping cylinder M_p of p, with L=X as its bottom subcomplex. The cellular telescope projection p has image in the corresponding cells of K, so M_p is a CW complex and X is a subcomplex. Its retraction onto K and the already proved weak equivalence of p show that X→M_p meets the filling hypotheses. Let k:K→M_p be the top inclusion. The map q=rk:K→X satisfies pq≃1_BC by projecting H on that top inclusion. The cylinder path from x to k(p(x)), followed by r, gives qp≃1_X. These are whole homotopies on the specified spaces. This completes the actual homotopy-equivalence claim in(396), rather than merely its action on homotopy groups or compact restrictions.

R1. The disk-attachment gluing step

For a diagram A←Z×∂Δ^n→Z×Δ^n, its pushout has the same homotopy type as its double mapping cylinder. The second arrow is a closed cofibration with an explicit collar: use the radial coordinate from the barycentre of Δ^n to its boundary, with an outer annulus as collar. Attaching an extra cylinder to that collar only lengthens its radial intervals. Rescaling those intervals, fixed at their inner ends, gives the comparison with the ordinary attachment. The same argument works component by component and with Z arbitrary; n=0 is a disjoint union.

A map of two such diagrams which is a homotopy equivalence on each of A, Z×∂Δ^n and Z×Δ^n therefore induces a homotopy equivalence of the attachments. Here is the usual cylinder argument, in the form needed here. Choose inverses on the three pieces and their inverse homotopies. The inverse pieces commute with the attaching maps up to homotopy: paste the inverse homotopy on the target piece, the original strictly commuting square, and the inverse homotopy on the source piece. On each intervening cylinder use that pasted track, allocating successive thirds of its interval to the three tracks. This defines an inverse map on the double mapping cylinders, agreeing on their ends. Pasting the same inverse homotopies gives homotopies of both composites to the identity; subdividing the interval once more keeps the end maps fixed. Rescaling the radial collars transfers them to the ordinary attachments. This proof uses actual homotopy equivalences on the pieces, rather than an unqualified weak-equivalence gluing rule.

R2. Compact parameter images have bounded fat dimension

Let Z_• be a semisimplicial space whose levels are T1. A compact subset of ||Z_•|| is contained in some finite fat skeleton. Otherwise choose points y_j in that subset with strictly increasing minimal dimensions n_j, using the unique interior representative in its minimal simplex. The inverse image of y_j in a fixed level Z_k×Δ^k is empty if n_j>k. For n_j≤k it is a finite union of closed sets: prescribe the zero barycentric coordinates of a face, prescribe its remaining coordinates, and take the inverse image of the closed base point under the face map. There are only finitely many faces. Thus the inverse image in every level of {y_j:j∈J}, for any subset J of the selected indices, is closed. The weak quotient topology makes every such subset closed in the realization. The selected set is consequently a closed discrete subset of the original compact set. It would be compact and infinite discrete, which is impossible. This proves the dimension bound. It makes no assertion that compact images meet finitely many base points or arrow charts in a fixed dimension.

The face-only quotient has no other identifications of interior representatives, which is why minimal dimension is available here. The argument does not use a Hausdorff arrow space. It does require the T1 condition at each level, verified below in the actual application.

R3. Level homotopy equivalences give a fat weak equivalence

Suppose a semisimplicial map Z_•→Y_• is a homotopy equivalence in each level, and both sets of levels are T1. Its fat realization is a weak homotopy equivalence. Indeed the n-skeleton is obtained from the (n−1)-skeleton by the attachment in R1 with Z=Z_n. The comparison on its boundary piece is also a homotopy equivalence, by the level inverse times the identity of ∂Δ^n. Induction using R1 gives an actual homotopy equivalence on every finite fat skeleton. A sphere, disk or finite homotopy-cylinder image in either full realization is compact and hence lies in a finite skeleton by R2. Surjectivity and injectivity on all homotopy groups follow from the finite-skeleton equivalences, enlarging that skeleton when a null disk is used. The same path argument gives the bijection of components. No compatibility of the separately chosen skeletal inverses is required for this weak equivalence statement.

R4. Cell cylinders and the fat-to-ordinary comparison for simplicial sets

For any simplicial set S, its fat realization maps weakly equivalently to its ordinary realization. Here is a proof which does not require closed degeneracies for a topological groupoid. For the representable simplicial set Δ[n], its fat realization is contractible. A simplex is an ordered string of vertices in {0,…,n}, allowing repetitions. Append vertex n and give that final vertex weight s, multiplying all old weights by 1−s. This respects every face relation, gives the identity at s=0, and is the constant final vertex at s=1. Its ordinary realization is the contractible geometric n-simplex. Thus the comparison for Δ[n] is a homotopy equivalence.

Both fat and ordinary realization preserve the pushouts which attach the nondegenerate simplices along their boundaries. The pair (||Δ[n]||,||∂Δ[n]||) is a CW pair: one cell is present for every simplex, including degenerate ones, and the simplicial subset supplies a subcomplex. Induction on nondegenerate dimension first proves the comparison for the boundary, then for a skeleton of an arbitrary S using these attachment pushouts. All their spaces are CW complexes. Their weak-equivalence comparisons are homotopy equivalences by the relative cell-filling proof in B4; the mapping-cylinder gluing argument of R1 applies to these CW cofibrations as well. Their homotopy-extension property is explicit: extend over each relative cell using the retraction of D^k×I onto D^k×{0}∪∂D^k×I, obtained by radial projection from a point above the centre of its top face. It fixes that bottom-and-side subset. Induction on cells and the CW weak topology give extension on the whole pair. Applying this extension to the cylinder-end homotopies gives the same ordinary-pushout to double-mapping-cylinder comparison used in R1. No global collar of an arbitrary CW subcomplex is being presumed. Disjoint unions handle any number of simplices in a dimension. This proves the weak comparison on every nondegenerate skeleton.

Finally a compact sphere, disk or homotopy image in either realization meets only finitely many of its CW cells, by the finite-cell argument in B4. Each of those fat cells belongs to the degeneracy of a simplex of finite nondegenerate dimension. Thus the compact image lies in some nondegenerate skeleton. The preceding comparisons prove the weak equivalence of the full realizations, with all components retained. For countable S both realizations are countable CW complexes, so B4's cell-filling argument supplies a full homotopy equivalence if desired.

A1. A labelled atlas groupoid with every actual arrow

Use the countable contractible basis U of the Hausdorff transverse object manifold T from B1. Put T'=coprod_(U∈U) U. Define H' to have objects (U,z), z∈U, and arrows

\[ ((U,z),(V,z'),g),\qquad g:z\longrightarrow z'\text{ in }H. \tag{397} \]

Its topology is the pullback topology from H together with the discrete chart labels; composition and inversion use the exact H products. The forgetful Q:H'→H is a continuous functor. Arrow spaces of H' can still be non-Hausdorff. No two different isotropy or holonomy arrows are identified in(397), even when they have the same endpoints.

A2. A locally finite partition on objects

Choose continuous functions λ_U:T→[0,1], with sum_U λ_U=1, locally finite closed supports and supp λ_U⊂U. Here supports, rather than the entire countable basis U, are required to be locally finite. Existence follows from a countable locally finite shrinking of the coordinate-disk cover on the locally compact second-countable Hausdorff manifold T and its subordinate partition. If several refined members are assigned to the same U, sum their functions. Their closed supports form a locally finite family, so their union is closed and still contained in U. The merged family retains all stated properties.

There is one useful local consequence. Near a fixed finite list x_0,…,x_n of objects, only finitely many supports can occur. A label U whose closed support omits x_i can be removed on a smaller neighbourhood if necessary. Every retained label with x_i in its support has x_i∈U and hence remains a valid object chart near x_i. Thus a finite expanded string below can be chosen on a neighbourhood even at points where some of its weights vanish. The resulting map does not try to retain an invalid object (U,x_i) outside U with a zero weight. Fix any total order of the countable chart labels.

A3. Weighted vertex splitting gives both actual homotopies

Write a fat H simplex as (x_0→…→x_n; t_0,…,t_n), t_i≥0, sum_i t_i=1. For every vertex i, replace it by its finitely many labelled copies (U,x_i), in the fixed label order, with weights t_i λ_U(x_i). Copies at the same vertex are connected by the actual unit 1_(x_i). Between blocks i<j use the actual composite g_j⋯g_(i+1):x_i→x_j of the old arrows. Intermediate blocks whose weights vanish are deleted using that identical composite. This defines

\[ S:\|N(H)\|\longrightarrow\|N(H')\|. \tag{398} \]

Continuity is explicit. On a neighbourhood of a given simplex's object list, A2 gives a fixed finite valid list of labels. All its arrows are compositions of the original continuously varying arrows or units; all its weights are continuous. Hence the formula is a continuous map to one finite-dimensional nerve level and then to its fat realization. When a weight vanishes, deletion by a face agrees with the neighbouring expanded formula. When an original vertex has zero weight, its whole block disappears and the old face product gives exactly the composite between the remaining blocks. Consequently these local formulas agree under all fat face relations and descend continuously in the weak quotient topology. Local finiteness is only on T. No cover or partition of H_1 was selected.

For QS≃1_(||N(H)||), place, in each block i, the original vertex x_i followed by its expanded copies. Give them respectively

\[ (1-s)t_i,\qquad s t_i\lambda_U(x_i),\qquad 0\le s\le1. \tag{399} \]

All within-block arrows are 1_(x_i); the arrows between blocks are the same old composites. At s=0 the expanded vertices disappear, giving the original fat simplex exactly. At s=1 the original vertices disappear, giving QS exactly. The sum of all weights is (1−s)sum_i t_i+s sum_i t_i sum_U λ_U(x_i)=1. All weights are nonnegative. The same face and local-continuity argument proves a whole homotopy, including all endpoints and all dimensions. A product of a quotient map with the compact locally compact interval is a quotient map, so this levelwise formula descends as a continuous homotopy on the product of the fat realization with I.

For SQ≃1_(||N(H')||), use exactly(399), retaining the original labelled vertex (V_i,x_i) as its first vertex. The arrow from an old or new copy at x_i to another copy at x_i is now the H' arrow whose H value is 1_(x_i), with its specified source and target labels. This exists whenever both labels are present; A2 guarantees that condition on each local formula. Arrows between blocks keep their actual H values and the expanded endpoint labels. At s=0 one obtains the original H' simplex and at s=1 SQ. Thus

\[ \|N(Q)\|S\simeq1_{\|N(H)\|},\qquad S\|N(Q)\|\simeq1_{\|N(H')\|}. \tag{400} \]

These are full fat homotopies, not just equivalences on individual homotopy groups. No degeneracy relation was used to combine repeated vertices: their removal at the endpoints is a genuine zero-weight face relation. The proof therefore retains the possible nonclosed unit locus of the non-Hausdorff H arrow space.

All identities and compositions used here also hold after applying the actual normal derivative representation of H. Within a block the derivative is the identity, and between blocks it is the exact old derivative product. Thus this atlas factor introduces no new orientation, determinant line or transverse twist. This is a check of the exact transition maps under the comparison, not a substitute for the universal cocycle construction in U and its complete classifying comparison in V and Q.

U1. The indexed arrow join and its quotient

Let I run over nonempty finite subsets of N={0,1,…}. The I-piece of E_M H consists of weights t_i≥0, sum_(i∈I)t_i=1, and actual arrows g_i with a common source x. Delete a zero-weight arrow and its index by a face relation. Give E_M H the resulting weak quotient topology of these finite simplex/arrow fibre products. The index of each retained arrow stays fixed under a face map. Thus every point has finitely many nonzero indexed weights. Right multiplication by h:z→x sends every g_i to g_i h and retains every weight. Define B_M H as the orbit quotient by this actual right H action. Distinct arrows with the same endpoints have not been identified before that specified principal action. Denote the orbit projection by q. For b∈B_M H the indexed weights t_i(b) are well-defined continuous functions, with sum_i t_i(b)=1.

The right action is jointly continuous in the stated weak topology. This needs a check because an arbitrary product of quotient maps would not suffice. Cover the acting arrow h by étale bisections B. On such a bisection, h is uniquely and continuously determined by t(h)=x, the common source of the tuple. The corresponding part of E_M H×_(T)B is homeomorphic to the open subset with x∈t(B). On each finite piece, multiplication by that determined h is continuous and respects every face. The weak quotient restricted to this open subset is still quotient, so multiplication descends continuously there. These open pieces cover the action fibre product. This proves joint continuity without assuming that H_1 is Hausdorff or that its product with a quotient is automatically quotient. It also proves continuity of the inverse local chart below, by the same bisection argument.

Set O_i={b:t_i(b)>0}. On q^−1(O_i), normalize all arrows by

\[ (g_j)_j\longmapsto(g_jg_i^{-1})_j, \qquad g_ig_i^{-1}=1_{t(g_i)}. \tag{401} \]

This is continuous on each finite piece and respects every face. It is invariant under right H: (g_jh)(g_ih)^−1=g_jg_i^−1. The restriction of q to this open saturated set is a quotient map, so(401) descends continuously. Its range Z_i consists of the tuples whose ith arrow is a unit. The induced map O_i→Z_i is inverse to q|_(Z_i); their two composites are literal identities. In particular the local anchor u_i(b)=t(g_i) is continuous. On O_i∩O_j the invariant actual arrow

\[ c_{ji}(b)=g_jg_i^{-1}:u_i(b)\longrightarrow u_j(b) \tag{402} \]

is continuous. The equations c_ii=1, c_ij=c_ji^−1 and c_kj c_ji=c_ki follow by actual cancellation. They are equations of arrows, rather than leaf-image relations. Thus (u_i,c_ji) is an actual H-arrow cocycle on the whole candidate B_M H.

It is the actual local principal cocycle of q. The map sending a tuple over O_i to (its orbit b, g_i) is a homeomorphism onto {(b,h):b∈O_i, t(h)=u_i(b)}. Its inverse multiplies the normalized tuple(401) on the right by h. Both maps are continuous by the normalization and the groupoid action, and both composites are identities. This checks principality locally without imposing Hausdorffness on H_1 or on the quotient candidate.

U2. A globally numerable cover, even on the weak quotient

The functions t_i themselves need not have locally finite supports. There is an explicit numerable replacement. Put

\[ m(b)=\max_i t_i(b)>0,\quad a_i(b)=(t_i(b)-m(b)/2)_+,\quad \lambda_i(b)=a_i(b)\big/\sum_j a_j(b). \tag{403} \]

Every sum or maximum here is finite at a point. More importantly, these are continuous functions in the specified weak topology: on every finite join piece they are the corresponding continuous finite expressions, agree on zero-weight faces, and are invariant under the H action. The denominator is positive, since a coordinate attaining m contributes m/2. Their sum is one.

Their closed supports are subordinate and locally finite. The closure of {λ_i>0} lies in {t_i≥m/2}⊂O_i, by continuity and m>0. At b_0 let I_0 be its finite positive support and m_0=m(b_0). The function u(b)=sum_(i∉I_0)t_i(b)=1−sum_(i∈I_0)t_i(b) is continuous and is zero at b_0. On the open neighbourhood {m>m_0/2, u<m_0/8}, every i outside I_0 satisfies t_i≤u<m_0/8<m/2 and hence λ_i=0 throughout that neighbourhood. None of their closed supports meets it. This proves local finiteness on the whole B_M H, without assuming the quotient paracompact. Therefore the cover O_i and actual cocycle(402) are numerable.

U3. The precise finite-dimensional normal bundle

On O_i take u_i*τ. Glue these vector bundles by the exact derivatives D c_ji. They satisfy the inverse and triple equations because the normal derivative is a representation of actual holonomy arrows. The local gluing gives a continuous rank-q vector bundle E_M on the candidate with no orientation or spin-c choice. It is numerable by(403). A metric is explicit: choose the existing metric on τ over T, transport its local pullbacks to the common fibre using D c_ji, and sum them with the weights λ_i. Every sum is locally finite and positive definite. Its local coefficients are continuous; closed subordination lets each weighted summand extend by zero outside O_i. Consequently its full graded Clifford bundle and graded-opposite bundle are actual continuous bundles.

This records the entire derivative twist, including the rank, orientation character and any obstruction to a spin-c choice. No scalar Chern character or numerical pairing replaces that bundle.

U4. Every eligible parameter cocycle has a whole map into it

Let f be an actual continuous H-cocycle on a locally compact Hausdorff second-countable X. Refine to countably many charts indexed by a∈N and choose a locally finite partition ρ_a with closed supports contained in those charts. At x use weights ρ_a(x). Choose any a_0 with ρ_(a_0)(x)>0 and arrows f_(a,a_0)(x):f_(a_0)(x)→f_a(x) for the indices with positive weights. This tuple has a common source and defines an orbit

\[ \Phi_f(x)=[(\rho_a(x),f_{a,a_0}(x))_a]\in B_M H. \tag{404} \]

Changing a_0 multiplies every arrow on the right by the same actual transition arrow, so the orbit is independent of a_0. For continuity fix a positive a_0 on a neighbourhood of a point. Only finitely many closed partition supports occur near it. Labels whose supports miss that point can be removed by shrinking further; each remaining label has its valid cocycle chart on that neighbourhood. Thus even its possible zero-weight columns have defined transition arrows there. Formula(404) is a continuous map into one finite join piece followed by q. These local quotient maps agree, proving a continuous map of the entire X, without taking compact-stage limits.

The pullback of(402) to {ρ_a>0} is literally f_ba: f_(b,a_0) f_(a,a_0)^−1=f_ba. Its anchors are the given f_a. This positive-support cover refines the original cover and still covers X. Hence Φ_f pulls the actual candidate cocycle back to f up to the specified refinement. Its normal bundle Φ_f*E_M is canonically f*τ by those identical derivative transitions. A G-cocycle first passes to H by the actual plaque-arrow equivalence of B1, giving the same statement for its full normal twist.

M1. Actual equivalence supplies a combined arrow cocycle

For this proof an equivalence of actual H-cocycles is given by actual equivalence arrows on a common refinement, satisfying the transition equations. A concordance is an actual cocycle on X×I whose restrictions are equivalent to the two endpoint cocycles. These are the conventions used by C5 and B1.

Write f^0 on charts U_i and f^1 on charts V_j. On a common refinement W_r⊂U_(i_r)∩V_(j_r), let θ_r:f^0_(i_r)→f^1_(j_r) be its equivalence arrow. On U_i∩V_j define the cross arrow, wherever x∈W_r, by

\[ \theta_{j,i}(x)=f^1_{j,j_r}(x)\,\theta_r(x)\, f^0_{i_r,i}(x). \tag{405} \]

On an overlap of refinement charts the equivalence equation is θ_s f^0_(i_s,i_r)=f^1_(j_s,j_r) θ_r. Substitution into(405) and the two original triple equations give the same θ_(j,i), independently of r. Thus these local actual-arrow maps glue continuously on every cross overlap. Within each family retain the original transitions; in the other direction use θ_(j,i)^−1. Their inverse and triple equations follow from this displayed equivalence equation, including the triples with vertices from both families. This is an actual cocycle on their disjoint labelled union of charts.

Any smaller chart copying an anchor from the first family can be adjoined to this combined cocycle with its exact restricted transition arrows. Hence the auxiliary charts used below have consistent actual arrows to both original families and to one another. There is no selection of an arrow from its two endpoints alone.

M2. Fresh indices are chosen locally, with finite avoidance

Let α_i and β_i be the two countable locally finite closed-subordinate partitions used to construct the maps Φ_0, Φ_1 of U4 for equivalent cocycles. Both use indices in N; unused indices have zero weight. Choose a countable locally finite precompact cover W_j whose compact closures lie inside charts of a common refinement. Choose a partition ρ_j with closed supports inside W_j. Its anchor γ_j is the copied first-family anchor on that refinement chart. M1 supplies its actual combined transitions.

For each j let I_j be the union of the original numeric indices whose α_i or β_i closed support meets the compact closure of W_j. The two support families are locally finite, so I_j is finite. Recursively choose

\[ \nu_j>\max\bigl(I_j\cup\{\nu_0,\ldots,\nu_{j-1}\}\cup\{-1\}\bigr). \tag{406} \]

This gives pairwise distinct auxiliary indices. Give γ_j weight ρ_j at color ν_j and zero weight at unused colors. U4 defines the auxiliary whole map Φ_* into B_M H. If an original α_i or β_i is positive at x and ρ_j is positive at x, then x lies in both original support and the closure of W_j, so i∈I_j and i≠ν_j. The same exclusion holds when x belongs to the two closed supports, even if one of the weights is zero. Consequently a neighbourhood of any point has finitely many valid original and auxiliary labels, with no collision among their possible active colors. This is a local condition on the whole X; it does not require a finite bound for all active indices on X.

An auxiliary color can occur as an original color elsewhere on X. That causes no collision there: its auxiliary support is contained in a W_j whose finite avoidance set excluded exactly that simultaneous occurrence. Thus no globally disjoint relabelling of the two old infinite index sets is presumed.

M3. Both choices are joined to that same whole auxiliary map

Use the combined cocycle to form, at x, one indexed tuple with weights

\[ (1-s)\alpha_i(x)\text{ at color }i, \qquad s\rho_j(x)\text{ at color }\nu_j, \qquad 0\le s\le1. \tag{407} \]

The anchors are the corresponding old anchor and γ_j. Choose any positive-weight anchor as common source; all columns are the actual combined transition arrows from it. Changing that anchor multiplies all arrows on the right by the same actual arrow. Therefore the orbit is independent of this choice. M2 prevents two distinct columns being assigned to the same color where either could be present. The weights are nonnegative and sum to (1−s)+s=1.

For continuity near any (x,s), choose a positive source column there and a neighbourhood on which it stays positive. The closed support families and M2 give a fixed finite valid list of columns on a further neighbourhood, with disjoint colors. All combined arrows are continuous on their chart overlaps. This is a continuous tuple in a single finite join piece, followed by its quotient. At the endpoints one family has zero weight and is deleted by faces. Hence it gives the actual whole homotopy Φ_0≃Φ_*. Applying the identical construction with β_i gives Φ_1≃Φ_*. The middle tuple uses the same γ_j, ν_j and ρ_j, with the same actual transitions in both constructions, so their middle maps agree literally. Concatenating one homotopy with the reverse of the other proves Φ_0≃Φ_1 as maps on the entire X.

This proves independence of refinement, partition, enumeration and actual-cocycle equivalence. Every re-enumeration is another choice to which the same finite-avoidance argument applies. The pulled normal bundle along each displayed homotopy is the normal bundle of that whole combined cocycle, by U4's literal derivative identities. Its endpoint comparisons retain the full twist; an odd coefficient has not been traced or replaced by numerical data.

M4. A global cutoff homotopy recovers every continuous map

Let R:B_M H→B_M H retain the actual arrow columns of a tuple and replace its weights t_i by the λ_i of U2. It is well-defined: λ_i>0 implies t_i>0, so no new column is needed. More generally retain those arrows and replace the weights by

\[ t_i(s)=(1-s)t_i+s\lambda_i,\qquad0\le s\le1. \tag{408} \]

They sum to one, respect all zero-weight face relations, and are invariant under the common right H action. On every finite join piece the formula is continuous, including the deletion of cutoff-zero columns at s=1. The finite-piece quotient and the right-action quotient remain quotient maps after product with the compact locally compact interval. Thus(408) defines a continuous homotopy of the entire candidate from its identity to R. No assumption that its raw t_i supports are locally finite was needed for this global homotopy.

For any continuous F:X→B_M H, pull the actual cocycle of U1 back to the charts F^−1(O_i). The partition λ_i∘F has locally finite closed supports subordinate to them by U2. Construct its classifying map with exactly those indices and weights. Its arrows are the old normalized columns of F and its weights are λ_i(F). Therefore it is literally RF. Composing(408) with F proves that this choice of classifying map is homotopic to F on the whole X. The full normal bundle is also the literal pulled E_M of U3.

M5. The natural classification bijection, including concordances

Let Coc_H(X) be equivalence classes of actual numerable H-cocycles, further identified by concordance. Pullback of U1 gives a map P:[X,B_M H]→Coc_H(X), since a whole map homotopy pulls back a whole actual cocycle on X×I. Constructing U4 gives Q in the other direction. M3 proves its independence from all representative and partition choices.

If an actual cocycle is given on X×I, perform U4 once on that entire eligible base. Its endpoints have the given endpoint cocycles up to their specified equivalences. M3 on X compares its endpoint partitions with any previously selected ones. These endpoint homotopies, pasted with the whole interval map, give a homotopy of the selected endpoint classifying maps. Thus Q is well-defined on concordances, not only on equivalent cocycles.

U4 proves PQ=1: the pulled cocycle equals the original on its positive-weight refinement. M4 proves QP=1: a pulled cocycle classifies to RF≃F. Consequently

\[ [X,B_M H]\ \cong\ \operatorname{Coc}_H(X) \tag{409} \]

is a bijection of the full homotopy/concordance sets for every eligible X. It is natural for every continuous h:Y→X between such spaces, including nonproper maps. The pulled closed-subordinate partition α_i∘h remains locally finite and subordinate; using it in U4 gives exactly Φ_f∘h. M3 removes dependence on the partition chosen separately on Y. Pullback of cocycles is already literal. The two maps in(409) therefore commute with h at the full class level, with the canonically pulled normal bundle.

The same proof applies to the whole base X×K for every compact finite polyhedron K, since it remains locally compact, Hausdorff and second countable. This asserts the classification of whole families. It does not assert a prescribed relative boundary filling or simultaneous choices on all faces of an infinite realization.

By B1 the actual G-cocycle/concordance functor has the same comparison, with its specified short plaque-arrow equivalences and transported τ. No C*-algebra Morita theorem is required for that statement; the analytic algebra in χ remains C*r(G).

W1. The relative CW lifting lemma

Let f:Y→Z be a weak homotopy equivalence. Let (K,L) be a CW pair. Given b:K→Z, a:L→Y and a homotopy f a≃b|L, there exist a':K→Y extending a and a homotopy f a'≃b extending the prescribed boundary homotopy. No CW structure on Y or Z is required.

To prove it, include Y at the bottom of the mapping cylinder M_f. Its retraction to Z shows that Y→M_f has the same component and homotopy-group isomorphisms as f. The disk-filling step in B4 applies to this inclusion: its proof uses only those isomorphisms. A disk whose boundary is in Y first has a filling of that boundary in Y by injectivity on the preceding homotopy group. Correct the difference sphere by surjectivity on the disk's homotopy group, then fill its null difference in M_f. In dimension1 use endpoint components and difference loops; in dimension0 use paths of corresponding components. This gives a disk homotopy to Y with the boundary fixed.

On L use the mapping-cylinder path from a to f a followed by the specified homotopy to b|L. Induct over the relative cells of (K,L). The boundary homotopy already constructed on each cell is appended as a collar to its b-valued disk, exactly as in B4. The disk-filling step extends it, ending in Y with its prescribed boundary values. This gives a' and a homotopy in M_f on the entire K. Project to Z. On L the extra cylinder path projects to a constant initial segment before the given homotopy. Remove that segment by a homotopy of its interval parametrization, fixed at its ends. The homotopy-extension property of the CW pair (K×I, L×I∪K×{0,1}) extends this correction, so the projected boundary homotopy is exactly the specified one. R4's cell-cylinder retraction proves that extension property. The weak topology and its product with the finite interval make the whole construction continuous. This proves the lemma, including infinite K.

W2. Weak equivalences of spans give a weak equivalence of cylinders

Write P(A,C,B) for the double mapping cylinder of A←C→B. A strictly commuting map of spans which is a weak homotopy equivalence on A,C,B induces a weak homotopy equivalence of P. Here is the finite-parameter proof, including the relative step needed for injectivity.

The cylinder has a continuous height function, equal to0 on A, to1 on B, and to t on C×I. Its two open subsets U_A={height<2/3}, U_B={height>1/3} cover P. They deformation retract to A and B by moving the height to their respective ends. Their intersection is C×(1/3,2/3), with its projection to C. These retractions commute with every map of spans; the map also preserves height, so the inverse images of these two open subsets are precisely the corresponding open subsets of the source cylinder.

Let g:K→P be a map from a compact finite polyhedron. Pull back these two opens. Choose a continuous partition p_A+p_B=1 with closed supports inside them. Approximate p_A by a piecewise linear function r within1/12 on a sufficiently fine triangulation. Set K_A={r≥1/3} and K_B={r≤2/3}; subdivide at those two levels. They are finite closed subpolyhedra covering K. Their intersection K_C={1/3≤r≤2/3} maps into U_A∩U_B, because both p_A and p_B are at least1/4 there. The end retractions give maps

\[ a:K_A\to A,\qquad c:K_C\to C,\qquad b:K_B\to B, \quad a|_{K_C}=\ell c,\quad b|_{K_C}=r_C c, \tag{410} \]

where ℓ and r_C are the two span arrows, not the piecewise linear function r. This is a strictly commuting map of finite source spans. The collapse p_K:P(K_A,K_C,K_B)→K is a homotopy equivalence: K is their ordinary union pushout and both subpolyhedron inclusions are CW cofibrations; the cylinder comparison proved in R4 applies.

The assembled span map G:P(K_A,K_C,K_B)→P(A,C,B) is homotopic to g p_K. On K_A move g's height toward0; on K_B move it toward1. On K_C×I, if g(x)=(c(x),v(x)), use height (1-s)v(x)+s t. At the two ends this agrees with the preceding two retractions. It gives the desired pasted homotopy, including all points of A or B. Thus every finite probe can be replaced, up to its full homotopy, by these exact finite span data.

Now apply this construction to a map into the target cylinder of a weak-equivalence span map F. Lift its c-map up to homotopy through F_C using W1. Lift the a-map through F_A relative to K_C, prescribing there the new source map ℓ c and the homotopy ℓ' H_C. W1 gives an exact extension a with a|_(K_C)=ℓ c. Do the same for b. The three resulting homotopies form a strictly commuting homotopy of span data. Their assembled cylinders therefore give a source map whose image is homotopic to the original target probe. The homotopy equivalence p_K transfers it to K. This proves surjectivity.

For injectivity, take a target null disk or homotopy cylinder with its boundary the image of a given source probe. Subdivide that entire finite polyhedron using the same two opens. Since F preserves height, the source boundary also lies in the corresponding source opens. Its source retractions give the boundary values of a,c,b. Lift c by W1 relative to that boundary, with its constant comparison homotopy there. Lift a relative to the union of K_C and its source boundary; their prescribed maps agree on the intersection, and the prescribed homotopies agree because H_C is constant there. Lift b in the identical way. These are finite CW pairs after the chosen subdivision. The resulting source span data extend the boundary span data exactly.

Their assembled source cylinder extends its boundary assembly. To transfer that extension back to the original disk, choose a homotopy inverse of its source collapse p_K relative to the desired boundary inverse. W1 applied to p_K provides it: prescribe the boundary inverse and its known comparison homotopy, then extend over the disk. Composing with the assembled map gives a source disk whose boundary is homotopic to the original source probe by the preceding explicit assembly homotopy. Hence that probe is null. For two endpoint probes the same construction on their homotopy cylinder proves equality. Paths and a marked basepoint can be included in the prescribed boundary subpolyhedron; the usual basepoint-change path is retained in the filling step of W1. This proves injectivity in every based homotopy group and the bijection of components. It proves W2 without a global inverse of a weak map, a CW assumption on A,C,B, or a compactness claim about those target spaces.

W3. The full levelwise-weak fat realization theorem

Let Z_•→Y_• be a semisimplicial map which is a weak homotopy equivalence in every degree, and suppose every level is T1. Then its fat realization is a weak homotopy equivalence. At a finite skeleton use the attaching span ||Z||_(n−1)←Z_n×∂Δ^n→Z_n×Δ^n. The disk-boundary arrow has the actual collar of R1, so its ordinary attachment and double mapping cylinder are homotopy equivalent. The maps on both new pieces are weak equivalences: products with the fixed sphere or disk preserve components and homotopy-group isomorphisms. Induction with W2 proves the comparison on every finite skeleton. R2's T1 dimension-bound argument places every sphere, null disk and homotopy-cylinder image in some finite skeleton. The finite comparisons therefore give the full weak equivalence. In degree0 the assertion is the given level map; the empty boundary for that degree introduces no extra condition.

This is the exact stronger version required when an augmented étale or open-cover comparison gives only weak equivalences. It does not assert that contractible point fibres by themselves give such level weak equivalences; that remains a separate input.

W4. An open-cover groupoid has the correct weak realization

For an open cover {U_i} of any space Y, let C_U be the groupoid with objects (i,y), y∈U_i, and its unique actual arrow between (i,y) and (j,y) when y lies in both opens. Its fat realization maps weakly equivalently to Y by the common y coordinate.

Given a sphere or finite polyhedron map f:K→Y, take a finite closed-subordinate partition of unity on K for the pulled cover. Order its finitely many positive labels, put their weights at the objects (i,f(x)), and use the unique cover arrows. This is a continuous lift: near a point closed subordination gives a fixed finite valid label list, and zero-weight faces agree. Its projection is f exactly. Hence homotopy groups and components are surjected.

For any given lift a:K→||N(C_U)|| over f, join its original ordered string with such a partition string, retaining their common y=f(x). Give the two strings weights (1-s) times the old weights and s times the partition weights. The unique cover arrows connect the last old to the first new label. Repeated labels are allowed in this fat nerve, so there is no indexed join collision. At s=0 and s=1 faces delete the zero string, giving respectively a and the partition lift.

The homotopy is continuous without requiring a global partition on Y or a local simplex representative for a. Locally in K the new partition labels are a fixed finite valid list, and f takes values in their common open intersection. Over that open set, joining any old fat string to this fixed finite new string is continuous on every nerve piece and respects its faces. Product with the finite new simplex and interval preserves the quotient topology. Thus the local join maps compose continuously with a; they agree when new weights vanish. This proves the whole join homotopy. If f extends over a null disk, choose the partition on that entire disk and join a to its boundary lift. The boundary lift now bounds the lifted disk, proving injectivity. The same path argument handles components and basepoint change. Therefore the cover augmentation is a weak equivalence even when Y has no global subordinate partition or is non-Hausdorff.

For T1 open charts all its nerve levels are T1, and its fat realization is T1 as well: the inverse image of a point in each nerve piece is the finite closed-face union used in R2. Thus W3 can be applied to a face-compatible family of these cover resolutions. The face-compatible holonomy nerve resolution in Q applies this result to every required level.

V1. Forgetting colors gives an actual continuous nerve map

For a tuple representing B_M H, order its positive colors i_0<⋯<i_n. Put x_a=t(g_(i_a)) and give this vertex weight t_(i_a). Its arrow from x_a to x_b is the actual arrow g_(i_b)g_(i_a)^−1. Use the consecutive ones to form the nerve chain. This defines

\[ v:B_M H\longrightarrow B_f H. \tag{411} \]

On a finite indexed join piece use all its colors in increasing order, allowing zero weights. The arrows are continuous groupoid products. Deleting a zero coordinate produces the same chain as the corresponding nerve face: the two adjacent products cancel the omitted column. A common right multiplication cancels from every product. Thus the finite-piece formulas descend through the weak join quotient and its orbit quotient. They prove continuity of v on the whole space, including at the faces. No ordering of the arrow space or of the leaf space is being selected.

V2. Barycentric subdivision supplies a map in the other direction

For the chain x_0→⋯→x_n let h_a:x_0→x_a be its initial actual product, with h_0=1_(x_0). Subdivide Δ^n barycentrically. A simplex of that subdivision is indexed by a flag of nonempty faces

\[ I_0\subsetneq I_1\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq I_k \subseteq\{0,\ldots,n\}. \]

If u_0,…,u_k are its barycentric weights, put at color |I_j|−1 the arrow h_(min I_j) and weight u_j. The colors are distinct, because the face cardinalities strictly increase. All arrows have common source x_0. Pass to their Milnor orbit. On the finite subdivision pieces this is continuous. It defines

\[ d:B_f H\longrightarrow B_M H. \tag{412} \]

Here are all the gluing checks. On an intersection of subdivision simplices the positive subflag is the same; the other weights vanish and their columns are deleted. If an original coordinate t_a vanishes, then

\[ t_a=\sum_{j:a\in I_j}u_j/|I_j|=0. \tag{413} \]

Every positive face in the flag therefore omits a. After removing a its cardinality is unchanged. Its minimum is the same remaining vertex, with the changed numerical position in the shorter chain. The initial arrow to that vertex is unchanged when a>0. When a=0 it becomes h_b g_1^−1, where g_1:x_0→x_1 is the removed initial arrow. This is a common right multiplication of all retained columns, so the orbit is identical. Successive zero-coordinate deletions obey the same cancellation. These checks prove compatibility with every fat face, including the first face and all intersections of faces. Finite subdivision followed by the weak quotient now proves global continuity of d. No degeneracy identification is used.

V3. One entire fat homotopy is explicit

On one flag piece concatenate the original vertices x_0,…,x_n with the new vertices x_(min I_0),…,x_(min I_k). Give them weights

\[ (1-s)t_a\quad(0\le a\le n),\qquad s u_j\quad(0\le j\le k),\qquad 0\le s\le1. \tag{414} \]

The arrow between any two consecutive retained vertices x_a,x_b is h_b h_a^−1. This includes backward arrows when the successive face minima decrease. It is a valid chain because H is a groupoid. The weights are nonnegative and sum to one. At s=0 its second block is deleted and it is the original simplex. At s=1 its first block is deleted and it is exactly v d of that simplex, since the new colors increase with the flag cardinalities.

At a subdivision boundary the zero new vertices are deleted and the common subflag gives the same chain. At an original face the checks of(413) remove both the old zero vertex and any zero new vertex, while the actual consecutive arrow products cancel as in V1. A changed initial source multiplies all h_a on the right by the same actual arrow and leaves every chain arrow unchanged. Thus(414) defines a whole continuous homotopy

\[ 1_(B_f H)\simeq v d. \tag{415} \]

Continuity follows first on each finite subdivision piece times I, then through the face quotient, whose product with the locally compact interval is quotient. The argument includes the full infinite realization; no finite-stage homotopy is pasted by a limit. At a vertex x the track is the fat unit 1-simplex at x, with weights (1−s,s). It need not be constant in the fat realization. Its loop is null: inside the fat nerve of the one-object category with just 1_x, append that same object with weight r and multiply the old weights by 1−r. This gives a contraction, by the same face-compatible formula used in R4. Consequently this vertex track induces the identity basepoint-change action on all homotopy groups. This point is needed for the based conclusion in V5 below.

V4. The other composite has exactly the original actual cocycle

Let F:X→B_M H be any continuous map from an eligible parameter space X. Its original cocycle has anchors u_i on t_i(F)>0 and arrows g_j g_i^−1. The pullback by d v F of the U1 cocycle is equivalent to it by actual arrows. We check continuity of those arrows; there is no globally continuous choice of a subdivision flag.

At a finite tuple, order its positive weights by decreasing size, writing w_1≥⋯≥w_r>0 and w_(r+1)=0. The barycentric coefficient of the face of the k+1 largest original weights is

\[ u_k=(k+1)(w_(k+1)−w_(k+2)),\qquad0\le k<r. \tag{416} \]

Their sum is one by telescoping, and(413) recovers each original weight. Equal weights give a zero coefficient at that boundary, so the positive face is uniquely the top k+1 set at every positive new color k. Choose its least original color a. The new anchor at color k is exactly u_a. The comparison arrow from that new anchor to an original anchor u_i is

\[ g_i g_a^{-1}:u_a\longrightarrow u_i. \tag{417} \]

Where that new coefficient is positive, its top set and a are locally constant as sets of colors. This remains true when nearby tuples acquire arbitrarily many new raw colors. At the given point let I be the finite original positive support. The total outside weight 1−sum_(i∈I)t_i is continuous and zero there. Near that point it is smaller than a fixed fraction of the positive gap w_(k+1)−w_(k+2) and of w_(k+1). Each outside coordinate is bounded by that total. The finitely many coordinates in I are continuous. Shrink the neighbourhood so their strict top-set gap persists and every outside coordinate remains below it. The selected top k+1 set is then unchanged throughout that neighbourhood.

Thus(417) is a continuous actual-arrow map on every relevant positive new/old overlap, by the continuity of U1's normalized old arrows. Changing common source does not change it. The old and new transition equations are exactly cancellation of the g columns, so(417) gives an actual-cocycle equivalence on the joint positive refinement. Applying the normal derivative gives precisely the corresponding normal-bundle equivalence, with no loss of the twist.

M5 on the entire X now proves

\[ F\simeq d v F\quad\text{as whole maps }X\longrightarrow B_M H. \tag{418} \]

Only this eligible-domain conclusion is used. It does not assert a global homotopy 1≃d v on the possibly non-locally-compact candidate. For spheres, disks and finite polyhedra it retains all their actual cocycle data, rather than passing to separate point fibres.

V5. The comparison is a weak equivalence with the full twist

Equation(415) makes v surjective on every homotopy group at a vertex: apply d to a based sphere; its composite with v is homotopic to the original sphere. The vertex track is the null unit loop checked in V3, so this yields the same based class. For injectivity let F:S^n→B_M H have vF extending to a disk. Apply d to that disk. Its boundary is d v F. Equation(418), on the entire sphere, gives a homotopy of F to that boundary; appending its collar supplies a disk for F. A freely null sphere is also based null: its homotopy track gives a basepoint-change isomorphism, and that isomorphism sends the zero class to the zero class. This proves injectivity.

The identical argument with paths proves the component bijection. Every point of either space has a path to a vertex: decrease all but one positive weight linearly in its representing finite simplex. In B_M H a vertex at any color is connected to the color-0 vertex at the same target object using the two-color tuple of unit arrows. Hence the preceding based conclusion transfers to every component and every basepoint by actual paths. Thus v is a weak homotopy equivalence. The reverse map d is also weakly equivalent, by(415).

The comparison identifies the normal cocycle on every eligible probe by(417) and its exact normal derivatives. It proves a specific full holonomy comparison, not merely the weak type of orbit points. Part Q supplies a verified countable CW model with its actual universal cocycle, followed by the full twisted K group and the ordinary-manifold KK triangles.

V6. From the transversal to the full holonomy fat nerve

Choose the foliation boxes O_i of B1, labelled even when they overlap. Let G' have objects (i,z), z∈O_i, and every actual G arrow between those labelled endpoints. Its forgetful functor Q:G'→G has the same entire fat homotopy equivalence as A2–A3. Those proofs require a locally finite closed-subordinate partition only on the Hausdorff object manifold; the arrow space need not be étale. Their formulas use only units, continuous actual compositions, weights and valid endpoint charts. A countable locally finite partition for the O_i therefore gives both full homotopies for Q in exactly(398)–(400).

Let t_i:O_i→T_i be the plaque projection. Let a_i(z):z→t_i(z) be its continuously varying short plaque arrow, chosen to be the unit on the transverse section. Define R:G'→H by

\[ R(i,z)=t_i(z),\qquad R(g:(i,z)\to(j,w))=a_j(w)g a_i(z)^{-1}. \tag{419} \]

These are continuous maps, and the two middle short arrows cancel in a composite, so R is a functor. Let S:H→G' include its labelled transverse object into its own box and retain the actual arrows. Then RS=1 literally. The short arrows a_i(z) give a natural isomorphism 1_(G')→SR: for any g:z→w, R(g)a_i(z)=a_j(w)g. This equality is of actual G' arrows with the displayed endpoint labels.

For completeness it gives an entire fat homotopy without using degeneracy identifications. In each old vertex block, interleave the old object (i,z) of weight (1−s)t with its projected object (i,t_i(z)) of weight s t. Use a_i(z) within the block. Between the projected old vertex and the next old vertex use g_next a_i(z)^−1. All remaining arrows are their actual products. At s=0 the projected vertices disappear, leaving the old chain; at s=1 the old vertices disappear, leaving its SR chain. Zero old weights delete whole blocks, with the naturality equation ensuring equality of every face product. The levelwise formulas and quotient-times-I argument prove full continuity. Thus R,S are homotopy inverse on the whole fat realizations.

Combining these verified functors with V1 gives a specific weak equivalence from B_M H to B_f G, with each intermediate fat transversal/atlas comparison an entire homotopy equivalence. Every short-arrow derivative is the canonical normal transport; the displayed naturality equations remain true for those derivatives. No C*-algebra Morita equivalence or ordinary thin realization for a nonclosed unit locus was invoked.
