Lemma 8.15 (uniform calculus through the zero anchor). Suppose \(V\) is compact and the \(H\)-action is smooth. The family transformation groupoid \[ \mathcal G=\coprod_{v\in[0,1]}(V\rtimes H_v) \] has a compact-support source-fibre pseudodifferential calculus, with principal bundle \(V\times[0,1]\times\mathfrak h^*\). Its order-zero operators are multipliers of \(\mathfrak A_H(C(V))\); negative-order operators belong to that algebra. Completion gives the exact scalar symbol sequence \[ 0\longrightarrow\mathfrak A_H(C(V)) \longrightarrow\overline\Psi^0(\mathcal G) \xrightarrow{\sigma} C(V\times[0,1]\times S^{d-1})\longrightarrow0. \tag{59} \] Bundle corners have the corresponding assertion. At \(v=0\) the anchor is zero, while the source fibres still have dimension \(d\); this causes no degeneration in these estimates.

In rank zero, interpret \(S^{-1}\) as the empty cosphere. The family algebra is \(C(V\times[0,1])\), every kernel is smoothing, and (59) has zero symbol quotient. The following proof treats \(d\ge1\).

Proof. The source fibre at \((x,v)\) is \(H_v\). Use the fixed smooth coordinates near its identity from (53)–(54), and right-translate those coordinates to any point \(h_0\) of the fibre. The relative group coordinate of \(h=uh_0\) and \(h'=u'h_0\) is \(uu'^{-1}\), independent of \(h_0\). In the regular representation a coefficient \(b\) is evaluated at \(h x\), so on this patch its base point is \(h_0x\) followed by the small action of \(u\). This base point remains in compact \(V\). The needed derivatives in \(u\), the relative coordinate changes, and the normalized densities have bounds uniform in \(v\) and in this base point. Parameter derivatives of the original kernel are taken on its fixed compact groupoid charts; we do not assert bounded \(v\)-derivatives of a faraway moving point \(h_0x\). Such derivatives are not used in the regular norm bound. Right translation of left Haar introduces one constant modular factor for the patch; normalizing its \(L^2\) coordinate map cancels that constant. The remaining local factors are smooth positive densities on the small chart. No derivative of an inverse anchor, and no injectivity of the anchor, is used.

Here is why local estimates give a uniform bound on the entire, possibly noncompact, fibre. Equip \(H_v\) with the right-invariant metric specified by the fixed tangent basis. A sufficiently small coordinate ball and its slightly larger buffer work for every \(v\), since the near-identity metric coefficients depend smoothly on a compact parameter interval. Choose a maximal separated set and translated bump functions, then normalize them to a square partition \(\sum_i\phi_i^2=1\). Its overlap number and derivative bounds are uniform. Indeed disjoint smaller balls have uniformly bounded positive local volume; a finite cover of a buffered identity ball bounds their possible number in that ball. Right translation preserves the metric and changes Haar by a constant, so the same ratio bound holds on every translated ball.

For a kernel with a fixed compact relative group support \(K\), each input patch meets only a uniformly bounded number of output patches, and conversely. To verify this without a global coordinate-growth assumption, cover the compact set \(K\), and its products with the fixed small coordinate buffers, by finitely many small coordinate balls, uniformly in \(v\). Their products are compact because group multiplication is smooth on the compact parameter interval. The preceding packing bound applies to this finite cover. If all localized blocks have norm at most \(C\) and each row and column has at most \(N\) blocks, Cauchy–Schwarz gives norm at most \(NC\) for the matrix of blocks. The square partition is an isometric localization and a contractive reconstruction, so this is the bound for the original operator.

On each such patch, a compact-support conormal kernel reduces, by a smooth phase change, to \[ (2\pi)^{-d}\int e^{i(z-z')\cdot p} a(z,p;x,v)\,dz'\,dp. \] The phase change uses the integrated differential of the relative coordinate map; it is invertible on the fixed small buffer even at \(v=0\). Half-density and bundle changes are smooth bounded factors. The symbol estimates are \[ \|\partial_z^\gamma\partial_p^\eta a\| \le C_{\gamma\eta}\langle p\rangle^{m-|\eta|}, \] uniformly in \(x,v\) and the translated patches. Integrating by parts in the compact \(z\)-variable bounds its Fourier kernel by \(C_L\langle\zeta-p\rangle^{-L}\langle p\rangle^m\). For \(m=0\), choose \(L>d\) and apply the two-sided Schur bound, exactly as in the index lesson, Lemma 6.1. The finite-overlap argument just given makes this a uniform regular norm bound.

The same Taylor and integration-by-parts computation as in that lesson's Lemma 6.2 proves composition and adjoints: the local expansion is \(\sum_\gamma(\partial_p^\gamma a)(D_z^\gamma b)/\gamma!\), and after \(L\) terms the remainder has order \(m+n-L\). All required derivatives and supports are uniform in \(v\). Away from the units a conormal kernel is smooth. Composable products of two fixed compact arrow supports are compact, since the source-range equality is closed in the Hausdorff unit manifold. Thus the calculation globalizes. Smooth kernels remain smooth under these products, also at zero.

For \(m<0\), truncate the symbol at \(|p|\le R\), keeping the same compact physical kernel cutoff. The error's finitely many order-zero seminorms are at most \(C R^m\); derivatives of the frequency cutoff satisfy the same bound. Therefore its regular norm tends to zero uniformly in \(x,v\). The truncated kernels are jointly smooth compact kernels in the dense algebra of Theorem 8.14. The fibre-supremum norm proves membership in \(\mathfrak A_H(C(V))\). Multiplying an order-zero kernel on either side by a smooth compact kernel gives a smooth compact kernel. The norm bound and the adjoint bound extend these two products to a bounded adjointable multiplier. Finite bundle embeddings into trivial bundles give the identical statements in bundle corners.

We include the quotient-norm check. If \(c=\|\sigma(P)\|_\infty\), quantize the smooth positive square root of \((c^2+\varepsilon)I-\sigma(P)^*\sigma(P)\). Composition gives \(P^*P+Q^*Q=(c^2+\varepsilon)I+R\), with \(R\) of negative order in the algebra. Hence \(\|P+\mathfrak A_H(C(V))\|\le c\). For the opposite inequality, fix \(x,v\) and a unit covector at the identity source chart. A unit wave packet of radius \(h^{1/2}\) and phase \(e^{i\langle z,p_0\rangle/h}\) has \(\|Pu_h-\sigma(P)(x,v,p_0)u_h\|_2\to0\). Rescaling the packet and using degree-zero homogeneity proves this on bounded rescaled frequencies; the rapidly decreasing Fourier tail and the order-zero bound control the rest. Every smooth compact kernel takes this packet to zero in norm, by integration by parts, and algebra-norm approximation gives the same result for every element of \(\mathfrak A_H(C(V))\). This argument works in the additive source fibre at zero too. Taking the supremum proves equality of quotient and symbol norms. Smooth symbols are dense, and every one is quantizable; the norm identity proves surjectivity and that completion introduces no extra kernel. This proves (59).

Finally, an invertible principal bundle symbol has a smooth inverse on the compact parameter cosphere. Quantize both with fixed charts. Their two defects have order \(-1\), hence belong to the algebra, which suffices for a Fredholm index. If smoothing defects are desired, the recursive inverse symbols and the increasing-frequency Borel summation of the index lesson's Theorem 6.3 work uniformly on \(V\times[0,1]\). Each summand uses the same physical chart cutoff; growing products of actual operator supports are not summed. \(\square\)

The Dirac cycle over the deformation

The evaluations in Corollary 8.14a are already KK equivalences. To use them to compare geometric operators, one needs an actual cycle over their common domain. Fibrewise self-adjoint operators and a fibrewise compactness assertion do not provide that cycle. We construct it here for the ordered, globally framed solvable deformation of Theorem 8.14. The global vector-bundle equivalence is proved in Section 6. Its general longitudinal use and the geometric wrong-way comparisons require their further arguments.

Write \(I=[0,1]\), \(A_I^0=\mathfrak A_H(\mathbb C)\), and \(A_I^B=\mathfrak A_H(B)\). Fix the ordered basis \(e_1,\ldots,e_d\) used in (53), with \([e_i,e_j]_v=v\sum_k c_{ij}^ke_k\). The positive Clifford algebra \(C_d\) has odd self-adjoint generators \(\varepsilon_i\), satisfying \(\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j+\varepsilon_j\varepsilon_i=2\delta_{ij}\). All coefficient algebras \(B\) in the following statement are separable and trivially graded; Clifford tensor products retain their grading.

Lemma 8.15a (regularity and algebra-valued resolvents). On the standard graded module \(A_I^0\widehat\otimes C_d\), the differential operator \[ D=\sum_i D_i\widehat\otimes\varepsilon_i, \qquad U_i(s)=e^{-isD_i}, \qquad D_i=-iX_i^R, \tag{115} \] has a regular self-adjoint closure, with the jointly smooth compact group kernels as a graph core. Here \(X_i^R f(h)=\left.\frac{d}{ds}f(\exp_{H_v}(se_i)h)\right|_{s=0}\), and the Hilbert-space realization uses normalized left Haar measure. Its scalar functional calculus satisfies \[ f(D)\in A_I^0\widehat\otimes C_d\quad(f\in C_0(\mathbb R)). \tag{116} \] In particular this is an assertion about the whole interval algebra.

Proof. Suppose first that \(d>0\). Left translations preserve left Haar, so \(-iX_i^R\) is formally symmetric. The right-invariant metric making the fixed frame orthonormal is complete. Its volume is right Haar. Put \(\kappa_i(v)=X_i^R\log\Delta_v\); these are constants on each group, smooth in \(v\). Since \(dh_R=\Delta_v^{-1}dh_L\), the unitary from right-Haar to left-Haar realization is multiplication by \(\Delta_v^{-1/2}\). In the right-Haar realization (115) is therefore \[ D^R=\sum_i\bigl(-iX_i^R+\tfrac i2\kappa_i(v)\bigr)\varepsilon_i. \tag{117} \] Indeed \(\operatorname{div}_{dh_R}X_i^R=-\kappa_i(v)\). This verifies symmetry including the modular term. The principal symbol is \(\sum_i p_i\varepsilon_i\), whose square is \(|p|^2\). Its propagation speed for this metric is one.

We verify the uniform support condition needed to apply the energy argument of Lemma 8.19. A single compact identity-coordinate buffer \(Q\) and a radius \(r>0\) work for every \(v\), by smooth dependence of the metric on the compact interval. A path of length at most \(R\) splits into at most \(\lceil R/r\rceil+1\) pieces; right translation puts the increment of each piece in \(Q\). The union of the corresponding products of copies of \(Q\), over \(v\in I\), is compact by the smooth group multiplication of Theorem 8.14. It contains all radius-\(R\) balls. The same argument prevents a finite-length path from escaping a translated compact buffer and proves completeness without a global coordinate-growth estimate.

The local elliptic estimates and the deficiency-cutoff proof of Lemma 8.19 now apply on each source group, with the just verified principal symbol, formal symmetry and complete metric. Thus \(D_v\) is essentially self-adjoint on its smooth compact core. The energy identity with a moving cutoff gives propagation at most \(|t|\) for \(W_v(t)=e^{itD_v}\). These are Hilbert-space statements at this stage.

Here is their passage to the interval algebra. For a jointly smooth compact kernel \(a_v\), \(W_v(t)a_v\) has support in a common compact set for \(|t|\le T\), by the preceding reachable-set bound. It is jointly smooth, including at zero. To see the parameter assertion explicitly, trivialize densities on that compact set, differentiate \(\partial_t u_v=iD_vu_v\), and obtain \[ \partial_t(\partial_v u_v) =iD_v\partial_v u_v+i(\partial_vD_v)u_v. \] The variation-of-constants integral bounds this derivative in each local Sobolev norm by the corresponding norms of the initial data and one higher norm of \(u_v\). Source differentiation has the same energy estimate; induction treats every source and parameter derivative. All coefficients and their derivatives are bounded on the common compact set. The smooth group family extends locally past the interval endpoints, as in Theorem 8.14, so this also proves one-sided smoothness there. Local Sobolev embedding gives the stated joint smoothness. This argument uses compact relative coordinates, rather than derivatives at an uncontrolled faraway moving base point.

The differential operators commute with right regular translations. Consequently \(L_ta=W(t)a\) is a left convolution centralizer on the compact kernel algebra: \(L_t(ab)=(L_ta)b\). Its partner is \(R_ta=(L_{-t}(a^*))^*\). Formal symmetry, or integration by parts in the convolution product, gives \((R_ta)b=a(L_tb)\). In the faithful direct sum of fibre regular representations, \(L_ta\) is the product of a unitary and the convolution operator for \(a\). Thus \(\|L_ta\|\le\|a\|\), and the same holds for \(R_t\). The full and reduced norms agree here by Theorem 8.14. Both centralizers extend and define a unitary multiplier \(W(t)\) of \(A_I^0\widehat\otimes C_d\). The group identities hold in that faithful representation. On test kernels, \(\|(W(t)-1)a\|\le |t|\|Da\|\); applying this to adjoints proves strict continuity. Density extends it to every algebra element.

We give the module-domain argument, so that Hilbert-space regularity is not substituted for module regularity. On the standard module define \(D\) to be \(1/i\) times the norm generator of this strongly continuous unitary group. Difference quotients show that its domain is dense and that it is symmetric. It is closed: passing to a graph limit in \(W(t)x-x=i\int_0^tW(s)Dx\,ds\) gives the same identity for the limit, and hence its derivative. For \(\eta\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb R)\), time convolution \(\int\eta(t)W(t)x\,dt\) lies in the generator domain, with derivative obtained by moving the derivative to \(-\eta'\). Time approximate identities approximate every domain vector in graph norm. For a fixed such convolution, approximate its input by smooth compact group kernels; the derivative error is at most \(\|\eta'\|_1\) times the input error. The support and smoothness just proved put these convolutions back in the test-kernel algebra. This proves the asserted graph-core property.

The Laplace integrals \[ R_+=-i\int_0^\infty e^{-t}W(t)\,dt, \qquad R_-=i\int_0^\infty e^{-t}W(-t)\,dt \tag{118} \] converge strictly as multipliers and in norm after application to any module vector. Integration by parts gives both inverse identities \((D+i)R_+=R_+(D+i)=1\) and \((D-i)R_-=R_-(D-i)=1\), on their respective domains. The second identity on each side also proves injectivity. These integrals are not asserted to be norm Bochner integrals in the multiplier algebra. Unitarity gives \(R_+^*=R_-\), and the integrals commute. Surjectivity of both \(D\pm i\) proves self-adjointness: if \(y\in\operatorname{Dom}D^*\), take \(x=R_+(D^*+i)y\). The vector \(y-x\) is in \(\ker(D^*+i)\), orthogonal to \(\operatorname{ran}(D-i)\), and is zero. Moreover \(R_+R_-\) is the inverse of \(1+D^2\), with range in \(\operatorname{Dom}D^2\). That range is dense because each resolvent has dense range. Hence \(D\) is regular self-adjoint on its full module domain.

It remains to prove (116). Use Lemma 8.15 with \(V\) a point and finite Clifford matrices. The principal inverse \((\sum p_i\varepsilon_i)/|p|^2\), cut off near zero and quantized with a fixed compact physical-coordinate cutoff, gives an order-\(-1\) operator \(Q_\pm\). The composition formula gives \[ (D\pm i)Q_\pm=1-S_\pm, \qquad Q_\pm,S_\pm\in A_I^0\widehat\otimes C_d. \tag{119} \] Here the defect has order \(-1\); a smoothing defect is unnecessary. The principal symbol remains invertible at \(v=0\), and all estimates are uniform. On test kernels \(Q_\pm\) maps into the graph core and the displayed identity holds. Its bounded right side and closedness extend it to the whole module, with range in \(\operatorname{Dom}D\). Multiplication by the module inverse (118) therefore yields \(R_\pm=Q_\pm+R_\pm S_\pm\), which belongs to the interval algebra. The resolvent identity gives \(R_+-R_-=-2iR_+R_-\), so \(1-2iR_+\) is a unitary with adjoint \(1+2iR_-\). Continuous functional calculus for this bounded unitary therefore constructs the calculus in (116). Its restriction to functions vanishing at the circle point \(1\) is nondegenerate because the resolvent ranges are dense. The resolvents generate \(C_0(\mathbb R)\): the Cayley function \(u(x)=(x-i)/(x+i)\) identifies the one-point compactification with the circle, and \(u-1=-2i(x+i)^{-1}\), \(u^{-1}-1=2i(x-i)^{-1}\). Trigonometric approximation on the circle, subtracting the value at its distinguished point, uniformly approximates every function vanishing there by polynomials in these two differences. This proves (116), with norm approximation in the whole interval algebra. In dimension zero the algebra is \(C(I)\), \(D=0\) is everywhere defined, and all the assertions follow directly. \(\square\)

Lemma 8.15b (the coefficient Kasparov cycle). For a separable \(B\) with a point-norm continuous \(H\)-action, the operator of Lemma 8.15a induces a regular self-adjoint operator on \[ E_I=A_I^B\widehat\otimes C_d, \qquad \phi:C(I,B)\longrightarrow\mathcal L(E_I). \] With the usual coefficient representation, its bounded transform \[ F=D(1+D^2)^{-1/2} \tag{120} \] defines \(T_D\in KK_d(C(I,B),A_I^B)\), in the ordered Clifford model of Section 0.

Proof. Integration of the scalar group kernels gives a nondegenerate homomorphism \(j:A_I^0\to M(A_I^B)\). Indeed a scalar approximate identity supported in shrinking common identity buffers converges on the dense compact coefficient kernels, uniformly over \(I\). Extend \(j\) strictly, and include the Clifford factor. The wave multipliers and the two Laplace resolvents transfer through this extension. The generator proof in Lemma 8.15a applies on the coefficient standard module: both resolvents are inverses, and their ranges are dense. For the latter assertion, approximate scalar algebra elements by vectors in the scalar resolvent range and use density of \(j(A_I^0)A_I^B\). This proves regular self-adjointness over \(A_I^B\).

A graph core is the linear span of \(j(k)x\), for smooth compact scalar Clifford kernels \(k\) and \(x\in E_I\). To prove this, first time-smooth a domain vector as in Lemma 8.15a. Approximate its input by finite such vectors, using nondegeneracy. Their time convolutions are again of this form, since \(W(t)j(k)=j(W(t)k)\) and the scalar time convolution is a smooth compact kernel. The derivative error is bounded by \(\|\eta'\|_1\) times the input error. Thus they approximate the original vector in graph norm; no Hilbert-space spectral theorem with coefficients is involved.

For \(a\in C(I,B)\) and \(f\in C_0(\mathbb R)\), the localization statements are \[ \phi(a)j(f(D)),\ j(f(D))\phi(a) \in A_I^B\widehat\otimes C_d=\mathcal K(E_I). \tag{121} \] For a compact scalar group kernel these products are compact coefficient group kernels, by convolution covariance and the continuous family action. Approximate the scalar element of (116) in its interval-algebra norm by such kernels. The multiplier bounds extend the conclusion to all \(a\) and \(f\). No unlocalized compactness for a nonunital coefficient algebra is being claimed.

Let \(B^\infty\) be the elements smooth for the original group action. Orbit convolution by compact smooth approximate identities proves density. Finite sums of continuous interval functions times elements of \(B^\infty\) are dense in \(C(I,B)\); all of their group derivatives are uniformly bounded. On this subalgebra, covariance and the negative physical phase give \[ [D,\phi(a)]=C_a=i\sum_i\phi(v\delta_i a)\varepsilon_i. \tag{122} \] Indeed differentiating \(U_i(s)\phi(a)U_i(s)^*=\phi(\alpha^v_{\exp(se_i)}a)\) gives \(-i[D_i,\phi(a)]=\phi(v\delta_i a)\). We check the domain assertion on the preceding core. Move \(\phi(a)\) through each integrated group unitary by \(\phi(a)U_h=U_h\phi(\alpha^v_{h^{-1}}a)\). On the compact kernel support this coefficient is smooth in \(h\), continuous in \(v\), with bounded first group derivatives. It can be approximated, together with those derivatives, by finite sums of scalar coordinate functions times elements of \(B\): use a finite coordinate partition, ordinary smooth approximation and the compactness of the coefficient and derivative ranges. Multiplying the scalar functions by \(k\) gives vectors in the same graph core. Differentiating their integrated expressions shows graph convergence, since the kernel and its first derivative errors bound the algebra norm by their uniform \(L^1\) norms. Thus \(\phi(a)j(k)x\) lies in the domain and (122) holds there. Its bounded right side and closedness extend it to every domain vector.

For \(b=(1+\tau^2)^{1/2}\) and \(R_\tau=(D^2+b^2)^{-1}\), the resolvent identity on the core, extended by the bounded factors below, gives \[ [DR_\tau,\phi(a)] =C_aR_\tau-D^2R_\tau C_aR_\tau -DR_\tau C_aDR_\tau. \tag{123} \] To justify the identity using only bounded factors, put \(R_z=(D-z)^{-1}\). Domain preservation by \(\phi(a)\) gives \([R_z,\phi(a)]=-R_zC_aR_z\). Since \(DR_\tau=(R_{ib}+R_{-ib})/2\), expanding these two first-order resolvents gives \(b^2R_\tau C_aR_\tau-DR_\tau C_aDR_\tau\). Substituting \(b^2R_\tau=1-D^2R_\tau\) gives (123). No domain-preservation assertion for the Clifford-valued \(C_a\) is needed. Every term is compact: \(C_aR_\tau\) and \(C_aDR_\tau\) are finite sums of the localizations (121), and the other displayed factors are bounded multipliers. Their combined norm is at most \(9\|C_a\|/(4(1+\tau^2))\), since \(\|R_\tau\|\le b^{-2}\), \(\|DR_\tau\|\le(2b)^{-1}\), and \(\|D^2R_\tau\|\le1\).

The scalar identity \(h(x)=(2/\pi)\int_0^\infty x/(1+x^2+\tau^2)\,d\tau\) gives (120) as a strict limit of bounded partial integrals. The partial scalar functions are bounded by one and converge uniformly on compact spectral sets; the resolvent's dense range proves strict convergence. Formula (123), in contrast, is norm integrable. Consequently \([F,\phi(a)]\) is the norm integral of these compact commutators. The bound \(\|[F,\phi(a)]\|\le2\|a\|\) extends compactness from the smooth subalgebra to all coefficients. Finally \((F^2-1)\phi(a)=-R_0\phi(a)\) is compact by (121), and \(F\) is odd self-adjoint. This proves every Kasparov defect. The standard module is countably generated because the parameter algebra is separable. Dimension zero gives the coefficient homomorphism cycle \((C(I,B),\phi,0)\). \(\square\)

Lemma 8.15c (the ordered zero-fibre comparison). Put \(s_d=(-1)^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}\). Evaluation at zero sends the cycle of Lemma 8.15b to the positive physical Bott class, with the following exact comparison to the native ordered real iteration: \[ T_D[q_0]=s_d[e_0]\Theta_0 \quad\text{in }KK_d(C(I,B),B\otimes C_0(\mathfrak h^*)). \tag{124} \]

Proof. At zero the group is additive, the action is trivial and the modular character is one. The transform \(\widehat f(p)=\int e^{-i\langle p,h\rangle}f(h)\,dh\) sends \(-i\partial_{h_i}\) to \(p_i\). Hence the evaluated operator is \[ F_d(p)=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^d p_i\varepsilon_i}{\sqrt{1+|p|^2}}. \tag{125} \] The evaluated coefficient representation is \(a\mapsto a(0)\). The resolvents agree with these Fourier multipliers on the compact core and hence on their full domains, so evaluation of the regular calculus gives exactly this cycle.

We check its product, rather than identify it by its K-group action. For one coordinate (125) is the trivial-action cycle (109). Suppose the first \(m\) ordered factors have been identified, and write \(x\in\mathbb R^m\), \(y=p_{m+1}\). The tensor module for the next trivial real Thom factor is the standard module over \(B\otimes C_0(\mathbb R^{m+1})\widehat\otimes C_{m+1}\), with the old Clifford generators followed by \(\varepsilon_{m+1}\). The candidate product operator is \(F_{m+1}(x,y)\).

For a homogeneous creation vector \(\xi\in B\otimes C_0(\mathbb R^m)\widehat\otimes C_m\), the connection error with the lower operator \(y\varepsilon_{m+1}/\sqrt{1+y^2}\) has two parts. One has the coefficient \((\sum x_i\varepsilon_i)\xi(x)/\sqrt{1+|x|^2+y^2}\); the other has the coefficient \[ (-1)^{|\xi|}\xi(x)y\varepsilon_{m+1} \left(\frac1{\sqrt{1+|x|^2+y^2}}-\frac1{\sqrt{1+y^2}}\right). \] Both are in \(B\otimes C_0(\mathbb R^{m+1})\widehat\otimes C_{m+1}\). For large \(|x|\), use the small norm of \(\xi(x)\) and boundedness of each scalar multiplier. On bounded \(x\), the first expression tends to zero as \(|y|\to\infty\), and so does the parenthesis multiplied by \(y\), uniformly there. The adjoint connection error has the identical estimate. First using finite elementary vectors and then norm approximation proves the connection condition for every creation vector, with the displayed grading sign.

The positivity condition of Definition 0.3 is even exact: \[ \{F_m\widehat\otimes1,F_{m+1}\} =\frac{2|x|^2}{\sqrt{1+|x|^2}\sqrt{1+|x|^2+y^2}}\ge0. \tag{126} \] The cross term cancels by the Clifford anticommutation. The cycle defects of \(F_{m+1}\) are the scalar \(C_0\) defect and exact coefficient commutation. Thus it is a product operator.

The preceding connection and positivity calculations prove the product on the unreduced standard Clifford module with the old generator block first. They also identify the positive ordered geometric Bott class after its specified consecutive-pair reduction. We must still compare that reduction with the native parity product of Lemma 0.13; its odd–odd target has the second-cycle coefficient first.

Write \(B_m\) for the positive geometric class of (125), reduced by the first \(2a\) generators when \(m=2a+\epsilon\), retaining the last right \(C_1\) generator if \(\epsilon=1\). Write \(t_{m+1}\) for the next positive one-dimensional trivial real Thom class. When \(m=2a\), the native product has the full module \[ B\otimes C_0(\mathbb R^{m+1})\otimes\Sigma_a\widehat\otimes C_1. \] The old physical generators act on \(\Sigma_a\), and the new one is \(\Gamma_a\otimes L_\varepsilon\). The connection estimates and exact positive anticommutator above prove that the normalized sum is the actual product. Thus \(B_{2a}\cdot t_{2a+1}=B_{2a+1}\).

When \(m=2a+1\), the second-cycle coefficient precedes the retained old odd coefficient in (104). The full reduced module is \[ B\otimes C_0(\mathbb R^{m+1})\otimes\Sigma_a\otimes\mathbb C^{1|1}. \] Its first \(2a\) physical generators are unchanged. Its last two physical generators and grading are \[ p_m:\ \Gamma_a\otimes\sigma_y, \qquad p_{m+1}:\ \Gamma_a\otimes\sigma_x, \qquad \Gamma_a\otimes\sigma_z. \] The same creation-map estimates and positivity calculation apply with precisely this order, so this is the actual native product operator. In the positive geometric reducer, those last two physical generators instead have order \(\Gamma_a\otimes\sigma_x,\Gamma_a\otimes\sigma_y\). The explicit unitary \[ U=1_{\Sigma_a}\otimes\frac{\sigma_x+\sigma_y}{\sqrt2} \] fixes every earlier generator, exchanges these last two, and anticommutes with the total grading. It preserves the right action and inner product and is onto. Consequently it is an even module unitary from the grading reversal of the geometric cycle to the native cycle. This right coefficient algebra is trivially graded. The grading operator is therefore right-linear; conjugating the additive inverse cycle \((\Pi E,-F)\) by it identifies that inverse with \((\Pi E,F)\). It follows, as an identity of full cycles and KK classes, that \[ B_{2a+1}\cdot t_{2a+2}=-B_{2a+2}. \] This last scalar-target argument is used only after the two odd coefficients have been contracted. On a module with a retained right odd Clifford coefficient, its grading operator is not right-linear, and cannot justify that shortcut.

Starting with the rank-zero identity and the rank-one class (109), bilinearity and these actual product operators give \[ \Theta_0=(-1)^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}B_d, \qquad B_d=(-1)^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}\Theta_0. \] Equivalently, the native physical generator list is \((2,1,4,3,\ldots,2a,2a-1[,d])\); each consecutive exchange contributes the displayed grading reversal. Coefficient multiplication is even, and all compactness tests remain localized by the tested coefficient, as in Lemma 0.13. The argument therefore holds for every separable trivially graded \(B\), including nonunital coefficients.

For completeness this normalization preserves both inverse products. Let \(A_d\) be the full geometric inverse obtained from Lemmas 6.0a–b and Theorem 6.0c by the prescribed source-to-target transfer and parity reduction of Lemma 7.20. Those complete module evaluations give \(B_d A_d=1\) and \(A_d B_d=1\). The inverse of the native accumulated real product is therefore \(s_d A_d\), where \(s_d=(-1)^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}\); uniqueness identifies it with the reverse chronological product of the real inverses. Both products are \(s_d^2\) times the corresponding geometric identity and hence equal one. This statement uses the actual geometric inverse and its entire finite Clifford transfer, without substituting an independently normalized positive Dirac cycle. Combining the Fourier evaluation with \(B_d=s_d\Theta_0\) proves (124). In rank zero all classes are the coefficient homomorphism class. \(\square\)

Theorem 8.15d (the framed longitudinal Dirac representative). In the precise ordered solvable deformation, \[ T_D=s_d\Theta_I,\qquad [\iota_B]T_D[q_1]=s_d\Theta_1, \qquad \iota_B(b)(v)=b. \tag{127} \] These are KK-class equalities for separable coefficients, not merely equalities of induced K-group maps. For a smooth locally free action whose holonomy groupoid is \(V\rtimes H\), take \(B=C_0(V)\). The endpoint cycle is the Dirac cycle of the ordered global longitudinal frame, with its homogeneous source metric and induced spin structure. It is also the corresponding Levi-Civita spin Dirac class, with the same Clifford and chirality conventions.

Proof. Naturality in Corollary 8.14a gives \(\Theta_I[q_0]=[e_0]\Theta_0\). Lemma 8.15c gives \(T_D[q_0]=s_d[e_0]\Theta_0=s_d\Theta_I[q_0]\). Multiply this equality on the right by the explicit KK inverse of \([q_0]\). Associativity gives the first identity in (127). Evaluating at one and precomposing with the constant coefficient inclusion gives the second, since \([\iota_B][e_1]=1_B\). The inclusion need not be equivariant; this use is an ordinary KK product. The preceding lemmas supplied the actual interval cycle and its zero-fibre product, so no representative comparison is inferred just from evaluation being an isomorphism.

We verify the last geometric assertion. On a source fibre the ordered right-invariant frame has constant structure coefficients \(-c_{ij}^k\). The Koszul formula therefore makes every Levi-Civita connection coefficient constant in that frame. For negative Clifford multiplication set \(c_i=-i\varepsilon_i\). The spin Dirac operator \(\sum_i c_i\nabla_{X_i^R}\), in the right-Haar realization, has principal part \(\sum_i-iX_i^R\varepsilon_i\). Its connection term differs from the modular correction in (117) by a constant, odd, self-adjoint Clifford endomorphism \(K_v\). This difference is self-adjoint because both differential operators are formally symmetric for metric volume. Its norm is uniformly bounded over \(I\), since the structure constants and modular logarithmic derivatives depend smoothly on \(v\). No compactness or ambient bounded geometry of \(V\) is needed: the coefficients are intrinsic to the homogeneous source groups. At zero the frame is flat, \(K_0=0\).

For completeness the bounded perturbation gives an actual Kasparov homotopy. Put \(D_s=D+sK\), \(0\le s\le1\), on \(\operatorname{Dom}D\). Choose \(\lambda>\max(1,\|K\|)\). A Neumann series for \(1+sK(D\pm i\lambda)^{-1}\) proves surjectivity of \(D_s\pm i\lambda\). Symmetry and the inverse-domain argument of Lemma 8.15a prove self-adjointness. Their product \(S=(D_s^2+\lambda^2)^{-1}\) has dense range and satisfies \(0\le S\le\lambda^{-2}\). The bounded operator \(1+(1-\lambda^2)S\) is positive invertible, bounded below by \(\lambda^{-2}\); hence \(S(1+(1-\lambda^2)S)^{-1}\) is the inverse of \(1+D_s^2\). This proves regularity. The scalar resolvents belong to the parameter algebra, first by the Neumann series and then at every nonreal parameter by the resolvent identity. Also \([D_s,\phi(a)]=[D,\phi(a)]\), since the scalar Clifford endomorphism \(K\) commutes with coefficients. Thus (121)–(123) give all localized cycle defects.

The transforms \(F_s\) are norm continuous. Indeed, for \(b=\sqrt{1+\tau^2}\), \[ D_s(D_s^2+b^2)^{-1} =\tfrac12\bigl((D_s-ib)^{-1}+(D_s+ib)^{-1}\bigr). \] The resolvent identity bounds the difference of these expressions for \(s,t\) by \(|s-t|\|K\|/b^2\). Integrating their difference, which is norm integrable although the individual transform integrals need only converge strictly, gives \(\|F_s-F_t\|\le |s-t|\|K\|\). Localized resolvent defects and commutators are continuous by the same estimates and their integrable tails. This is a Kasparov homotopy on the interval module. The ordered Clifford Morita contractions of Section 0 convert its Clifford-valued cycle into the spinor cycle, including odd dimension. In even dimension \(d=2\ell\), its grading is \(i^\ell c_1\cdots c_d=(-i)^\ell\varepsilon_1\cdots\varepsilon_d\), precisely the grading of the index lesson, Lemma 6.24.

For the graph action, source-fibre constructions and right translations give the longitudinal operator and its coefficient representation on the convolution module. The principal bundle frame is the given ordered identification \(F\cong V\times\mathfrak h\); its zero-fibre symbol is (125). This proves the stated framed Dirac comparison with the explicit native normalization \(s_d\). Corollary 6.0d tracks the chosen spin-c structure and proves the nontrivial vector-bundle Thom equivalence. Its use in the general longitudinal deformation, general foliation wrong-way factorization and assembly still need their own comparisons. \(\square\)

Figure 8.15d. The analytic steps establish a cycle in the parameter algebra before cancellation by the proved inverse of \([q_0]\). The middle positivity formula proves the raw Clifford product. The native odd–odd contraction exchanges each final pair; the explicit finite spinor unitary gives \(s_d=(-1)^{\lfloor d/2\rfloor}\) before the last comparison of actual KK classes. Lemmas 8.15a–c and Theorem 8.15d give the full proofs; the geometric statement is restricted to the indicated global frame. The real-action deformation method is due to Fack and Skandalis, as credited in Section 0; the product connection criterion is due to Connes and Skandalis, Appendix A.

Theorem 8.16 (solvable longitudinal symbol index). Let \(V\) be compact, and suppose a smooth locally free action of a simply connected solvable group \(H\) has orbit holonomy groupoid \(G=V\rtimes H\). Then the full longitudinal symbol index is an isomorphism \[ \operatorname{Ind}_a:K_c^0(V\times\mathfrak h^*)\xrightarrow{\cong} K_0(C(V)\rtimes H). \] More precisely, with the Fourier identification at zero and the ordered tangent identification at one, \[ \operatorname{Ind}_a=(\mathrm{ev}_1)_*(\mathrm{ev}_0)_*^{-1}. \tag{60} \] The analogous suspended statement holds in degree one. This is a comparison with the actual analytic symbol map, without an assembly or wrong-way independence assumption.

Proof. A compact relative symbol class is a triple \((B_0,B_1,a)\) over the disk and sphere of \(V\times\mathfrak h^*\). Radial contraction transports each disk bundle to a bundle from \(V\), as proved in the Hilbert-module lesson, Theorem 6.6. Smooth approximation preserves the sphere isomorphism. Keep this triple constant in \(v\), and quantize it with Lemma 8.15. A quantization \(P\) and its inverse-symbol quantization \(Q\) have both defects in \(\mathfrak A_H(C(V))\).

Apply the exact elementary-matrix index construction (11)–(12) of that lesson in the two finite bundle corners. It gives \(I(a)\in K_0(\mathfrak A_H(C(V)))\). Direct sums, smooth symbol homotopies, changed quantizations, and triples whose sphere isomorphism extends to the disk preserve the index, by the same continuous-parametrix argument. Thus \(I\) is defined on the full relative K-group. Evaluation of each matrix factor gives the endpoint index; this establishes naturality by the explicit formula, not by an asserted constancy of fibre Fredholm operators.

At zero the group acts trivially. Fourier transformation converts \(P\) to a bounded matrix function \(P_0(x,p)\), with radial limit \(a(x,p/|p|)\), and \(Q\) has the inverse radial limit. A compact physical cutoff changes the uncut Fourier symbol by a negative-order function, which vanishes at infinity and leaves this relative class unchanged. Compactify each \(\mathfrak h^*\) radially to its disk. On the boundary the elementary matrix \(W\) is exactly the diagonal map \(\operatorname{diag}(a,a^{-1})\), so its first range bundle is \(B_0\) identified with \(B_1\) by \(a\). Extend its range idempotent by the fixed trivial complements as in formula (12). Its difference from the reference idempotent is precisely the disk/sphere clutching construction of \((B_0,B_1,a)\). Hence \[ (\mathrm{ev}_0)_*I(a)=[B_0,B_1,a]. \] This also fixes the sign: a zero-dimensional fibre gives \([B_0]-[B_1]\), the kernel-minus-cokernel convention. The construction retains the actual source and target bundles and their complements; it does not require those bundles themselves to be trivial.

At one, the source-fibre calculus is the holonomy-cover calculus for \(G=V\rtimes H\). The module corner and index matrices are exactly those of the Hilbert-module lesson's Theorem 6.6. Thus \((\mathrm{ev}_1)_*I(a)=\operatorname{Ind}_a(a)\). Theorem 8.14 makes both evaluations K-isomorphisms, proving (60) and surjectivity as well as injectivity.

For degree one, suspend the coefficients and all the index matrices. Smooth compact-support suspension kernels are dense; their estimates use the same fixed supports in the additional parameter on each compact set. The natural suspension identifications then give the degree-one statement. If \(d=0\), the family is constant and the index is the difference of its two finite bundle modules, so (60) holds directly. \(\square\)

Corollary 8.17 (the complete compact trace-image formula). Under the hypotheses of Theorem 8.16, let \(\Lambda\) be a locally finite invariant transverse measure. Then formula (20) holds, with the parity there stated.

Proof. The ordered fundamental fields identify \(F\) with \(V\times\mathfrak h\). Thus \(\operatorname{Td}(F\otimes\mathbb C)=1\). By Theorem 8.16 every class of \(K_0(A)\) is a full relative-symbol index. The all-symbol measured theorem, Theorem 6.37 of the index lesson, gives \[ \tau_{\Lambda*}(\operatorname{Ind}_a\alpha) =\epsilon_d\langle\pi_!\operatorname{ch}(\alpha),[C_\Lambda]\rangle, \qquad \epsilon_d=(-1)^{d(d+1)/2}. \tag{61} \]

We check the entire symbol lattice. Stable Bott periodicity gives an external-product isomorphism \[ K^{d\bmod2}(V)\longrightarrow K_c^0(V\times\mathbb R^d), \qquad x\longmapsto x\boxtimes b_d, \] where \(b_d\) is a scalar generator in \(K_c^{d\bmod2}(\mathbb R^d)\). Its Chern normalization has absolute value one. In even dimension this is the ordered trivial spin-c computation of the index lesson's Theorem 6.29, whose fibre character is \((-1)^{d/2}\). In odd dimension tensor that even generator with \(u_+(p)=(p-i/2)/(p+i/2)\). Its one-form satisfies \[ \int_{\mathbb R}\frac1{2\pi i}u_+^{-1}du_+=1. \] The suspension isomorphism is the external product with this winding generator, as fixed in Corollary 8.10 and the stable Bott conventions above. Multiplicativity of the even and suspension Chern characters follows from tensor curvature and its transgression; the latter is obtained by differentiating a connection path and integrating its exact Chern derivative. Hence, after a possible replacement of \(b_d\) by \(-b_d\), its top fibre character integrates to \(+1\).

With base differentials preceding the ordered positive fibre differentials, fibre integration gives \(\pi_!\operatorname{ch}(x\boxtimes b_d)=\operatorname{ch}(x)\). If the suspension product is ordered in the opposite way, the Koszul sign on the only component pairing with the \(d\)-current is the fixed sign \((-1)^d\); it can equivalently be absorbed in \(b_d\). Thus the stated subgroup image is independent of this order, while (61) retains its actual analytic sign. Every symbol class is one such product, including torsion classes whose character and trace vanish by (61). As \(x\) runs through a group, multiplication of every pairing by \(\epsilon_d\) leaves its image subgroup unchanged. This proves (20). No equality of the three source maps is inferred from equality of their numerical images. \(\square\)

Figure 3. Proposition 8.12 and Theorems 8.14–8.16. The parameter is \(v\); at zero the anchor vanishes but the group fibre is \(\mathbb R^d\). Haar densities and the positive-parameter kernel factor are exact. The bottom comparison uses the uniform source-fibre calculus of Lemma 8.15. It establishes the compact trace formula of Corollary 8.17. Example 8.13 shows why the measure-existence assertion needs compactness. Assembly and independence of geometric wrong-way factorizations remain further obligations.

Compact support on a noncompact base

Compactness of \(V\) made the preceding heat traces individually finite. For a noncompact \(V\) the two traces may both be infinite. The appropriate replacement is an actual relative index matrix with a finite trace difference. We now construct it. Throughout this subsection the action is smooth and locally free, \(H\) is simply connected and solvable, and the orbit holonomy graph is \(V\rtimes H\). Put \[ B=C_0(V),\qquad A=B\rtimes H. \] Full and reduced completions agree by Lemma 8.3. The chosen fundamental frame orients and trivializes \(F\). The measure \(\Lambda\) is invariant and geometrically locally finite. Write \(\mu\) for its unit measure using the right-invariant leafwise volume of this frame, and \(C=C_\Lambda\) for its closed tangent current. Neither \(\mu(V)<\infty\) nor unimodularity of \(H\) is assumed.

Lemma 8.18 (the full compact-support symbol map). The conclusion (60) of Theorem 8.16 holds with \(C(V)\) replaced by \(C_0(V)\), in both degrees. For \(d>0\), every class of \(K_c^0(V\times\mathfrak h^*)\) can be indexed by an operator \[ P=I+P_K \] on a finite trivial bundle, whose order-zero principal symbol is unitary and equals \(I\) outside a compact subset \(K\subset V\). The operator \(P_K\) has compact base and relative group support. Its inverse-symbol parametrix can have the same form.

Proof. The disk/sphere extension for the trivial real bundle is \[ 0\longrightarrow C_0(V\times\mathbb R^d) \longrightarrow C_0(V\times\overline{\mathbb B}^d) \longrightarrow C_0(V\times S^{d-1})\longrightarrow0. \tag{62} \] Contracting the disk identifies its K-groups with those of \(B\). Restriction of the constant disk functions to the sphere is injective on K-groups: evaluation at any fixed point of the sphere is a left inverse. Consequently the six-term sequence makes the boundary from \(K_1(C_0(V\times S^{d-1}))\) onto the \(K_0\) group of the ideal surjective. This is an integral assertion, including torsion. Its sign is the disk/sphere clutching sign of Theorem 8.16.

Represent a sphere \(K_1\)-class by a finite matrix unitary in the unitization. After a constant unitary homotopy its scalar value is \(I\). Uniform convergence to \(I\) at base infinity permits a compact cutoff of \(u-I\): choose a larger compact set on whose complement \(\|u-I\|<1/4\). The cutoff matrix remains invertible on the transition region and is unchanged on the inner compact set. Its polar part is a unitary equal to \(I\) off a compact set and homotopic to \(u\). Smooth approximation on that compact set, followed by the same polar operation, makes it smooth without changing its class.

Quantize \(u-I\) with a fixed small physical kernel cutoff and compact base cutoff, and set \(P=I+\operatorname{Op}(u-I)\). Quantize \(u^{-1}-I\) similarly. All source derivatives used in Lemma 8.15 are now bounded on fixed compact enlargements of \(K\), instead of on all of \(V\). Products only replace \(K\) by the image of \(K\) under a fixed compact set of group elements. Such images are compact, uniformly over the parameter \(v\). The homogeneous group geometry, right-translation density normalization, finite-overlap localization and Fourier–Schur estimate of that lemma require no compactness of the base. Hence they apply verbatim to these coefficients. Negative-order compact-base kernels belong to \(\mathfrak A_H(B)\) by the frequency cutoff estimate \(CR^m\), \(m<0\). The two inverse defects therefore belong to this algebra.

For clarity, the completed compact-base calculus has quotient \(C_0(V\times[0,1]\times S^{d-1})\); adding \(I\) gives the scalar unitized quotient needed here. The quotient-norm argument still works. Its upper bound quantizes the positive square root after subtracting its constant value at base infinity. Its lower bound freezes one finite base point and one covector; algebra kernels annihilate the shrinking wave packet. Surjectivity follows by smooth compact approximation. Thus no extra quotient kernel appears on completion.

Keep \(u\) constant in \(v\) and apply the elementary index matrices of Theorem 8.16. At zero they give its disk/sphere boundary class, and at one its actual longitudinal index. Theorem 8.14 applied to \(B\) makes both evaluation K-maps invertible. Surjectivity of the boundary in (62) proves (60) for every symbol class, not just a chosen set of differential symbols. Suspension of (62) and of these matrices proves the other degree. For \(d=0\), the algebra is \(B\) and the index is directly the difference of the coefficient projections. \(\square\)

Lemma 8.19 (relative wave calculus). Suppose \(d>0\). A class \(x\in K_0(B)\) has smooth finite matrix projection representatives \(p_0,p_1\) with the same constant projection \(p_\infty\) outside a compact set \(K\). The twisted leafwise spin Dirac operators on their ranges, with the usual spinor grading when the source dimension is even, admit a functional calculus with the following properties:

  1. Their self-adjoint extensions are unique, and their wave groups have propagation at most the absolute wave time.
  2. A Schwartz function with Fourier support in \([-\delta,\delta]\) gives a smooth kernel of group propagation at most \(\delta\). The difference of the two twisted kernels is supported over a compact enlargement of \(K\).
  3. All these assertions also hold on \(G\times(S^1\times S^1)\), with source fibre \(H\times S^1\), and coefficients compactly supported in the \(V\)-direction.

Here propagation refers to the complete right-invariant source metric, and the circle in part 3 has its usual complete metric. It does not refer to distance in an arbitrary ambient metric on \(V\).

Proof. Begin with continuous projections in a finite matrix algebra over \(B^+\). Stabilization and a scalar unitary arrange their common scalar projection to be \(p_\infty\). Smooth a self-adjoint approximation which is exactly \(p_\infty\) outside a larger compact set and is within \(1/8\) of the projection. The spectral cut at \(1/2\) is smooth, is exactly \(p_\infty\) there, and is homotopic to the original projection through the same spectral cut. This proves the representative assertion without a finite cover of the whole noncompact manifold.

On the full trivial coefficient bundle use the Hermitian connection \[ \nabla^p=d+[p,dp]. \tag{63} \] The commutator is skew-adjoint. Differentiating \(p^2=p\) gives \([ [p,dp],p]=-dp\), so \(\nabla^p p=0\); its restriction to the range is the projection connection \(p\,d\). The resulting full spin Dirac operator \(D_p\) preserves this range and its orthogonal complement. Outside \(K\) it is the common homogeneous operator \(D_\infty\). Its principal symbol is \(ic(\xi)\), with the chirality fixed in Lemma 6.24 of the index lesson.

Every invariant metric on a connected Lie group is complete. One elementary verification is to cover a small buffered identity ball by finitely many still smaller balls and translate this cover along a metric path. A finite-length path crosses only finitely many such buffers; a Cauchy path tail stays in a translated compact coordinate buffer and converges. The Hopf–Rinow argument then makes each closed metric ball compact. Curvature, a positive injectivity buffer and all metric jets are uniform by translation. The coefficient jets of (63) are uniform too: they vanish off \(K\), and repeated derivatives along fundamental fields are bounded on each fixed compact enlargement. On a translated source chart they are exactly these derivatives at its translated base point. The circle product retains these bounds and the finite-overlap bounds.

Local elliptic estimates imply that an \(L^2\) distributional deficiency vector is locally smooth. Choose source cutoffs \(\eta_R\), tending to one and satisfying \(\|d\eta_R\|_\infty\le C/R\). If \((D_p\pm i)w=0\), integration by parts against \(\eta_R^2w\), justified first on compact buffers, gives \[ \|\eta_Rw\|_2^2 \le \frac{C}{R}\|\eta_Rw\|_2\|w\|_2. \] Letting \(R\) tend to infinity shows \(w=0\). This proves essential self-adjointness. The energy identity for a moving spatial cutoff uses \(\|[D_p,\eta]\|=\|c(d\eta)\|\le\|d\eta\|_\infty\). Choosing its level sets to recede with unit speed makes the exterior energy nonincreasing. A solution initially supported in a set therefore stays in its \(|s|\)-neighbourhood at wave time \(s\). Approximation by smooth data proves this for the full unitary wave group. The same estimate applied to the difference of two wave solutions proves equality in any causal region where their coefficients agree.

The metric volume on \(H\) is right Haar. If the convolution realization uses left Haar, the change of realization is multiplication by \(\Delta_H^{-1/2}\), since \(dh_R=\Delta_H^{-1}dh_L\). This is a unitary between the two \(L^2\) spaces, preserves support and has value one at the unit. Its logarithmic source derivatives are constants fixed by the modular character. Thus all estimates and the unit diagonal density remain valid for nonunimodular \(H\).

Here are the algebra and smoothing details. The wave group maps a smooth compact test kernel to one with compact relative group support: finite speed enlarges that support by a fixed compact metric ball. Source energy estimates preserve every Sobolev order, and differentiation with respect to a parameter on a compact base set uses the differentiated wave equation and its finite-time Duhamel integral. It therefore preserves smooth test kernels and their adjoints. The regular norm is at most one. On a test kernel \(a\), \[ \|(e^{isD_p}-1)a\|\le |s|\,\|D_pa\|, \] and the adjoint estimate gives strict continuity. These double centralizers define the wave multipliers; the faithful direct sum of regular representations gives their stated norm bounds and group identities.

Use the coefficient algebra \(\mathcal B=B^+\rtimes H\), not the scalar unitization \(A^+\). Compactly supported Fourier integrals of the wave group are its multipliers. If the spectral function is Schwartz, then \(D_p^j f(D_p)\) is bounded for every \(j\). Uniform elliptic estimates and local Sobolev embedding give a smooth kernel with all source derivatives bounded. Its relative group support is compact by finite speed. Off a fixed compact enlargement of \(K\) it is exactly the kernel of \(f(D_\infty)\), by equality in causal regions. The latter is a smooth compact kernel in \(C^*(H)\); the difference is a smooth compact kernel in \(A\). Hence \(f(D_p)\in\mathcal B\). These Schwartz functions are uniformly dense in \(C_0(\mathbb R)\), so the assertion holds for that whole functional calculus. It is nondegenerate: for \(f_n(z)=(1+z^2/n^2)^{-1}\), the bound \(\|(1-f_n(D_p))a\|\le n^{-2}\|D_p^2a\|\) on the test core proves strict convergence to one. This also supplies the regular functional calculus on the coefficient module.

For the relative support assertion, a wave kernel between two source points depends only on coefficients within the wave-time neighbourhood of those points. If such a region misses the pullback of \(K\), the two kernels agree. At the units all possibly contributing base points therefore lie in \(H_RK\), for a fixed compact ball \(H_R\subset H\); off-diagonal support has the same bound with a larger fixed \(R\). The image of \(H_R\times K\) under the action is compact. Local finiteness gives \(\mu(H_RK)<\infty\). No estimate of \(\mu(V)\) is used. The circle product changes this set only to its product with a compact circle. \(\square\)

Proposition 8.20 (an exact finite propagation relative index matrix). Under Lemma 8.19's hypotheses with even source dimension, let \(E_i=\operatorname{ran}p_i\), and let \(\alpha\) be the difference of their graded Dirac symbol classes. There are idempotents \(e_i(t)\) with \(e_0(t)-e_1(t)\) a smooth compact arrow kernel such that \[ \tau_{\Lambda*}(\operatorname{Ind}_a\alpha) =\int_V\operatorname{str}\!\left( p_0r_t(D_{p_0})^2-p_1r_t(D_{p_1})^2 \right)(1_x)\,d\mu(x),\qquad t>0. \tag{64} \] The integrand is supported in one fixed compact set, independent of \(t\). It is not the difference of two separately integrated infinite heat traces.

Proof. Choose an even \(\chi\in C_c^\infty((-\delta,\delta))\), with \(0\le\chi\le1\) and \(\chi=1\) on \([-\delta_0,\delta_0]\), \(0<\delta_0<\delta\). Define \[ \begin{split} \rho_t(s)&=a_t\chi(s)(4\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-s^2/(4t)}, & a_t^{-1}&=\int_{\mathbb R}\chi(s)(4\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-s^2/(4t)}\,ds,\\ r_t(z)&=\int_{\mathbb R}\rho_t(s)e^{isz}\,ds, & q_t(z)&=\frac{1-r_t(z)}z . \end{split} \tag{65} \] Normalization is essential: \(r_t(0)=1\), so \(q_t\) extends smoothly and oddly at zero. The even real function \(r_t\) is Schwartz. The Fourier distribution of \(q_t\) is a constant multiple of the primitive of \(\delta_{\{0\}}-\rho_t\), where \(\delta_{\{0\}}\) is the point mass at zero. Its total integral is zero, so the primitive can be chosen with support in \([-\delta,\delta]\). Consequently \(q_t(D_p)\) has propagation at most \(\delta\). It has order \(-1\): away from bounded spectral frequency it is \(D_p^{-1}\) modulo a smoothing function, and the local elliptic parametrix identifies this assertion in each source chart. Equivalently the compactly supported Fourier primitive has its only nonsmoothness at zero, which gives the inverse principal symbol.

Restrict to \(X=S^+\otimes E_i\) and \(Y=S^-\otimes E_i\). Put \(D=D_{p_i}^+:X\to Y\), \(Q=q_t(D_{p_i})^-:Y\to X\), \(S_0=r_t(D_{p_i})|_X\), and \(S_1=r_t(D_{p_i})|_Y\). Functional calculus gives \[ QD=1-S_0,\quad DQ=1-S_1,\quad DS_0=S_1D,\quad QS_1=S_0Q. \] The following matrix is bounded, despite the unbounded \(D\): \[ e_i(t)= \begin{pmatrix} S_0^2&S_0(1+S_0)Q\\ S_1D&1-S_1^2 \end{pmatrix}. \tag{66} \] Indeed its nonconstant entries are Schwartz functions of the full \(D_{p_i}\). The four displayed relations prove \(e_i(t)^2=e_i(t)\) by direct multiplication; for example the upper-left entry is \(S_0^4+S_0^2(1+S_0)(1-S_0)=S_0^2\). Extend this matrix by zero on the source coefficient complement and by identity on the target complement. Then both matrices act on the same finite trivial graded bundle. Each differs from \(e_{\rm ref}=\operatorname{diag}(0,I)\) by an element of \(M_{2N}(\mathcal B)\). Its nonconstant entries have propagation at most \(3\delta\). Equality of the two coefficient systems in causal regions shows that their difference is a smooth compact arrow kernel, supported in a fixed compact group ball and over, for example, \(H_{6\delta}K\). Enlarge the ball slightly if coordinate cutoffs are used.

We verify that the matrices give the actual symbol index. Put \(G=(1+D_{p_i}^2)^{-1/2}\). Conjugation on the source by \(G^{-r}\), \(0\le r\le1\), changes the two off-diagonal entries to \[ G^{-r}S_0(1+S_0)Q,\qquad S_1DG^r \] and leaves the diagonal entries fixed. The scalar functions in these entries are Schwartz times a polynomial weight; they are norm continuous in \(r\). Their kernels remain in \(\mathcal B\), with relative difference in \(A\): compact Fourier approximation of a Schwartz function has this property, and functional calculus gives norm convergence. At \(r=1\) the formula is the bounded-parametrix index matrix for \[ T=DG:X\to Y,\qquad Q'=G^{-1}Q:Y\to X. \] Their defects are \(S_0,S_1\), and their principal symbols are the normalized Dirac symbol and its inverse. On coefficient complements set \(T=Q'=I\). The elementary Fredholm boundary construction of the Hilbert-module lesson therefore identifies \([e_i-e_{\rm ref}]\) with this symbol index in \(K_0(\mathcal B)\). Varying \(t\) gives the same class by the same norm continuous formulas.

This absolute coefficient algebra is only an intermediate device. Exactness and its constant splitting give \[ 0\longrightarrow A\longrightarrow\mathcal B \longrightarrow C^*(H)\longrightarrow0. \tag{67} \] Both matrices have the same image \(e_\infty(t)\) in the quotient. For any idempotents \(e,f\) with \(e-f\in M_n(A)\), set \[ J_f=\begin{pmatrix}f&1-f\\1-f&f\end{pmatrix}, \qquad \widetilde e=J_f\operatorname{diag}(e,1-f)J_f. \tag{68} \] One has \(J_f^2=I\), and \(J_f\operatorname{diag}(f,1-f)J_f=\operatorname{diag}(I,0)\). Thus \(\widetilde e-\operatorname{diag}(I,0)\in M_{2n}(A)\) defines a genuine relative class \([e:f]\in K_0(A)\), even if \(f\) is not a scalar idempotent. Direct sums, conjugations and continuous idempotent homotopies show that it maps to \([e]-[f]\) in \(K_0(\mathcal B)\). The split sequence (67) makes this inclusion injective. Naturality of the bounded symbol construction, with the common exterior bundle trivialization retained, consequently identifies \([e_0(t):e_1(t)]=\operatorname{Ind}_a\alpha\). It is not necessary to invert or discard an infinite reference trace.

The invariant transverse measure makes the weight of Theorem 7.10 of the transverse-measure lesson a trace. Lemma 7.9 there places every smooth compact arrow kernel in its linear trace ideal. Hence \(e_0-e_1\) has finite absolute trace in the measured algebra. This ideal is preserved by bounded multipliers, and cyclicity gives \[ \tau(\widetilde e-\operatorname{diag}(I,0)) =\tau(e_0-e_1). \] The trace pairing of a finite-trace relative idempotent is this number: replacing its range by the orthogonal range projection, or applying the usual idempotent-to-projection homotopy, preserves the value by cyclicity on this ideal. This is the same normalization used for the Fredholm boundary index. The two diagonal entries of (66) now give exactly the supertrace in (64). The compact support and diagonal formula justify that integral absolutely. \(\square\)

Theorem 8.21 (the relative measured formula in even rank). If \(d\) is even, every \(\alpha\in K_c^0(F^*)\) satisfies \[ \tau_{\Lambda*}(\operatorname{Ind}_a\alpha) =\epsilon_d\langle\pi_!\operatorname{ch}(\alpha),[C]\rangle, \qquad \epsilon_d=(-1)^{d(d+1)/2}. \tag{69} \] All forms paired with the current have compact base support. The same theorem holds for the even-dimensional product source fibres \(H\times S^1\), with the circle pair groupoid and compact support in \(V\).

Proof. We first compute on the relative Dirac classes of Proposition 8.20. Integration by parts in (65) gives, for every fixed integer \(j\ge0\), \[ \sup_{z\in\mathbb R}(1+z^2)^j |r_t(z)^2-e^{-2tz^2}| \le C_jt^{-M_j}e^{-c/t},\qquad 0<t\le1, \tag{70} \] for some \(c>0\). To verify the estimate, subtract the uncut normalized Gaussian. Its removed tails and every fixed derivative have \(L^1\) norm at most a polynomial in \(t^{-1}\) times \(e^{-\delta_0^2/(8t)}\); the same bound holds for \(a_t-1\). Multiplication by \(z^m\) is integration by parts in \(s\). For the square, subtract the convolution of the uncut Gaussians and use the \(L^1\) convolution inequality for each fixed derivative. Reducing \(c\) absorbs the finite polynomial factors. This proves (70), including its polynomial spectral weights.

Uniform source elliptic estimates give a diagonal estimate \[ |f(D_p)(1_x)|\le C_j \sup_z(1+z^2)^j|f(z)|,\qquad j>d/2. \tag{71} \] In detail, evaluation on a fixed unit chart is bounded on \(W^j\), uniformly in \(x\); its dual point distribution is bounded in \(W^{-j}\). The all-real spectral Sobolev comparison follows from the integer elliptic estimates, interpolation and duality exactly as in Lemma 6.7 and Theorem 6.8 of the index lesson, using Lemma 8.19's uniform source jets and localization. Pairing the two point distributions with \((1+D_p^2)^{j/2}f(D_p)(1+D_p^2)^{j/2}\) gives (71). Larger \(j\) treats kernel derivatives. Applying it to (70) bounds the diagonal error by \(Ct^{-M}e^{-c/t}\).

We also check the use of the local heat coefficient on these noncompact source covers. The radial transport recursion and Clifford degree calculation in Lemmas 6.24–6.25 and Theorem 6.26 of the index lesson use finitely many jets in a buffered source chart. Lemma 8.19 supplies bounds for each required jet, the inverse metric, the density and the finite-overlap partition on every such chart. The cut-off heat parametrix has compact relative group support. Its residual Taylor remainder and the separated-cutoff remainder have the same uniform Sobolev norm bounds as in Theorem 6.12 there, by the Fourier–Schur and row/column argument of Lemma 8.15. Increasing the finite recursion order gives any prescribed positive remainder power. Duhamel's remainder estimate uses the contraction bound of the self-adjoint heat semigroup and those Sobolev bounds; it has no integration over the unit space. It therefore proves the actual local expansion uniformly here. With the stated chirality and curvature convention, its supertrace density is \[ \operatorname{str}\bigl(p_i e^{-sD_{p_i}^2}\bigr)(1_x) =[\widehat A(F)\operatorname{ch}(E_i)]_d(x)+O(s). \tag{72} \] All negative powers cancel pointwise by the full-word Clifford supertrace. This verification extends the local calculation; it does not assume that either heat trace over \(V\) is finite.

Let \(K'=H_{6\delta}K\) contain the support in (64). It is fixed and has finite unit measure. Equations (70)–(71) show that replacing the wave-cutoff diagonal by the heat diagonal on \(K'\) changes the integral by at most \(C\mu(K')t^{-M}e^{-c/t}\). Equation (72), at \(s=2t\), then shows that its limit is \[ \langle\widehat A(F) (\operatorname{ch}(E_0)-\operatorname{ch}(E_1)),[C]\rangle. \tag{73} \] The characteristic difference vanishes off \(K\); its integral over \(K'\) is its full current pairing. The left side of (64) is independent of \(t\), so (73) is its value.

The fundamental frame makes \(F\) a trivial oriented spin bundle, with trivial determinant line. Chern–Weil transgression from its connection to a flat trivial connection makes \(\widehat A(F)-1\) exact. Multiplying its transgression by the closed compactly supported character difference gives a compactly supported primitive. Closedness of \(C\) therefore replaces \(\widehat A(F)\) by \(1\) in (73). This step uses compact support of the difference, even though the transgression itself need not have compact support.

Every class of \(K_c^0(V\times\mathbb R^{2\ell})\) is the integral spin Thom image of a class in \(K_0(B)\). This is stable Bott periodicity with coefficients \(B\); it applies to all of a noncompact \(V\) and does not require a finite cell decomposition. Lemma 8.19 supplies relative projection representatives for each such class. The projection connection Dirac symbol is that Thom representative, and \(\pi_!\operatorname{ch}(\alpha)=(-1)^\ell\widehat A(F)^{-1} (\operatorname{ch}(E_0)-\operatorname{ch}(E_1))\), with the sign computed in Theorem 6.29 of the index lesson. Since \(\epsilon_{2\ell}=(-1)^\ell\), (73) is (69) for the entire integral symbol lattice, including torsion.

For the circle product the source fibres are \(H\times S^1\). The same energy, local Sobolev and relative kernel arguments hold by Lemma 8.19, and the unit trace is \(\tau_\Lambda\otimes\operatorname{Tr}\). The tangent frame, including the positive circle field, is again trivial. Even Bott periodicity now has coefficient algebra \(C_0(V\times S^1)\). Relative projection representatives are constant outside a compact subset of \(V\times S^1\), and all the preceding estimates apply. The compact-base product calculus and its full relative symbol boundary are obtained by the same local proof as Lemma 8.18, independently of any solvable parameter deformation. This proves its measured assertion in the stated product scope. Rank zero is simply the trace of the relative coefficient projection, and satisfies (69) directly. \(\square\)

Proposition 8.22 (the compact-support circle product). Let \(d>0\), with \(V\) possibly noncompact, and let \(\kappa\) be the circle class of (36) in the index lesson. For every \(\alpha\in K_c^0(F^*)\), \[ \tau_{\Lambda,\mathrm{product}*} (\operatorname{Ind}_a(\alpha\boxtimes\kappa)) =-\tau_{\Lambda*}(\operatorname{Ind}_a\alpha). \tag{74} \] The product algebra is \(A\otimes\mathcal K(L^2(S^1))\). Its exterior reference operator is genuinely invertible; ellipticity alone on the noncompact base would not suffice for this assertion.

Proof. Use Lemma 8.18 to represent \(\alpha\) by a unitary sphere symbol \(u=I\) off \(K\) and \(P_0=I+\operatorname{Op}(u-I)\). Its inverse defects are in \(A\). The smooth compact algebra lies in the finite trace ideal by the factorization of Lemma 7.9 in the transverse-measure lesson. Consequently \(A\) is contained in the norm closure of the finite-trace ideal in the measured algebra. Applying the random-operator Fredholm theorem of Proposition 6.28 of the index lesson gives \[ \tau_{\Lambda*}(\operatorname{Ind}_a\alpha) =\tau_\Lambda(\ker P_0)-\tau_\Lambda(\ker P_0^*), \] with both dimensions finite. This use of the Fredholm theorem needs no finite heat trace: a parametrix modulo the trace-compact ideal is exactly its hypothesis. For example a small-norm approximation of its defects by finite-trace operators bounds each kernel projection by a finite-trace spectral projection. The finite module boundary index and the measured Fredholm boundary agree by the same explicit matrix map as in that proposition.

Let \(H_1=1+\Delta\) be the homogeneous connection-Laplacian operator on the full first coefficient bundle; the trivial bundle representation makes the same choice possible in source and target. Its all-real powers have the Sobolev and multiplier calculus used here. One can verify its resolvent algebra membership by the complete-metric wave equation for \(\sqrt{\Delta}\): the scalar energy proof gives finite speed, compact Fourier Schwartz functions give smooth compact group kernels, and uniform functional approximation gives \((1+\Delta)^{-1}\in C^*(H)\). The local elliptic estimates then give integer powers, interpolation and duality give real powers, and the parametrix expansion gives their stated principal symbols, as in the Hilbert-module lesson's Section 6. Put \(P=P_0H_1^{1/2}\). Uniform elliptic graph estimates give the unique closed realization on \(W^1\). The order \(-1\) parametrix gives the maximal-domain assertion: if \(Pv\in L^2\) distributionally, it first gives \(v\in W^1\), and then the graph estimate. Smooth compact sections are dense there. The same holds for the adjoint. On \(\ker P_0\), elliptic regularity bounds all Sobolev norms by the \(L^2\) norm, so \(H_1^{1/2}\) and its inverse give bounded equivariant identifications of the source kernels. The distributional identity \(P^*=H_1^{1/2}P_0^*\), and injectivity on \(W^{-1}\), identify the adjoint kernels. Thus \(P\) has the same two finite measured dimensions as \(P_0\).

On the circle use \(Q_0=P_+M_{e^{i\theta}}P_++P_-\), with \(P_+\) the modes \(n\ge0\), and \(Q=Q_0H_2^{1/2}\), \(H_2=1-\partial_\theta^2\). It has no source kernel and its adjoint kernel is the constant line. Form \[ A_1=\begin{pmatrix}0&P^*\\P&0\end{pmatrix},\quad A_2=\begin{pmatrix}0&Q^*\\Q&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \mathcal D=A_1\otimes1+\Gamma_1\otimes A_2, \quad \Gamma_j=\operatorname{diag}(1,-1). \tag{75} \] The positive squares of the separate factors strongly commute. On joint bounded spectral cuts the two odd summands anticommute, and \[ \mathcal D^2=A_1^2\otimes1+1\otimes A_2^2,\qquad \|\mathcal Dv\|^2=\|(A_1\otimes1)v\|^2+\|(1\otimes A_2)v\|^2. \] The cuts exhaust their intersected first-order domain. The bounded resolvents \((\mathcal D\mp i)(1+A_1^2\otimes1+1\otimes A_2^2)^{-1}\) prove self-adjointness on that domain, as in the explicit argument in Proposition 6.36 of the index lesson. No tensor-domain assertion is being inferred just from the formal square.

Put \(H=H_1\otimes1+1\otimes H_2\) on this graded product and \(T=\mathcal D H^{-1/2}\). The joint-cone proof of Lemma 6.35 there applies to the current uniform source seminorms: where \(|\xi|\ge c_\delta(|\xi|^2+\eta^2)^{1/2}\), separate first-factor symbol derivatives are joint symbol derivatives. Off a slightly larger cone, integration by parts in the intermediate first coordinate gives arbitrary negative joint order. The bounded-frequency part is smoothing in both factors. Compact first-factor remainders are approximated by smooth compact kernels and have the same assertion on this cone. Finally its complement contributes norm at most \(\|B_1\|\sqrt{2\delta}\), where \(B_1=A_1H_1^{-1/2}\). Interchanging the factors proves the second term. Thus \[ T=(B_1\otimes1)\sqrt Z+(\Gamma_1\otimes B_2)\sqrt{1-Z}, \qquad Z=(H_1\otimes1)H^{-1}, \] lies in the completed product order-zero calculus. The continuous principal odd map is \[ s(\xi,\eta)= \frac{a_1(\xi)\otimes1+\Gamma_1\otimes a_2(\eta)} {\sqrt{|\xi|^2+\eta^2}}, \tag{76} \] where \(a_1\) is \(|\xi|\) times the graded unitary matrix of \(u\), and \(a_2\) is \(|\eta|\) times the graded circle symbol. Each is zero at its own origin. The anticommuting square gives \(s^2=1\) off the joint zero section. At either axis the vanishing numerator factor supplies continuity. Uniform smooth approximation on its joint sphere preserves invertibility and its relative class.

We spell out the exterior Fredholm check. Work first in the product calculus over \(\mathcal B=B^+\rtimes H\). All coefficients and their source jets extend to the added base point as their homogeneous values. Lemma 8.18's localization and quotient-norm proof gives its exact symbol quotient as well as the compact ideal \(\mathcal B\otimes\mathcal K\). Evaluation at base infinity maps it onto the homogeneous product calculus. The image \(P_\infty=H_1^{1/2}\) is invertible, and the image \(\mathcal D_\infty\) satisfies \[ \mathcal D_\infty^2=H_1\otimes1+1\otimes A_2^2\ge1. \] Its graph norm is equivalent to the product \(W^1\) norm by the separate elliptic estimates. Therefore \(T_\infty=\mathcal D_\infty H^{-1/2}\) is a bounded invertible operator on the product Hilbert space. It belongs to the homogeneous calculus closure; the faithful regular representation and spectral permanence of a unital C*-subalgebra put its inverse there too.

Choose a product inverse-symbol parametrix \(R_0\) for \(T\). Its two defects are in \(\mathcal B\otimes\mathcal K\). In the exterior calculus, \(T_\infty^{-1}-R_{0,\infty}\) has zero principal symbol and hence belongs to \(C^*(H)\otimes\mathcal K\). Lift it by the constant coefficient splitting of (67) and add that lift to \(R_0\). The resulting \(R\) has \[ TR-1,\ RT-1\in \ker(\mathcal B\otimes\mathcal K\longrightarrow C^*(H)\otimes\mathcal K) =A\otimes\mathcal K. \tag{77} \] This proves actual Fredholmness over the required algebra, not merely over the algebra with a constant exterior coefficient.

Its relative symbol class is \(\alpha\boxtimes\kappa\). The tensor product of the two relative two-term complexes has odd map \(a_1\otimes1+\Gamma_1\otimes a_2\); cancellation of mixed terms makes it invertible wherever either complex is invertible. Radial normalization and smoothing of (76) preserve that class. On the exterior base set, the first complex is the identity complex and is contractible. Its actual invertible operator \(P_\infty\), and hence \(T_\infty\), supplies this exterior trivialization. More explicitly, the usual tensor symbol comparison first gives equality of the two boundary indices in \(K_0(\mathcal B\otimes\mathcal K)\); the exterior identity complex contributes zero, since its quantization above is invertible. The split version of (67), tensored with \(\mathcal K\), makes \(K_0(A\otimes\mathcal K)\) inject into this group. Equality there therefore proves equality of their compact-support indices. This also proves independence of the exterior inverse lift and the quantization by the elementary boundary homotopy. Keeping the exterior trivialization is essential in this comparison.

The finite-rank circle kernel proof in Proposition 6.36 gives the completed algebra \(A\otimes\mathcal K\) and trace \(\tau_\Lambda\otimes\operatorname{Tr}\) here too. It uses finite matrices over \(A\), squared-kernel Fubini and increasing circle projections; it has no compact-base assumption. The circle constant projection has kernel \(1/(2\pi)\) and trace one. The dense finite-trace ideal and (77) therefore make \(T^+\) trace Fredholm.

Finally \(H^{1/2}\) gives a bounded equivariant isomorphism between \(\ker T^+\) and \(\ker\mathcal D^+\), by the elliptic graph estimate. The adjoint identity \((T^+)^*=H^{-1/2}\mathcal D^-\) on distributions, injectivity of \(H^{-1/2}:W^{-1}\to L^2\), and the maximal-domain assertion identify the adjoint kernels. The nonnegative square in (75) forces \[ \ker\mathcal D^+=(\ker P^*)\otimes\mathbb C1,\qquad \ker\mathcal D^-=(\ker P)\otimes\mathbb C1. \] Their product trace is the reversed difference of the two original finite dimensions. This proves (74). \(\square\)

Theorem 8.23 (the noncompact measured formula and entire trace image). For the hypotheses of this subsection, in every dimension, \[ \tau_{\Lambda*}(\operatorname{Ind}_a\alpha) =\epsilon_d\langle\pi_!\operatorname{ch}(\alpha),[C_\Lambda]\rangle \quad(\alpha\in K_c^0(F^*)), \tag{78} \] and \[ \tau_{\Lambda*}(K_0(A)) =\{\langle\operatorname{ch}(x),[C_\Lambda]\rangle: x\in K_c^{d\bmod2}(V)\}. \tag{79} \] Every value on the right is finite. Nonzero invariant transverse measure on noncompact \(V\) need not force \(H\) to be unimodular.

Proof. Even rank is Theorem 8.21. If \(d\) is odd, apply its even-rank product assertion to \(\alpha\boxtimes\kappa\). The explicit circle character computation (44)–(45) in the index lesson uses only a compact cotangent cutoff and therefore retains its compact-base support here: \[ \pi_{\mathrm{product}!}\operatorname{ch}(\alpha\boxtimes\kappa) =(-1)^d\pi_!\operatorname{ch}(\alpha)\wedge\frac{d\theta}{2\pi}. \] The product current is \(C_\Lambda\times[S^1]\), with the first leaf followed by the positive circle. Integration of \(d\theta/(2\pi)\) is one. Proposition 8.22 and \(\epsilon_{d+1}=(-1)^{d+1}\epsilon_d\) now give \[ -\tau_{\Lambda*}(\operatorname{Ind}_a\alpha) =\epsilon_{d+1}(-1)^d \langle\pi_!\operatorname{ch}(\alpha),[C_\Lambda]\rangle =-\epsilon_d\langle\pi_!\operatorname{ch}(\alpha),[C_\Lambda]\rangle. \] This proves (78). In rank zero the foliation algebra is \(C_0(V)\), and the diagonal trace on relative coefficient projections gives it directly.

Lemma 8.18 makes every \(K_0(A)\) class a full compact-support symbol index. Coefficient Bott periodicity identifies its entire symbol lattice with \(K_c^{d\bmod2}(V)\), exactly as in Corollary 8.17, now with coefficient algebra \(C_0(V)\). Even Bott character integral \((-1)^{d/2}\), the positive odd winding integral one and the fixed ordered product convention give a scalar generator with fibre integral \(+1\), after changing its sign if necessary. Its external product has fibre character \(\operatorname{ch}(x)\). Multiplication by the fixed \(\epsilon_d\) preserves the subgroup image. Equations (78) and surjectivity therefore give (79), integrally and with torsion retained. Smooth representatives are constant outside a compact set; their relative characters have compact support, so local finiteness of the current gives finite pairings.

The numerical assertion of the historical corollary is now proved in its noncompact as well as compact scope. Its measure-existence parenthesis still needs the explicit correction: Proposition 8.12 proves it for nonempty compact \(V\), whereas Example 8.13 refutes it for noncompact \(V\). These are exact scope statements, not an added compactness hypothesis on (79). Equality of the three geometric and topological maps and general assembly remain separate obligations. \(\square\)

The finite propagation method has a classical precedent in Gorokhovsky–Lott, Appendix A. Their paper's proper cocompact setting is not being used as a noncompact-base theorem here. The relative matrix, compact reachable set, normalized wave cutoff and exterior inverse checks above supply that extension in the present transformation-groupoid scope.

Figure 4. Lemma 8.18 through Theorem 8.23. The wave-time curve is a numerical sample of the declared smooth plateau cutoff, not a proved asymptotic bound; its reproducible source uses Simpson normalization. The group metric ball defines the reachable compact set and supplies no ambient metric on the base. Matrix (66), relative conjugation (68), estimates (70)–(72) and the two circle signs give the actual proof. Exercises 18–21 check the normalization, nonscalar reference, parity and affine-group example.
