With \(c=(\lambda-1)/n\), multiplication of the first two factors gives \[ \begin{pmatrix}1+nc&n\\c&1\end{pmatrix}. \] Multiplying on the right by \(\overline U_{-n/\lambda}\) makes the upper-right entry \(n-(1+nc)n/\lambda=0\); the lower-right entry is \(1-cn/\lambda=\lambda^{-1}\). The other entries are \(\lambda,c\), proving the identity. For \(F(g)=\langle\pi(g)w,w\rangle\), upper-unipotent invariance of \(w\) on each side gives \(F(\overline U_nU_c\overline U_{-n/\lambda})=F(U_c)\). Only \(c\to0\) is used; no boundedness of the outer parameters is assumed. Continuity then gives \(F(D_\lambda)=\|w\|^2\), with \(D_\lambda=\operatorname{diag}(\lambda,\lambda^{-1})\). Since \[ \|\pi(D_\lambda)w-w\|^2 =2\|w\|^2-2\operatorname{Re}F(D_\lambda)=0, \] \(w\) is diagonal-fixed. Now \(D_\lambda U_sD_\lambda^{-1}=U_{s/\lambda^2}\). Unitarity and diagonal invariance make the norm of \(\pi(U_s)w-w\) equal to that of \(\pi(U_{s/\lambda^2})w-w\), which tends to zero. Upper and lower elementary matrices generate \(L\), including its centre, so the vector is \(L\)-fixed.

Exercise 24 (advanced). In the proof of Theorem 8.26, justify uniform mixing on the moving family \(y=a_{-t}x\). Check the Haar density and the limiting order needed to replace the thickened averages by flat horocycle averages. What fails if one uses just ergodicity?

Solution. For fixed smooth compact group probability \(k_\varepsilon\), its pushforward densities \(h_y\) form a compact subset of \(L^2(X,m)\). Given \(\eta>0\), choose a finite \(\eta\)-net \(h_{y_i}\). Mixing controls each of their finitely many matrix coefficients. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the discrepancy for an arbitrary \(h_y\) by \(\|f\|_2\eta\); all densities have integral one, so the constant term is the same. This estimate is uniform in \(y\), and therefore applies to every \(a_{-t}x\). In the ordered \((v,r,s)\) chart the determinant of the Maurer–Cartan columns is \(e^r\). Multiplication by \(e^{-r}\) in (87) leaves exactly the probability \(\phi_\varepsilon(v,r)h(s)\,dv\,dr\,ds\). Conjugation sends \((v,r,s)\) to \((v/T,r,Ts)\); its coordinate Jacobian is one and its \(e^r\) Haar factor is unchanged. For each fixed \(\varepsilon\), first let \(T\to\infty\) using uniform mixing. The difference from the weighted orbit average is at most \(\omega_f(\varepsilon)\); next let \(\varepsilon\to0\). Finally approximate \(1_{[0,1]}\) by smooth integral-one \(h\) in \(L^1\), using the bound \(\|f\|_\infty\|h-1_{[0,1]}\|_1\) independent of \(T,x\). An almost-everywhere ergodic theorem alone leaves exceptional orbits uncontrolled and does not exclude another singular invariant probability. Uniform convergence permits integration against every invariant probability, giving unique ergodicity and then uniqueness of the transverse measure up to scale.

Exercise 25 (advanced). For a closed one-form \(\omega\) on \(X\), calculate \(C_m(\omega)\) from the left fundamental-field bracket. Explain how zero trace can coexist with a nonzero \(K_0(C(X)\rtimes_U\mathbb R)\), and why “the only transverse measure” needs a normalization.

Solution. For left fundamental fields the bracket is the negative Lie bracket, so \([A^\#,N^\#]=-N^\#\). Closedness gives \[ A^\#(\omega(N^\#))-N^\#(\omega(A^\#))+\omega(N^\#)=0. \] Invariance of Haar under both flows makes the integrals of the first two terms zero. Thus \(C_m(\omega)=0\). In dimension one the current pairs only with the closed degree-one component of an odd Chern character. The entire symbol-index/trace formula gives zero trace on all of \(K_0\). However the compact-support odd Bott class inserted in an oriented three-dimensional ball of \(X\) has nonzero top Chern integral; its extension by identity is a nonzero class in \(K^1(X)\). The actual analytic isomorphism sends it to a nonzero \(K_0\)-class. A trace pairing need not detect it. Multiplying \(C_m\) by any \(c>0\) gives another nonzero positive closed current and transverse measure. The unique probability normalization is \(m(X)=1\), using the density that makes \(N^\#\) unit; without it uniqueness means precisely positive scalar multiples.

Exercise 26 (basic). On \(\mathbb C^2\), graded by \(\operatorname{diag}(1,-1)\), take \[ F=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\qquad F'=\begin{pmatrix}0&-i\\i&0\end{pmatrix}. \] Compare the square of \((1-t)F+tF'\) with that of the bridge operator (97). Explain the reason for its normalization.

Solution. Both matrices are self-adjoint odd unitaries, and their anticommutator is zero. Thus the square of the straight segment is \(((1-t)^2+t^2)I\), which at \(t=1/2\) is \(I/2\). Here \(P=0\), so (97) gives \(F_\theta=\cos\theta F+\sin\theta F'\), whose square is \(I\) for every \(\theta\). More generally the anticommutator contributes \(\cos\theta\sin\theta H\); the outside fourth-root factors divide its square by \(1+\cos\theta\sin\theta P\) in the localized quotient. The endpoint factors are exactly one.

Exercise 27 (intermediate). Let \(J=\mathcal K(\ell^2(\mathbb N))\), \(u_n=v_n\) the projection onto the first \(n\) standard basis vectors, \(A_2=\mathbb C I\), and \(w=I\). The products \(u_jw\) lie in \(J\), and \((1-v_n)u_jw=0\) for every \(j\le n\). Show why this information alone does not give (92). Which extra term does the one-step lookahead control?

Solution. With \(b_n=(v_n-v_{n-1})^{1/2}\), we have \(b_n\) equal to the rank-one projection onto the \(n\)-th vector, and \[ b_n^2u_nw=b_n,\qquad b_nu_nb_nw=b_n. \] Both norms are one; the latter terms have no summable norm bound. Indeed their strict sum is \(I\), so its product with \(A_2\) is not compact. The condition \(j\le n\) at the \(n\)-th step gives no smallness for \((1-v_{n-1})u_nw\). Requiring \(j\le n+1\) at that step gives its bound at step \(n-1\), namely \(4\epsilon_n^2\); the current-step bound is \(\epsilon_n^2\). Their sum gives the exact \(5\epsilon_n^2\) in the proof. This example concerns the omitted approximation condition; it does not refute the separator theorem.

Exercise 28 (advanced). Let \(p\) be a rank-one projection on an infinite-dimensional Hilbert space \(H_1\), and let \(H_2\) be infinite-dimensional. Prove that \(p\otimes I_{H_2}\) is not compact. Explain how the first positive term in (101) remains valid when a compact error on \(E_{12}\) is tensored with the last module.

Solution. Choose a unit vector \(\xi\) in the range of \(p\), and an orthonormal sequence \(\eta_n\) in \(H_2\). The images of \(\xi\otimes\eta_n\) under \(p\otimes I\) are the same orthonormal sequence, so no subsequence converges. This excludes compactness. In the product proof the equality \(C_a=P_a+K_a\) holds before the last tensor, with \(P_a\ge0\) and \(K_a\in\mathcal K(E_{12})\). The separator includes \(\mathcal K(E_{12})\widehat\otimes1\) in \(A_1\), so \(M^{1/4}(K_a\widehat\otimes1)\) is compact on the final module. Hence its sandwiched contribution is compact. The remaining \(M^{1/4}(P_a\widehat\otimes1)M^{1/4}\) is positive. One keeps this positive contribution; tensoring alone supplied no compactness.

Exercise 29 (advanced). Let \(B=C([0,1])\), \(D=\{f\in B:f(0)=0\}\), \(E=B\) with trivial grading, and \(\phi:D\to\mathcal L(E)\) multiplication. Show that \((E,\phi,0)\) is a Kasparov cycle, but \(E^{\rm ess}=D\) has no orthogonal complement. Explain why the essential-module homotopy does not require such a complement.

Solution. The zero operator is odd, its commutators and adjoint defect vanish, and its square defect is \(-\phi(d)\in B=\mathcal K(E)\). Also \(\overline{DE}=D\). An adjointable projection on \(E=B\) is multiplication by a continuous projection-valued scalar function \(p:[0,1]\to\{0,1\}\). Its range equals \(D\) only if \(p(0)=0\) and \(p(t)=1\) for all \(t>0\), contradicting continuity. In the homotopy the module consists of continuous \(E\)-sections whose final value lies in \(D\). At the initial parameter its fibre is \(E\); at the final parameter it is \(D\). The connection is built by stabilization on this module, and its defects are tested against constant elements of \(D\). No projection onto \(D\) inside \(E\) is used.

Exercise 30 (introductory). On \(H=\ell^2(\mathbb N)\), let \(P_n\) project onto the first \(n\) basis vectors. Prove that \(P_n\to1\) strictly in \(M(\mathcal K(H))\), although \(\|1-P_n\|=1\). Explain why the infinite diagonal sums used in the multiplier swindle need not converge in norm.

Solution. For a rank-one operator \(\theta_{\xi,\eta}\), \[ \|(1-P_n)\theta_{\xi,\eta}\|\le\|(1-P_n)\xi\|\,\|\eta\|\to0, \qquad \|\theta_{\xi,\eta}(1-P_n)\|\le\|\xi\|\,\|(1-P_n)\eta\|\to0. \] Finite rank sums and their norm density in \(\mathcal K(H)\) prove the two strict convergence tests. The bound \(\|1-P_n\|\le1\) allows passage from finite ranks to every compact operator. A unit basis vector beyond the first \(n\) has unchanged norm under \(1-P_n\), so its norm is exactly one. The identity is the strict sum of its orthogonal rank-one diagonal terms; no norm sum has been asserted. The same compact tests define a multiplier diagonal on a countable Hilbert-module direct sum. This is the convergence used in Lemma 0.13 and Theorem 0.14.

Exercise 31 (intermediate). For \(a>0\), let \(S_a\) be the half-line operator in Lemma 0.16. For \(\lambda>0\), define \((Q_\lambda f)(t)=\sqrt\lambda f(\lambda t)\). Prove \[ Q_\lambda S_aQ_\lambda^*=S_{a\lambda}. \] Find the normalized cokernel vector of \(S_a\), and compute the index of \(S_a^*\). Explain the role of this adjoint in the positive physical Wiener–Hopf boundary.

Solution. A change of variable shows that \(Q_\lambda\) is unitary, with adjoint \(Q_{1/\lambda}\). In the Volterra term, substitute \(r=\lambda u\). Its coefficient becomes \(2a\lambda\), its exponential becomes \(e^{-a\lambda(t-u)}\), and its upper limit becomes \(t\). This gives the claimed conjugacy. The defect projection of \(S_a\) has kernel \(2ae^{-a(t+r)}\), so its range is the line generated by \[ e_a(t)=\sqrt{2a}\,e^{-at},\qquad \|e_a\|_2^2=\int_0^\infty2ae^{-2at}\,dt=1. \] The identity \(S_a^*S_a=1\) gives zero kernel for \(S_a\); \(S_aS_a^*=1-\theta_{e_a,e_a}\) gives its one-dimensional cokernel. Thus its index is \(-1\). The adjoint is onto and has kernel this line, so its index is \(+1\). Under the positive physical half-line convention, the lift of \(u_+\) is the coisometry, hence its boundary is positive. The intermediate Fourier compression in Lemma 0.16 instead uses \(\eta=-t\), explaining its opposite index. No index is changed by the dilation.

Exercise 32 (advanced). Let \(B=C_0(\mathbb R)\), choose a nonzero real \(\theta\in C_c(\mathbb R)\), and put \[ p(t)=\begin{pmatrix} \cos^2\theta(t)&\cos\theta(t)\sin\theta(t)\\ \cos\theta(t)\sin\theta(t)&\sin^2\theta(t) \end{pmatrix},\qquad p_0=\operatorname{diag}(1,0). \] Show that \(p-p_0\in M_2(B)\). Explain why \((pB^2,1,0)\) is not a scalar Kasparov cycle over \(B\), and why the relative two-representation cycle in Theorem 0.14 is legitimate. Compute its KK class.

Solution. The column \((\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\) has unit norm, so \(p\) is a projection. It equals \(p_0\) outside the compact support of \(\theta\), proving the compact-coefficient difference. However, the identity compact operator of \(pB^2\) would be \(p\in pM_2(B)p\). Its norm tends to one at infinity, so it does not belong to that compact algebra. The square defect for the zero operator is \(-p\); therefore the proposed individual cycle fails.

On \(B^2\oplus(B^2)^{\rm op}\), use representations \(p,p_0\) and the off-diagonal identity. Its square and adjoint defects vanish, and its commutator with a scalar representation has off-diagonal entries \(p-p_0\), which are compact. It is thus a legitimate relative cycle. Replace \(\theta\) by \(u\theta\), for \(0\le u\le1\). The resulting projection differences form a norm-continuous compact-coefficient homotopy. At zero both representations are \(p_0\), so the cycle is degenerate. Its KK class and its relative \(K_0(B)\)-class are zero. The general unitization argument in Theorem 0.19 uses legitimate projection cycles over \(B^+\), subtracts the scalar reference, and then restricts; this exercise explains why that order matters.

Exercise 33 (advanced). Put \(I=C([0,1],C_0(\mathbb R))\), with \((\beta_t f)(w,x)=f(w,x-wt)\), and let \(e_v\) be evaluation at \(v\). Prove that the constant coefficient inclusion \(c_v(b)(w,x)=b(x)\) is an ordinary KK inverse of \(e_v\), but need not be equivariant for \(\beta\) and \(\beta^v\). Explain why this does not prevent the formula \(d_C[c_v]t_I\) in Corollary 8.14a from being a crossed-evaluation inverse, and check both of its products.

Solution. Evaluation and the constant inclusion are *-homomorphisms, with \(e_vc_v=1\). The interval contraction \(f(w,x)\mapsto f((1-s)v+sw,x)\) gives \(c_ve_v\sim1_I\), uniformly in the \(C_0(\mathbb R)\)-norm. Thus their ordinary KK products are identities. On the other hand \[ \beta_t(c_v b)(w,x)=b(x-wt),\qquad c_v(\beta_t^v b)(w,x)=b(x-vt). \] For a nonzero compactly supported bump, choose \(w\ne v\) and \(t\ne0\) so these translations differ. Thus \(c_v\) is not equivariant in general and cannot simply be crossed as a coefficient homomorphism. The expression \(x=d_C[c_v]t_I\) is nevertheless a well-typed ordinary KK product: its successive algebras are \(C\rtimes\mathbb R,C,I,I\rtimes\mathbb R\). Naturality is used only for the equivariant map \(e_v\), giving \([e_{\mathbb R}]=d_I[e_v]t_C\). Associativity and the four real inverse identities yield \([e_{\mathbb R}]x=d_I[e_v][c_v]t_I=d_It_I=1\), and \(x[e_{\mathbb R}]=d_C[c_v][e_v]t_C=d_Ct_C=1\). No equivariance of \(c_v\) enters either calculation.

Exercise 34 (intermediate). In the conventions of Lemma 8.15a, derive the modular correction in (117) and the Lie bracket of the generators. Explain why setting the anchor to zero does not destroy ellipticity.

Solution. Let \(M\) be multiplication by \(\Delta_v^{-1/2}\). For a smooth compact function,

\[ M^{-1}(-iX_i^R)Mf=-iX_i^Rf+(i/2)(X_i^R\log\Delta_v)f. \]

This is (117). Also \(dh_R=\Delta_v^{-1}dh_L\) and left translation preserves \(dh_L\), so \(\operatorname{div}_{dh_R}X_i^R=-\kappa_i(v)\). Consequently the displayed correction is exactly half the divergence correction for \(-iX_i^R\), with the required sign. Right-invariant fields obey \([X_i^R,X_j^R]=-v\sum_k c_{ij}^kX_k^R\). Hence \[ [D_i,D_j]=iv\sum_kc_{ij}^kD_k, \qquad D^2=\sum_iD_i^2+iv\sum_{i<j,k}c_{ij}^kD_k\varepsilon_i\varepsilon_j. \] The extra term is first order. At zero the source group is still \(\mathbb R^d\), the operator is \(-i\sum\partial_i\varepsilon_i\), and its principal square is \(|p|^2\). A zero anchor concerns the map to the base tangent bundle, whereas this ellipticity is along the nonzero-dimensional source fibres.

Exercise 35 (advanced). Complete two checks that cannot be replaced by fibrewise statements. First, show how a principal parametrix proves interval-algebra membership of \((D+i)^{-1}\). Second, check the two-coordinate Bott product explicitly. Explain why neither check by itself proves a general vector-bundle KK Thom theorem.

Solution. Quantization of \((p\cdot\varepsilon)/|p|^2\) with a low-frequency cutoff and compact physical support gives \(Q\) of order \(-1\). The uniform composition calculus gives \((D+i)Q=1-S\) with \(S\) also of negative order, so both \(Q,S\) belong to the interval algebra. On the graph core the identity proves that \(Q\) maps into \(\operatorname{Dom}D\); closedness and the bounded right side extend this to the whole module. The regular module inverse \(R=(D+i)^{-1}\) therefore satisfies \(R=Q+RS\). The right side is an algebra element, proving the assertion with joint norm approximation. Separate fibrewise compactness would not prove this identity in the parameter algebra.

For coordinates \(x,y\), take \(F_1=x\varepsilon_1/\sqrt{1+x^2}\) and \(F_2=(x\varepsilon_1+y\varepsilon_2)/\sqrt{1+x^2+y^2}\). Their graded anticommutator is \(2x^2/(\sqrt{1+x^2}\sqrt{1+x^2+y^2})\), a nonnegative multiplier. For an old creation vector \(\xi(x)\), the connection errors are sums of \(x\varepsilon_1\xi(x)/\sqrt{1+x^2+y^2}\) and \[ (-1)^{|\xi|}\xi(x)y\varepsilon_2((1+x^2+y^2)^{-1/2}-(1+y^2)^{-1/2}). \] Their norms tend to zero on the joint complement of compact sets: use \(\xi(x)\to0\) for large \(|x|\), and the scalar limits for bounded \(x\) and large \(|y|\). Adjoint errors have the same bound. Definition 0.3 and Theorem 0.6 now give the old-first unreduced Clifford product class, with its product-operator homotopy. For the native odd–odd product, (104) instead puts the new coefficient first, so its full matrix numerator is \(x\sigma_y+y\sigma_x\), with grading \(\sigma_z\). The unitary \((\sigma_x+\sigma_y)/\sqrt2\) exchanges the two physical generators and reverses that grading; after this scalar coefficient contraction the native class is the negative of the positive geometric \(F_2\) class. This verifies \(s_2=-1\) by the actual finite module. Both arguments use a fixed global frame. The global bundle construction and both inverse products require the additional argument supplied in Lemmas 6.0a–b and Theorem 6.0c.

Exercise 36 (intermediate). For a metric real line, use the basis \(1,e\) of its exterior algebra. Write the matrices of \(a=e+\iota\), \(c=e-\iota\), \(D\) and \(Q\). Determine the kernel parity and spectral gap of \(Q^2\). Then check the rotation in (143), including which grading occurs in the second Clifford action. Explain why an orthogonal frame reversal does not twist the Gaussian kernel line.

Solution. In the indicated order, \[ a=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad c=\begin{pmatrix}0&-1\\1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad \Gamma=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix},\quad Q=\begin{pmatrix}0&-\partial_v+v\\\partial_v+v&0\end{pmatrix}. \] Here \(D=c\partial_v\). If \(L=-\partial_v^2+v^2\), then \(Q^2=\operatorname{diag}(L-1,L+1)\). The Hermite eigenvalues are \(2n\) on even degree and \(2n+2\) on odd degree. Its unique zero vector is \(\pi^{-1/4}e^{-v^2/2}\) in even degree, and the positive square-spectrum starts at two.

On the underlying ordinary tensor product, \(A=a\otimes1\) and \(B=\Gamma\otimes L_\varepsilon\). Hence \(A^2=B^2=1\), \(AB=-BA\), \([AB,A]=-2B\) and \([AB,B]=2A\). Differentiation of \(e^{-\theta AB/2}Ae^{\theta AB/2}\) and the analogous expression for \(B\) gives \(A\cos\theta+B\sin\theta\) and \(-A\sin\theta+B\cos\theta\). At \(\pi/2\), \(D+Bz\) becomes \(D-Az\), while the left Clifford action becomes \(B\). The graded notation for this second action is \(1\widehat\otimes L_\varepsilon\): adding another \(\Gamma\) to that graded tensor would insert the sign twice and destroy the required anticommutation.

A frame reversal sends \(v\) to \(-v\) and \(e\) to \(-e\). The exterior vacuum \(1\) and the radial Gaussian are fixed. Thus the kernel line is trivial even for a nonorientable real line bundle. Its target still retains the Clifford bundle twist; this observation does not give a spin-c structure to that line bundle.

Exercise 37 (advanced). Supply three global checks in the reverse product proof. Show that localized resolvents in (133) vanish at \(z\)-infinity uniformly down to \(t=0\), prove their norm continuity from the strong wave construction, and explain why the later representation contraction remains a cycle at \(s=0\). Finally derive the inverse proper-pullback identity and the order of the direct-sum inverse in (148).

Solution. Let \(R=(T_{t,z}\pm i)^{-1}\) and let \(\chi\) have support in \(|v|\le R_0\). From \(\|R\|,\|T_{t,z}R\|\le1\) and the potential-independent cutoff commutator, \(h=\chi R\xi\) satisfies (135). For \(|z|>2R_0+1\), its potential obeys \(|tv-z|\ge |z|-R_0\), so \[ \bigl((|z|-R_0)^2-r\bigr)\|h\|^2 \le C_\chi^2\|\xi\|^2. \] For the remaining bounded \(z\), use \(\|h\|\le\|\chi\|\|\xi\|\), enlarging the constant. This proves \(\|\chi R\|\le C/(1+|z|)\), with no lower bound on \(t\). The gradient part of (135) bounds the outputs in a fixed compact-support \(H^1\) ball, hence a relatively compact \(L^2\) set. At convergent parameters, both resolvents and their adjoints are strongly continuous by the Laplace wave formula. If \(K_n=\chi R_n\), then for any unit inputs \(\xi_n\) and any fixed \(\eta\), \(\langle(K_n-K_0)\xi_n,\eta\rangle=\langle\xi_n,(K_n^*-K_0^*)\eta\rangle\to0\). The differences of the output sets are relatively compact, so a norm-nonzero convergent output subsequence would contradict this weak limit. Thus \(\|K_n-K_0\|\to0\). Finite Clifford coefficients and compact base cutoffs give the stated module compactness.

For the representation \(u(z+sv)\), use a finite-rank spectral approximation of \(f(Q)\). On each of its finitely many fixed Hermite vectors, dominated convergence gives parameter continuity, and a compact \(v\)-cutoff makes vanishing at large \(z\) uniform in \(s\in[0,1]\). The omitted Hermite tails and spectral tail have arbitrarily small norms. Therefore \(u(z+sv)f(Q)\) is a compact operator field vanishing at target infinity on the whole interval. Its derivative commutator has \(s\partial_i u(z+sv)\); the same argument and the norm-integrable bound (132) apply. At \(s=0\) the derivative vanishes, and coefficients depend only on \(z\). The even Gaussian kernel then carries exactly the target identity action. Moving fibrewise centres alone would not prove these norm-continuity and compactness statements.

Write \(H=[h^*]\), \(J=[\widetilde h^*]\) and use (146). Multiplying \(Hb_{h^*E}=b_EJ\) first by \(d_E\) on the left and then by \(d_{h^*E}\) on the right gives \(d_EH=Jd_{h^*E}\), with all domains matched. If \(b_{E\oplus F}=b_Eb_F^{\mathrm{Cl}E}\), the inverse is \(d_F^{\mathrm{Cl}E}d_E\), because its two products cancel adjacent inverse pairs. Reversing that order is not even a composable pair of these KK morphisms. No interchange of odd Clifford blocks occurs.

Exercise 38 (intermediate). On the real line take the radius \(r=1\) compression in (152). For a function supported in \([-A,A]\), find one compact set containing the supports of its whole homotopy, and the smaller endpoint support. Check the derivative of \(q_1\) at zero and its inverse. Give a \(C_0(\mathbb R)\) function whose restriction to \((-1,1)\) is not in \(C_0((-1,1))\). Explain which map, and which actual cycle, prove that disk extension preserves the Thom class.

Solution. The function \(v\mapsto v/\sqrt{1+sv^2}\) is increasing, so the support at \(s\) is contained in \[ \left[-\frac{A}{\sqrt{1+sA^2}},\frac{A}{\sqrt{1+sA^2}}\right]\subset[-A,A]. \] At one this is the compact interval with radius \(A/\sqrt{1+A^2}<1\). The union of the supports over the parameter interval is therefore compact. The explicit inverse in (152), followed by the compact-level-set argument there, proves joint continuity across the moving boundary and uniform norm continuity; separate pointwise continuity would not suffice. Differentiation gives \(q_1'(v)=(1+v^2)^{-3/2}\), so \(q_1'(0)=1\). Its inverse on \((-1,1)\) is \(w/\sqrt{1-w^2}\).

The function \(f(x)=e^{-x^2}\) lies in \(C_0(\mathbb R)\), but its restriction tends to \(e^{-1}\) at both boundary ends of \((-1,1)\). For \(0<\epsilon<e^{-1}\), its \(\epsilon\)-level set is the whole open interval, which is not compact there. Thus restriction does not give the needed \(C_0\) homomorphism. Instead use the extension-by-zero homomorphism from the open interval to \(\mathbb R\). The full family \(\Phi\) of (152), tensored with the identity of \(C_1\), represents a homotopy on the standard interval module with operator zero: its square defect against a coefficient \(a\) is \(-\Phi(a)\), a compact endomorphism. Its zero endpoint is the identity and its one endpoint is compression followed by disk extension. Multiplication by the invertible Thom class proves (150); invertibility then permits the cancellation used for two nested disks. No improper restriction map or fibrewise-only homotopy is used.

Exercise 39 (advanced). Let \(i:\{1\}\hookrightarrow S^1\) be the point embedding and \(j:S^1\hookrightarrow S^1\times\mathbb R\) the zero-height embedding. Use the positive tangent to the circle for the first normal line and the increasing real coordinate for the second. Equip these trivial lines with their canonical spin-c structures. Construct normalized whole-bundle tubes and the composite tube. Write the actual ordered product multiplier and its positivity against the first factor. Explain why adding the two separately normalized multipliers does not give the required product cycle.

Solution. Identify the first normal coordinate with \(v\in\mathbb R\), measured in angle at \(1\), and put \[ \tau(v)=\exp\bigl(2i\arctan(v/2)\bigr),\qquad \sigma(y,w)=(y,w),\qquad \Omega(v,w)=\bigl(\tau(v),w\bigr). \] The angle derivative is \((1+v^2/4)^{-1}\), equal to one at zero; \(\tau\) is a diffeomorphism onto \(S^1\setminus\{-1\}\). The second tube is the identity of the trivial normal bundle, and the product connection makes its radial transport the identity. Thus \(\Omega\) is a normalized open tube of the point into the cylinder; its ordered normal coordinates are circle tangent first and vertical direction second.

Retain the two positive Clifford blocks, with \(\varepsilon_1^2=\varepsilon_2^2=1\) and \(\varepsilon_1\varepsilon_2=-\varepsilon_2\varepsilon_1\). The product representative on the sum module is \[ F(v,w)=\frac{v\varepsilon_1+w\varepsilon_2}{\sqrt{1+v^2+w^2}},\qquad \left\{\frac{v\varepsilon_1}{\sqrt{1+v^2}},F\right\} =\frac{2v^2}{\sqrt{1+v^2}\sqrt{1+v^2+w^2}}\ge0. \] For a compact old creation section, the old numerator divided by the joint normalizer and the difference from the new \(w\)-only normalization both tend to zero as \(|w|\to\infty\). Outside its compact old support, approximation makes the errors arbitrarily small. Their adjoints have the same property. These are the connection and positivity checks from (147), so this operator represents the actual product before extension along \(\Omega\). In an underlying ordinary tensor representation the second generator includes the old parity operator exactly once; that is what makes the two blocks anticommute.

The tempting sum \(G=v\varepsilon_1/\sqrt{1+v^2}+w\varepsilon_2/\sqrt{1+w^2}\) has \(G^2=v^2/(1+v^2)+w^2/(1+w^2)\). As both absolute coordinates tend to infinity, \(G^2-1\to1\). For the point's unit left coefficient this is a multiplier that does not vanish at infinity, hence is not compact on the finite spin-c section module. It fails the Kasparov square-defect condition. The joint normalization of \(F\) instead gives \(F^2-1=-1/(1+v^2+w^2)\), which vanishes at joint infinity. Finally (160) extends this checked product into the cylinder and proves the composition equality, preserving the chosen order and orientation.

Exercise 40 (advanced). On \(M=\mathbb RP^2\), put \(W=TM\), \(T=W\), and give \(L=W\oplus W\) its canonical complex spin-c structure. Choose a sufficiently large even-dimensional Euclidean embedding and construct its graph normal by Lemma6.0j. Determine the determinant line of that normal structure. Show that the orientation line \(\lambda=\det TM\) has nontrivial complexification \(H=\lambda_{\mathbb C}\), although \(H^{\otimes2}\) is trivial. What happens to the actual normal orientation module if the prescribed structure on \(L\) is twisted by \(H\)? Explain why its determinant line cannot detect this change.

Solution. Let \(Q=W\oplus W\). The given structure on \(L\) is exactly the canonical structure on \(Q\), so \(D_L=\det W_{\mathbb C}\). Lemma6.0j's full recovery gives \[ D_{E_j}\otimes\det W_{\mathbb C}\cong D_L, \qquad D_{E_j}\cong\underline{\mathbb C}. \] This conclusion uses the canonical double-bundle module; declaring its determinant contribution trivial in advance would give the wrong comparison.

To identify \(\lambda\), lift to the double cover \(S^2\to\mathbb RP^2\). Orient the tangent plane at \(x\in S^2\) by requiring its ordered basis together with the outward normal \(x\) to orient \(\mathbb R^3\). The antipodal map acts by \(-I\) in the ambient three-space, whose determinant is \(-1\). It carries the outward normal to the outward normal at \(-x\); hence it reverses the induced tangent orientation. Thus the orientation line is associated to the sign representation of this double cover. Its tensor square has transition \((-1)^2=1\) and is canonically trivial.

If \(H\) were trivial, a normalized nowhere-zero section would lift to a continuous map \(a:S^2\to S^1\) satisfying \(a(-x)=-a(x)\). Restrict to the equator parametrized by \(e^{it}\). Its continuous argument \(\theta(t)\) on an interval is obtained by subdividing into finitely many arcs on which a branch of argument exists and adjusting adjacent branches by integral multiples of \(2\pi\). The relation implies \(\theta(t+\pi)-\theta(t)=(2m+1)\pi\) with one integer \(m\), by continuity. Applying it twice gives equatorial winding \(2m+1\), which is odd. But this loop extends over the northern hemisphere through \(a\). Contracting the hemisphere radially gives a homotopy to a constant loop, whose winding is zero. Winding is invariant in this homotopy: at each sufficiently small parameter change a compact loop stays in argument neighbourhoods and its integer total change is continuous, hence constant; finitely many parameter neighbourhoods cover the interval. This contradicts the odd winding. Therefore \(H\) is nontrivial, while \(H^{\otimes2}\) is trivial.

Twisting the given structure replaces \(\mathscr M_{E_j}\) by \(\mathscr M_{E_j}\otimes H\). These modules are not isomorphic as graded Clifford bimodules. An isomorphism would tensor with the actual inverse Morita module and, by its two evaluation maps, give \(H\cong\underline{\mathbb C}\), contradicting what was just proved. Their determinant lines, however, differ by \(H^{\otimes2}\), which is trivial. They have the same determinant line and distinct full orientation data. The normal Thom multiplier remains the same local Clifford expression, but its transition module has changed. This is precisely the information the cancellation formula retains.

Exercise 41 (intermediate). Let \(i_s:S^1\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^2\), \(0\le s\le1\), be \(i_s(x)=x+(0,s)\). Use the outward radial normal, its trivial spin-c structure and a fixed \(0<\rho<1\). Write a normalized whole-bundle tube and the norm-continuous extension homomorphism of Lemma6.0g. For a function supported in \(S^1\times[-A,A]\), give one compact set containing all its image supports, separated from the moving tube boundary. Then stabilize by \(\mathbb R^2\), write the ordered product multiplier and explain the cancellation of the new Bott block.

Solution. Identify the normal bundle at every parameter with \(S^1\times\mathbb R\) by \(v\mapsto vx\). A normalized tube is \[ \tau_s(x,v)=\bigl(1+q_\rho(v)\bigr)x+(0,s), \qquad q_\rho(v)=\frac{v}{\sqrt{1+v^2/\rho^2}}. \] Its image is the annulus \(1-\rho<|z-(0,s)|<1+\rho\), because \(1+q_\rho(v)>0\). Its derivative in the normal coordinate at zero is \(x\), the specified unit normal. The map \((s,x,v)\mapsto(s,\tau_s(x,v))\) is an open embedding relative to the parameter interval: in the annulus, write \(r=|z-(0,s)|\), \(x=(z-(0,s))/r\), \(w=r-1\), and \(v=w/\sqrt{1-w^2/\rho^2}\). Thus the homomorphism is \[ \Theta(f)(s,z)= \begin{cases} f\!\left(\dfrac{z-(0,s)}{|z-(0,s)|}, \dfrac{|z-(0,s)|-1}{\sqrt{1-(|z-(0,s)|-1)^2/\rho^2}}\right), &\bigl||z-(0,s)|-1\bigr|<\rho,\\ 0,&\text{otherwise}. \end{cases} \] Let \(c=A/\sqrt{1+A^2/\rho^2}<\rho\). The supports for all parameters lie in the compact set \[ K_A=\{(s,z):0\le s\le1,\ 1-c\le|z-(0,s)|\le1+c\}. \] It is closed and bounded and is separated radially from each moving boundary by \(\rho-c>0\). On its open tube image the displayed inverse proves continuity. Outside that image, a compact level set of \(f\) has compact image strictly inside it, so the zero extension is continuous at the boundary as well. Its support stays in \(K_A\), and uniform continuity on a compact neighbourhood gives norm continuity in \(s\). Density and the bound \(\|\Theta(f)\|\le\|f\|\) give the assertion for all \(C_0\) functions. Tensoring with \(1_{C_1}\) gives the actual homomorphism used in Lemma6.0g. The standard interval module with zero operator represents its class, because against any coefficient its square defect is minus that coefficient, a compact module map. Multiplication by the fixed normal Thom class proves equality of the two endpoint embedding classes.

For the new even block \(w=(w_1,w_2)\), use \(\Omega_s(x,v,w)=(\tau_s(x,v),w)\). Retaining the old normal generator before the two new generators, the multiplier is \[ F(v,w)=\frac{v\varepsilon_0+w_1\varepsilon_1+w_2\varepsilon_2} {\sqrt{1+v^2+w_1^2+w_2^2}}. \] The three positive generators anticommute. Its square defect is \(-1/(1+v^2+|w|^2)\), and its anticommutator with the old normalized multiplier is \(2v^2/(\sqrt{1+v^2}\sqrt{1+v^2+|w|^2})\ge0\). For a compact old creation section the connection errors vanish at new infinity; its old tail is controlled by approximation, as in (147). Hence this is the actual ordered sum Thom product. Contract the last \(C_2\) factor by its canonical positive spinor module to obtain \((i_s)_!B_2^{C_0(\mathbb R^2)\widehat\otimes C_1}\). Compose with the even inverse \(A_2\) on that same coefficient algebra. The adjacent product \(B_2A_2=1\) gives \((i_s)_!\), by Lemma6.0h. The old odd generator has never been moved past an odd inverse: the new Bott class and its inverse are even after the specified contraction.

Exercise 42 (intermediate). Write both circles as \(\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\). On \(V=S^1_\theta\times S^1_y\), foliate by the circles with \(y\) fixed. Let \(M=S^1_x\) and let the smooth leaf-space map have the global lift \(f(x)=(0,mx)\), \(m\in\mathbb Z\). Use \(j(x)=(\cos2\pi x,\sin2\pi x)\), its outward radial normal, and the specified trivial spin-c structure on \(TM\oplus f^*\tau\). Give a global neighbourhood model for Lemma6.0l and an explicit étale replacement as in Lemma6.0m. Check its derivative, its ordered normal and its actual counting fibres. Finally replace \(mx\) by \(mx+c(s)\) for a smooth real function \(c\) on an interval. Explain precisely what proves equality of the two endpoint factorization classes.

Solution. Fix \(0<\epsilon<1/2\). The graph neighbourhood is \(H=S^1_x\times(-\epsilon,\epsilon)_\delta\), with transverse circle coordinate \(y=mx+\delta\), projection \(p(x,\delta)=x\), and section \(\delta=0\). The interval condition makes the difference \(y-mx\) unique whenever it lies in that interval. Its foliation is \(\ker(m\,dx+d\delta)\), where \(dx\) is the invariant circle one-form. In local real lifts this is exactly \(dy=0\); changing a lift adds an integer to \(y\) and preserves the one-form. Thus it is a genuine global foliated microbundle. Its normal quotient on the section is represented by \(\delta\), with the same trivial transverse line as \(f^*\tau\).

For \(0<\rho<1\) put \(N=S^1\times(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\times(-\rho,\rho)\), using the outward normal coordinate \(\eta\). Its local lift to \(V\times\mathbb R^2\) is \[ g(x,\delta,\eta)= \bigl(0,mx+\delta,(1+\eta)(\cos2\pi x,\sin2\pi x)\bigr). \tag{191} \] Its transverse map has coordinates \((y,z_1,z_2)\). In a local lift of \(x\), the determinant of its derivative, with columns ordered as \((x,\delta,\eta)\), is \[ \det\begin{pmatrix} m&1&0\\ -2\pi(1+\eta)\sin2\pi x&0&\cos2\pi x\\ 2\pi(1+\eta)\cos2\pi x&0&\sin2\pi x \end{pmatrix}=2\pi(1+\eta)>0. \tag{192} \] It is therefore étale. In fact this transverse map is injective onto its open image: the direction of the nonzero \(z\) determines \(x\), its length determines \(\eta\), and the unique small circle difference determines \(\delta\). The section \(k(x)=(x,0,0)\) has the ordered normal \((\eta,\delta)\), namely \(\nu_j\oplus f^*\tau\). Its orientation is the full module of Lemma6.0j constructed from the specified structure; a positive determinant for a different coordinate order is not used as a replacement for that module.

The holonomy groupoid of this product foliation is \(V\times_{S^1_y}V\). Indeed every leaf is a circle with identity transverse holonomy, so paths with the same endpoints define the same holonomy arrow. For a source unit \((\theta,y,z)\) of the product groupoid, an element of the principal counting fibre first requires a point of \(N\) with that transverse coordinate \((y,z)\). There is at most one such point by the preceding reconstruction. If it exists, there is exactly one arrow from \((\theta,y)\) to \((0,y)\). Thus each counting fibre is empty or a singleton. This conclusion uses the actual trivial holonomy, rather than just the numerical leaf dimension.

For the parameter family use the same \((x,\delta,\eta)\) domains and put \(y=mx+c(s)+\delta\). The vertical derivative determinant is unchanged. The normal structure on \(TM\oplus f_s^*\tau\) is the fixed specified structure pulled back over the interval. Lemma6.0n constructs the whole interval Hilbert module and gives its exact surjective endpoint evaluations; Theorem6.0o composes it with the whole normal Thom/tube cycle and the fixed Euclidean inverse. Its endpoints are the two factorization classes. This actual Kasparov homotopy proves their equality. An endpoint coincidence of leaf images, by itself, would not prove this conclusion.

Exercise 43 (advanced). Form the suspension \[ V=(\mathbb R_\theta\times\mathbb R_y)/ \bigl((\theta,y)\sim(\theta+1,2y)\bigr), \tag{193} \] with the foliation induced by the horizontal lines, and take the small transverse lift \(g:N=(-\epsilon,\epsilon)\to V\), \(g(y)=[0,y]\). At \(x_0=[0,0]\), determine the counting fibre of \(P_g\) and the regular source fibre of the holonomy groupoid. Write the map \(W_{x_0}\) for one short-plaque core vector. Verify directly that a rank-one module operator can act as a nonzero multiple of the identity on an infinite-dimensional counting fibre. Explain why this does not contradict Lemma6.0n.

Solution. The integer action is free and proper: on a compact set of \(\theta\)-coordinates only finitely many shifts can meet that set. Its quotient is therefore a smooth Hausdorff mapping torus, with the usual two overlapping interval charts in the \(\theta\) direction. The horizontal distribution is invariant because its derivative sends \(\partial_\theta\) to \(\partial_\theta\). The leaf of \(x_0\) is a circle. A positive one-turn path, lifted from \((0,y)\) to \((1,y)\), ends at \([0,y/2]\). Its transverse holonomy germ is \(y\mapsto y/2\); the \(k\)-turn germ is \(2^{-k}y\). These germs are distinct for every \(k\in\mathbb Z\). Consequently this leaf's holonomy covering is the real line, and the regular source fibre \(G_{x_0}\) is \(\mathbb R_t\), with range \([t,0]\). This follows directly from the definition of holonomy arrows: two lifted paths with the same endpoint differ by an integer winding, whose germ is identity only when that integer is zero.

Only \(g(0)\) lies on this leaf. Every winding gives a distinct principal lift over \(x_0\), so \(a^{-1}(x_0)=\{z_k:k\in\mathbb Z\}\), with \(z_k\) the \(k\)-turn arrow to \(g(0)\). The counting space is \(\ell^2(\mathbb Z)\), not the one-dimensional space obtained by forgetting the holonomy germs. Use the invariant positive longitudinal density \(dt\). Choose \(0<a<1/2\), \(b\in C_c^\infty((-a,a))\) with \(\int|b(t)|^2dt=1\), and a transverse cutoff \(\sigma\in C_c^\infty(N)\). Let \(\xi\) be the short-plaque source-anchor chart vector with coefficient \(b(-t)\sigma(y)\). Along this leaf, \(z_k\gamma_t^{-1}\) belongs to that chart precisely when \(|t-k|<a\); its short signed displacement is \(k-t\). The formula for \(W_x\) in Lemma6.0n therefore becomes \[ (W_{x_0}(\xi\otimes u))_k =\sigma(0)\int_{\mathbb R} b(k-t)u(t)\,dt. \tag{194} \] The row functions are translates supported in disjoint intervals \((k-a,k+a)\). Their squared norms equal one. Hence their Gram matrix is the identity, and the tensor image of \(\theta_{\xi,\xi}\) is \[ W_{x_0}(\theta_{\xi,\xi}\otimes1)W_{x_0}^{-1} =|\sigma(0)|^2\,1_{\ell^2(\mathbb Z)}. \tag{195} \] This is precisely the counting-fibre action of multiplication by \(|\sigma|^2\). For \(\sigma(0)\ne0\) it has infinite Hilbert-space rank and is not a Hilbert-space compact operator: the images of the orthonormal basis have fixed nonzero norm and no convergent subsequence.

The module operator is nonetheless the single rank-one operator \(\theta_{\xi,\xi}\), so is compact on \(\mathcal E_g\). Tensoring a Hilbert-module compact operator with an infinite-dimensional regular representation need not produce a Hilbert-space compact operator. Here the creation operator has infinitely many orthogonal rows, one for every genuine holonomy lift. The explicit calculation verifies both module compactness and the necessity of keeping those lifts; no finiteness of a holonomy counting fibre was assumed.

Exercise 44 (intermediate). On the cylinder \(X=S^1_\theta\times\mathbb R_s\), use the trivial Hermitian line with unitary connection \(\nabla=d+i\sin\theta\,ds+i\lambda\,d\theta\), \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\). Embed \(L=S^1\) by \(i(\theta)=(\theta,0)\), prescribe a normal spin-c structure, and use the whole normalized tube \[ \tau(\theta,v)=(\theta,q(v)),\qquad q(v)=\frac{v}{\sqrt{1+v^2}}. \tag{212} \] Compute the radial transport in Lemma6.0p. Show directly that it gives the onto even unitary between the two projection-formula modules, on the entire tube. Explain why neither a pullback homomorphism along the bundle projection nor a uniform bound on a connection derivative is needed. Retain an arbitrary full normal line twist in the calculation.

Solution. The path is \(t\mapsto(\theta,q(tv))\). Its angular coordinate is constant, so the \(i\lambda\,d\theta\) term does not enter its transport equation. With initial value one, that equation has solution \[ T_{\theta,v}=\exp\bigl(-i\sin\theta\,q(v)\bigr). \tag{213} \] Indeed its logarithmic derivative along the path is \(-i\sin\theta\,\partial_tq(tv)\), and integrating gives \(-i\sin\theta(q(v)-q(0))\). The formula is globally smooth and has norm one. The normal multiplier is \(F(v)=\varepsilon(v)/\sqrt{1+v^2}\) on the specified normal Thom module. Multiplication by \(T_{\theta,v}\) acts on the even coefficient line and commutes with that multiplier and all the coefficient actions.

The two completed modules have the same normal support space, with the coefficient fibre transported from \((\theta,0)\) to \((\theta,q(v))\). For compact core sections, pointwise multiplication by \(T\) preserves their inner product because \(\overline T T=1\). Its inverse is multiplication by \(\overline T\). Both maps preserve compact supports, so their images contain the opposite compact core; they extend to inverse onto isometries of the completed modules. The creation connections are exact, and the compact defects remain the localized Thom defects, tensored with a finite line. Both products therefore have precisely the operators in Lemma6.0p.

The tube is a diffeomorphism onto \(S^1\times(-1,1)\), so its essential open extension is legitimate. The base projection \(S^1\times\mathbb R\to S^1\) is nonproper: the pullback of the constant function one does not vanish at infinity. The calculation uses its bounded multiplier action, rather than that false \(C_0\) homomorphism. No derivative of \(T\) occurs in the bounded inner-product or operator-intertwining calculation. Smooth transport on finite compact parameter sets and the norm-one bound suffice. A normal twist stays in its separate module factor throughout, so its complete line, including phase transitions, survives the unitary.

Exercise 45 (advanced). Let \(M=S^1\), \(j(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\), and let \(f:M\to\{\mathrm{pt}\}\) have the stable orientation whose graph normal \(\nu_j\) has its outward positive frame. Let \(h:\{\mathrm{pt}\}\to M\) select \(\theta=0\), use \(u:\{\mathrm{pt}\}\hookrightarrow\mathbb R^2\), \(u=0\), and orient its graph normal by the ordered frame \((a,b,t)\), where \(a,b\) are the two new Euclidean directions and \(t\) is the positive circle tangent. These full normal modules determine the corresponding stable orientations by Lemma6.0v's recovery.

Both maps have odd parity. Compute the composed normal map into \(\mathbb R^2\oplus\mathbb R^2\), with the \(j\)-block first. Determine the grading of its recovered virtual rank-zero orientation and the scalar class \(h_!\# f_!\). Repeat after reversing the normal orientation of \(f\). Do not replace the two odd factors by an ungraded tensor product.

Solution. At \(\theta=0\), the tangent is \(t=(0,1)\) and the outward normal is \(\nu=(1,0)\). The two normal ranks are \(k_h=2-0+1=3\) and \(k_f=2-1+0=1\). Their ordered product has rank four and ordered frame \((a,b,t,\nu)\). The product étale map is the ordinary normal map of the circle times \(1_{\mathbb R^2}\). Thus the normal quotient map sends these four basis vectors, respectively, to \[ a\longmapsto(0,0,1,0),\quad b\longmapsto(0,0,0,1),\quad t\longmapsto(0,1,0,0),\quad \nu\longmapsto(1,0,0,0). \tag{214} \] Its matrix has determinant \(-1\): moving the new two-plane past the old two-plane has positive sign, whereas the old ordered frame \((t,\nu)\) reverses the standard \((x,y)\) orientation. This sign is the actual transported full normal orientation.

Here \(TL=0\) and \(T=0\), so there is no double-tangent factor. The cancellation in Lemma6.0v removes the canonical \(C_4\) Euclidean factor on both sides. A reversed real orientation gives the odd graded line. One can check the grading without a characteristic-class argument. An orientation-reversing orthogonal transformation is the product of a positive transformation and a reflection. The positive transformation has an even spin lift. Reflection is implemented in even Clifford rank by an odd Pin unit, up to that positive transformation. Multiplication by this odd unit identifies the resulting regular bimodule, by an even map, with the parity reversal of the canonical regular bimodule. The two finite Morita evaluations therefore leave the parity-reversed scalar line \(\Pi\mathbb C\), rather than \(\mathbb C\).

In the retained odd convention the two parity blocks are ordered \(C_1\widehat\otimes C_1=C_2\). The fixed \(\Lambda^*\mathbb C\) evaluation contracts them. The even triple cycles and wedge evaluations of Theorem6.0w identify this early contraction with contraction of the full ordered \(C_4\) normal module. The scalar Euclidean Thom/inverse identities then leave \[ h_!\# f_!=[\Pi\mathbb C,1,0]=-1 \quad\text{in }KK(\mathbb C,\mathbb C)=\mathbb Z. \tag{215} \] The last equality is the grading-inverse convention proved in Theorem0.7 and the scalar classification of Section0. This computation uses the two exact Euclidean inverse products; it assumes no Dirac-index comparison for the circle.

Reversing the one-dimensional normal orientation of \(f\) changes its positive frame to \(-\nu\). The composed determinant becomes \(+1\); the finite cancellation leaves the even scalar unit, and the product is \(+1\). Equivalently the two parity reversals cancel. Both cases have the same underlying virtual rank-zero bundle. Its stable orientation grading distinguishes the two classes, so the canonical even rank-zero unit cannot stand for both.

Exercise 46 (intermediate). On \(D=\mathbb R/2\pi\mathbb Z\), take \(Q=\{|\theta|\le\pi/2\}\) and its two-point boundary \(M\). Let \(0<\epsilon<\pi/4\), and give the two outward normals the coordinates \[ \tau_+(v)=\pi/2+q_\epsilon(v),\qquad \tau_-(v)=-\pi/2-q_\epsilon(v),\qquad q_\epsilon(v)=\frac{v}{\sqrt{1+v^2/\epsilon^2}}. \tag{236} \] Write the normal Thom unitary explicitly and construct its null-homotopy on the circle. Explain why the same argument fails for a single positively oriented point in this circle.

Solution. Put \(h(v)=v/\sqrt{1+v^2}\). On either collar the unitary is \(U(\tau_\pm(v))=\exp(\pi i(1+h(v)))\), and it is one elsewhere. The plus collar traversed in increasing \(\theta\) has its phase increase from zero to \(2\pi\). The minus collar traversed in that same circle direction has its phase decrease from \(2\pi\) to zero. The outgoing positive coordinate is \(v\), not increasing \(\theta\), at the minus point.

Define \(\Theta=0\) on the middle part of \(Q\), take \(\Theta=\pi(1+h(v))\) on each collar, and set \(\Theta=2\pi\) on the remaining outside arc. Its limits match at all four collar edges and at the circle identification. The bounded continuous function therefore defines the norm-continuous homotopy \(U_t=e^{it\Theta}\). Its norm modulus is at most \(2\pi|t-t'|\). This is the actual null class of Lemma 6.0y. Each of the two point classes separately has winding \(+1\) or \(-1\), while their signed sum is zero.

For a single positive point, cut the circle at an exterior point and follow a real phase continuously from zero. The collar increases that phase by \(2\pi\), and the unitary is constant on the rest of the circle. The ending phase is \(2\pi\), so it cannot be a single-valued continuous real function on the identified circle. The unitary has winding one. Winding is invariant under a continuous homotopy: subdivide a compact parameter square so each image lies in a circle arc with a continuous phase; changes between phase choices are integral multiples of \(2\pi\), locally constant in the parameter. Hence this unitary cannot have a null-homotopy. The separating hypothesis is exactly what allowed the two phase changes to cancel. \(\square\)

Exercise 47 (advanced). Let \(L,H\) be Hermitian complex lines over a compact smooth \(M\). Give \(W=L_{\mathbb R}\) its complex spin-c structure twisted by \(H\). Determine its full north/south spinor bundles, clutch bundle and sphere projection orientation. Check the normalization without discarding a two-torsion \(H\). Then perform the zero-rank calculation with the same line.

Solution. The exterior spin lift of a unitary line transition is \(\operatorname{diag}(1,g_L)\), as computed in Lemma 6.0j. The spinors are therefore \(S_W^+=H\) and \(S_W^-=L\otimes H\). Clifford multiplication from the positive to the negative part is \(1_H\otimes w\). Thus \(b_{W,H}\) is obtained by gluing \(\pi^*H\) in the north to \(\pi^*(L\otimes H)\) in the south using this full line-valued isometry. If \(b_{W,1}\) is the untwisted clutch bundle, the actual transition maps give \[ b_{W,H}\cong\pi^*H\otimes b_{W,1},\qquad n_!^H(1)=[b_{W,H}]-[\pi^*(L\otimes H)]. \tag{237} \] The inverse orientation of the projection has the tensor \(\pi^*H^*\). The full coefficient-transport theorem therefore gives \((\pi_!^H)_*(x)=(\pi_!^1)_*(x[\pi^*H^*])\). Applying Theorem 6.0ad and the projection formula yields, for every \(a\in K^0(M)\), \[ (\pi_!^H)_*(\pi^*a[b_{W,H}])=a,\qquad (\pi_!^H)_*(1)=0. \tag{238} \] These equations use \(H\otimes H^*\cong\mathbf1\), not a trivialization of \(H^{\otimes2}\). For example, the nontrivial two-torsion line on \(\mathbb RP^2\) proved in Exercise 40 has trivial square but is retained here: the north restriction of \(b_{W,H}\) is \(H\), whereas that of \(b_{W,1}\) is the trivial line. Their fibre restrictions alone would miss this difference. The inverse orientation cancels the actual \(H\).

In rank zero the sphere consists of \(M_+\sqcup M_-\). The Bott bundle is \((H,0)\), and the projection modules are the even \(H^*\) and the odd \(\Pi H^*\), respectively. Consequently \[ (\pi_!^H)_*(a_+,a_-)=H^*a_+-H^*a_-, \qquad(\pi_!^H)_*(H,0)=1. \tag{239} \] In particular its image of \((1,1)\) is zero. Assigning an even unit to both components would instead give the sum and would violate the boundary relation already for the interval. The retained zero-rank grading fixes that sign. \(\square\)

Exercise 48 (intermediate: the rank-zero orientation line). Give a compact manifold \(V\) its point foliation. Specify an arbitrary Hermitian line \(H\) as the rank-zero spin-c transition module. Determine the Dirac cycle, its coefficient action and the Thom map. For a vector bundle \(B\), check (246) on the symbol class \([B]\). Explain why replacing the Dirac module by the scalar identity while retaining this Thom map is generally incorrect.

Solution. The unit groupoid has algebra \(C(V)\). Its Dirac module is \(\Gamma(H)\), with even grading and operator zero. Every endomorphism of this finite bundle module is compact, so it is a cycle even though its square defect is minus the identity. Its class is \([H]\), and a coefficient bundle \(E\) gives \([E\otimes H]\). The chosen Thom map is multiplication by \([H]\), with inverse multiplication by \([H^*]\). Thus (246) gives

\[ \Theta_F^{-1}[B]\;\ell_!^{\mathrm{an}} =[B\otimes H^*][H]=[B]. \tag{247} \]

Replacing only the Dirac class by the scalar identity would instead give \([B\otimes H^*]\). For a concrete failure take \(V=S^2\), \(B=1\), and the line obtained by gluing two trivial lines over the hemispheres with equatorial transition \(e^{i\theta}\). The dual transition has winding minus one. Changing a frame over either disk changes that winding by zero: radial contraction of the disk gives a homotopy of its boundary frame function to a constant nonzero function. Winding is homotopy invariant, as proved in Exercise 46. Thus \(H^*\) is not trivial. If \(H^*\oplus\mathbb C^n\) were isomorphic to \(\mathbb C^{n+1}\), taking the top exterior power would trivialize \(H^*\), a contradiction. More generally an equality \([H^*]=[1]\) in the bundle Grothendieck group would give \(H^*\oplus E\cong1\oplus E\) for some bundle \(E\). Taking determinants and tensoring by \((\det E)^*\) gives the same contradiction. Hence \([H^*]\ne[1]\). The actual line and its dual must both be retained.

Exercise 49 (intermediate: a compact module map with a noncompact regular operator). On \(V=\mathbb T^2\), take the foliation generated by \(\partial_x+\alpha\partial_y\), with \(\alpha\) irrational. Let \(k\) be a nonzero nonnegative smooth function supported in \([-1,1]\), regarded as the arrow kernel independent of the unit. Show that left multiplication by this element of \(A\) is compact on the standard right module \(A\), while its operator on each holonomy-cover \(L^2(\mathbb R)\) is not compact. Give an explicit sequence witnessing the second assertion.

Solution. The action is free: if \((t,\alpha t)\in\mathbb Z^2\), then irrationality forces \(t=0\). Each leaf and its holonomy cover are therefore parametrized by \(\mathbb R\); the graph is \(V\times\mathbb R\). The kernel \(k\) is smooth with compact arrow support because \(V\) is compact. It belongs to the dense convolution algebra and hence to \(A\). On the standard module, \(\theta_{a,b}\) is left multiplication by \(ab^*\). An approximate identity shows these products span \(A\) densely, so \(\mathcal K_A(A)=A\), and left multiplication by \(k\) is compact.

On a cover it is convolution by \(k\). Choose a nonnegative smooth unit vector \(u\), supported in \([-1,1]\), which is not zero. Then \(v=k*u\) is nonzero, is supported in \([-2,2]\), and has norm \(c>0\). Put \(u_n(t)=u(t-6n)\). These unit vectors have disjoint supports, while their images are \(v(t-6n)\), also with disjoint supports. In particular,

\[ \|k*u_n-k*u_m\|_2=\sqrt2\,c \qquad(n\ne m). \tag{248} \]

No subsequence of the images converges in norm, which disproves ordinary compactness. Tensoring the construction with a finite Clifford module preserves the distinction. Thus (243) must be justified in the module compact ideal, as its proof does; ordinary finite-rank reasoning on an infinite cover would be invalid.

Exercise 50 (advanced). On the flat two-torus, let \(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\) be the ordered positive generators of \(C_2\). Lift the vertical operator with Fourier multiplier \(a(k)=k\varepsilon_1/\sqrt{1+k^2}\), and take the total multiplier \(q(k,l)=(k\varepsilon_1+l\varepsilon_2)/\sqrt{1+k^2+l^2}\). Show that the vertical lift is not compact, that its leading function does not extend continuously to the vertical zero-frequency axis, and that its anticommutator with the total operator is nevertheless nonnegative. Explain why the compactness step in Lemma 7.5 needs the vanishing-axis condition.

Solution. The exact anticommutator is \[ [a(k),q(k,l)] =\frac{2k^2}{\sqrt{1+k^2}\sqrt{1+k^2+l^2}}I\ge0. \tag{255} \] The positive-Clifford mixed terms cancel. At a fixed nonzero integer \(k\), the normalized vectors \(e^{i(kx+lz)}\otimes v\), with \(l\) tending through distinct integers and \(v\) a unit coefficient vector, are orthogonal. The norms of their vertical images are the same positive number \(|k|/\sqrt{1+k^2}\). Their images remain orthogonal, so the vertical lift is not compact. Its leading function for \(\xi\ne0\) is \(\operatorname{sgn}(\xi)\varepsilon_1\). Approaching \((0,1)\) from positive and negative \(\xi\) gives different limits. The total anticommutator's leading function is instead \(2|\xi|/\sqrt{\xi^2+\eta^2}\), which is continuous and zero there.

For the last assertion, let \(K\) be the rank-one projection onto a constant first-coordinate Fourier vector, and take \(G=I\). Then \((K\widehat\otimes1)G=K\widehat\otimes1\) has infinitely many orthonormal eigenvectors of eigenvalue one, indexed by the second Fourier coordinate. It is not compact, although \(K\) is vertically compact. The symbol of \(G\) is identity on the axis and violates Lemma 7.5's hypothesis. With a vanishing-axis symbol, Lemma 7.4 instead makes its compositions with creation vectors compact; this is precisely the step used in that lemma. No claim that every lifted vertical compact is a total compact is valid.

Exercise 51 (intermediate: the density correction). Give \(f:\mathbb T_x\times\mathbb T_y\to\mathbb T_y\) the vertical density \(a(y)\,dx\), where \(a>0\) is smooth, and horizontal lift \(\partial_y\). For a trivial coefficient line with metric connection \(\partial_y\), calculate (258). Check its sign on sections constant in \(x\). Then use density \(dx\) and horizontal lift \(\partial_y+\sin x\,\partial_x\); verify its corrected connection is skew-adjoint in the scalar total \(L^2(dx\,dy)\) inner product.

Solution. Formula (260) gives \(k_{\partial_y}=a'/a\), hence \[ \nabla^{E_f}_{\partial_y}=\partial_y+\frac{a'}{2a}, \qquad \partial_y\langle u,v\rangle =2\pi\bigl(a'\overline uv+a\overline{u'}v+a\overline uv'\bigr) \tag{267} \] for \(x\)-constant sections, with circle length \(2\pi\). The sum of the two corrected connection inner products is precisely the right side. Omitting the correction loses \(2\pi a'\overline uv\); using its negative doubles that error. In the second example \(v=1\), \(B=\sin x\), so \(k=\cos x\) and the corrected operator is \(L=\partial_y+\sin x\,\partial_x+\tfrac12\cos x\). Periodic integration by parts gives \((\sin x\,\partial_x)^*=-\sin x\,\partial_x-\cos x\) and \(\partial_y^*=-\partial_y\). Multiplication by \(\cos x/2\) is self-adjoint. Therefore \(L^*=-L\) on the smooth core. These computations explain the positive half-density sign in (258).

Exercise 52 (advanced: disconnected fibres and the compact ideal). Let \(V=\mathbb T\) with its full tangent foliation, and let \(W=V\sqcup V\) map to \(V\) by identity on each component. Use the canonical rank-zero vertical orientation. Determine \(H,R,\mathscr P_f\) and the inclusion (262). Explain why the compact correspondence \(\varepsilon_f\) does not give a Morita equivalence between \(C_r^*(H)\) and \(C_r^*(G)\). Verify the module and operator form of (264).

Solution. The connected circle has trivial transverse holonomy, so \(G=V\times V\). Write \(L=L^2(V)\). Its reduced algebra is \(\mathcal K(L)\): a smooth pair kernel acts by its integral operator; separated smooth kernels are finite rank and dense, and every regular representation is that same integral representation. The leaves of \(W\) are its two components. Thus \(H\) consists of two pair groupoids, whereas \(R\) has an arrow between any two points lying over the endpoints of a \(G\) arrow, including the two off-diagonal component choices. Accordingly \[ \begin{aligned} C_r^*(H)&=\mathcal K(L)\oplus\mathcal K(L),& A&=\mathcal K(L),\\ \mathscr P_f&=A\oplus A,&\mathcal K(\mathscr P_f)&=M_2(A). \end{aligned} \tag{268} \] The middle identification follows from \(E_f^0=C(V)^2\) and Lemma 7.8. The inclusion \(j_*\) is the block-diagonal inclusion into \(M_2(A)\). It has compact left action but does not cover the off-diagonal compact operators. A Morita equivalence would identify the two compact algebras (and their K-groups); here \(K_0(C_r^*(H))=\mathbb Z^2\) whereas \(K_0(A)=\mathbb Z\), by compact stability and scalar K-theory. The correspondence sends the two rank-one generators to the same generator, so cannot be an equivalence. The first module in (264) is \(C(V)^2\), with zero vertical operator. Its product with the base cycle is the direct sum of two base regular spinor modules. On the right, the two \(H\) modules extended by the block-diagonal inclusion give those same two summands, with the same direct sum operator. This verifies the entire product, while displaying why replacing \(H\) by \(R\) would change the asserted left algebra.

Exercise 53 (advanced: two rank-zero phase factors). Let \(f:W\to V\) be a finite smooth covering of compact manifolds and give \(V\) the point foliation. Specify a vertical rank-zero orientation line \(L_K\to W\) and a base rank-zero orientation line \(L_F\to V\). Determine both sides of (264) as actual modules with their left \(C(W)\) actions. Does the fibre cardinality determine the answer?

Solution. Here \(F_W=0\), \(G\) and \(H\) are the unit groupoids, and \(R=W\times_VW\). The first module is the finite vector bundle \(f_*L_K\), with fibre \(\bigoplus_{w\in f^{-1}(y)}(L_K)_w\). Its operator is zero and a function on \(W\) acts diagonally by its value at each \(w\). Tensoring with the base line gives \(f_*(L_K\otimes f^*L_F)\). On the right the full spin-c orientation on the zero bundle \(F_W\) is that same tensor line. Its \(C(W)\) line module tensored with \(\mathscr P_f\) gives the same fibre direct sums and diagonal left action. Both sides have zero operator and compact identity because they are finite bundle modules over \(C(V)\). Covering charts supply the bundle transitions, including the permutations of sheets and the two line phases. The number of sheets gives only the fibre rank; it determines neither these transitions nor the represented \(C(W)\) action. This is the rank-zero part of the ordered orientation in (256).

Exercise 54 (intermediate: infinitely many rank-zero sheets). Let \(W=\mathbb Z\times\mathbb T\), \(V=\mathbb T\), and \(f(n,y)=y\). Give both manifolds the point foliation and canonical rank-zero orientation lines. Identify the vertical module, its compact left action and the correspondence in (272). Explain why the zero vertical operator is a Kasparov cycle although the identity of the vertical module is not compact. Verify (273).

Solution. Compact subsets of \(W\) meet finitely many components. The vertical integration module is the standard module \(E_f^0=\ell^2(\mathbb Z)\widehat\otimes C(\mathbb T)\), whose inner product is \(\sum_n\overline{u_n}v_n\). The left algebra is \(C_0(W)=c_0(\mathbb Z,C(\mathbb T))\), acting diagonally. For \(g\) in that algebra, the finite-sheet diagonal truncations converge in norm, since their error norm is \(\sup_{|n|>N}\|g_n\|\to0\). Each finite-sheet diagonal is a finite sum of module rank-one maps, with the standard coordinate vectors and coefficient functions. Thus multiplication by \(g\) is compact. The identity is not compact: after evaluation at any \(y\), it becomes the identity on the infinite-dimensional Hilbert space \(\ell^2(\mathbb Z)\), while every module compact becomes an ordinary compact operator. The square defect of the zero phase is nevertheless \(-g\), which is compact for every allowed left coefficient.

Here \(G\) and \(H\) are unit groupoids, whereas \(R=W\times_VW\) has every pair of sheet indices over one \(y\). Thus \(\mathscr P_f=E_f^0\), \(C_r^*(R)=\mathcal K(\ell^2\mathbb Z)\otimes C(\mathbb T)\), and \(C_r^*(H)=C_0(W)\) includes as the diagonal compact action just proved. The base analytical class is the identity zero cycle on \(C(\mathbb T)\); the source analytical class is the identity zero cycle on \(C_0(W)\). Both sides of (273) are therefore the entire module \(E_f^0\) with its diagonal left action and zero operator. An assertion that \(H=R\), or that the identity of \(E_f^0\) must be compact, would give the wrong conclusion.

Exercise 55 (advanced: a smooth metric family need not be uniform at infinity). On \(\mathbb R^2\), with its full tangent foliation and trivial spin-c structure, set \(g_s=dx_1^2+e^{2s x_1^2}dx_2^2\), \(0\leq s\leq1\). Transport the Clifford module by the positive metric isometry. Write its normalized cotangent Clifford symbol \(q_s\) in the fixed positive generators \(\varepsilon_1,\varepsilon_2\). Show that the pointwise smooth family does not converge to \(q_0\) in the supremum symbol norm as \(s\downarrow0\). Explain which homotopy assertion of Lemma 7.11 still applies.

Solution. A coordinate covector \(\xi_1dx_1+\xi_2dx_2\) has dual norm squared \(\xi_1^2+e^{-2s x_1^2}\xi_2^2\). Positive transport gives \[ q_s(x,\xi)=\frac{\xi_1\varepsilon_1+e^{-s x_1^2}\xi_2\varepsilon_2} {\sqrt{\xi_1^2+e^{-2s x_1^2}\xi_2^2}}. \] Fix any \(s>0\), let \(|x_1|\to\infty\), and choose \(\xi_1=1\), \(\xi_2=e^{s x_1^2/2}\). Then \(q_0\to\varepsilon_2\) and \(q_s\to\varepsilon_1\). The two positive generators are self-adjoint, square to one and anticommute, so \((\varepsilon_1-\varepsilon_2)^2=2I\) and their difference has norm \(\sqrt2\). Consequently the supremum norm of \(q_s-q_0\) is at least \(\sqrt2\) for every positive \(s\). Pointwise smoothness has not supplied a global uniform symbol-norm path.

Lemma 7.11 instead constructs one adjointable bounded phase on the interval module, using compact parameter supports and a countable locally finite buffered atlas. Each compact left coefficient involves only finitely many charts, with uniform interval estimates and compact interval defects. Those are the assertions needed for a Kasparov homotopy. The equality of the endpoint classes follows; global operator-norm continuity of an arbitrarily chosen pointwise phase family was not its premise.

Exercise 56 (advanced: a domain projection does not reduce the phase). Take \(Y=\{\mathrm{pt}\}\), \(n=1\), \(U=(-1,1)\), and the full right \(C_1\)-module of Lemma 7.14. Show that \(PF(1-P)\ne0\). Explain why this does not obstruct (274), and verify the sign in both cutoff identities (278).

Solution. The one-dimensional off-diagonal kernel (279) is \(i\varepsilon_1 k(w)\), where

\[ k(w)=\frac{w}{2\sqrt\pi}\int_0^\infty t^{-3/2}e^{-t}(4\pi t)^{-1/2}e^{-w^2/(4t)}\,dt. \tag{283} \]

For \(w\ne0\) the integral is finite and strictly positive. Hence \(k(w)\) has the sign of \(w\). Choose a nonzero nonnegative smooth function \(v\) supported in \((2,3)\), with Clifford value (1). For \(-1<x<1\), the integral \(\int k(x-z)v(z)\,dz\) is strictly negative. Multiplication by the invertible \(i\varepsilon_1\) does not make it zero. Thus the inside component of \(Fv\) is nonzero although \(Pv=0\). The domain is not a reducing summand for this bounded phase.

If \(a\in C_c(U)\) and \(\chi=1\) on its support, then \(a\chi=a\), \(\chi(1-P)=0\), and \((1-P)\chi=0\). Expanding \(a[\chi,F](1-P)\) gives \(aF(1-P)\). Expanding \((1-P)[F,\chi]a\) gives \((1-P)Fa\). The commutators have the two opposite orders shown in (278). Each is compact, because \(\chi\) is a compact interior coefficient of the ambient analytical cycle. These localized compact terms permit the block homotopy and subsequent interior-symbol comparison. The proof requires that compactness, not a zero unlocalized inside–outside block.

Exercise 57 (intermediate: an exact whole tube and its Jacobian). Let \(f:S^1\to\{\mathrm{pt}\}\), \(u(\theta)=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)\), and let \(v\) denote the signed outward radial normal coordinate. Set \(\rho=1/4\). Compute the whole tube, its image, its vertical Jacobian with respect to \(d\theta\,dv\), and the image of \((\theta,v)=(0,1/(4\sqrt3))\). Explain why a flat phase on the image can be transported to the cylinder without a complete pulled-back metric assumption.

Solution. The bundle \(N\) is the radial real line bundle. Formula (281) becomes

\[ w(v)=\frac{v}{\sqrt{1+16v^2}},\qquad \Phi(\theta,v)=(1+w(v))(\cos\theta,\sin\theta), \qquad U=\{z:3/4<|z|<5/4\}. \tag{284} \]

The strictly increasing function \(w\) has derivative \((1+16v^2)^{-3/2}\) and range \((-1/4,1/4)\). Thus \((\theta,v)\mapsto(\arg\Phi,|\Phi|)\) is a diffeomorphism onto that annulus. Its polar area density is

\[ J(v)=(1+w(v))(1+16v^2)^{-3/2}>0. \tag{285} \]

For the separately chosen density \(d\theta\,dv\), the change-of-variables unitary sends \(h\) on the annulus to \(J(v)^{1/2}h(\Phi(\theta,v))\). This preserves the integral inner product and is onto by the inverse substitution. At the specified \(v\), \(w=1/8\), so the image is \((9/8,0)\). The pulled-back Euclidean metric is \(w'(v)^2dv^2+(1+w(v))^2d\theta^2\); a radial path to \(v=+\infty\) has finite length \(1/4-w(v_0)\), so this metric is incomplete. Lemma 7.11 constructs a bounded phase from interior charts with that principal symbol and locally compact defects. Lemma 7.14 then identifies it with the restriction of the flat ambient class. Neither completeness nor a self-adjoint boundary realization is needed for this bounded construction.

Exercise 58 (10 points; the rank-two block sign). In Lemma 7.16 take \(r=2\). Show that the normalized block volume is negative on \(\psi\), although \(\psi\) is even in the exterior/external module. Determine the grading and both physical generators after the contraction by \(\Sigma_2^*\). Give an even right-module unitary from that shifted module to the regular \(C_2\) module, and calculate the transported physical action. Explain why omission of the shift would change the full induced orientation.

Solution. Here \(k_2=1\). Moving \(B_1\) past \(A_2\) gives the single minus sign, so

\[ \begin{aligned} (-i)^2A_1A_2B_1B_2\psi&=-\psi,\\ \Sigma_2^*\widehat\otimes(T\widehat\otimes C_2)&\cong\Pi C_2, \qquad(C_1,C_2)^{\mathrm{contracted}}=(L_{t_1},L_{t_2}),\\ U:\Pi C_2\to C_2,\quad U(c)&=t_1c,\qquad (UC_1U^{-1},UC_2U^{-1})=(L_{t_1},-L_{t_2}). \end{aligned} \tag{296} \]

The first line uses that every \(-iA_iB_i\) fixes \(\psi\). The corner vector is even, but its corresponding vector of \(\Sigma_2\) is odd; the remaining module must therefore be shifted. The uncontracted corner generators are negative. The Koszul sign of the odd corner in the Morita tensor reverses both signs, giving the second line. The map \(U\) preserves the right action and inner product because \(t_1^*=t_1=t_1^{-1}\). It is even from the shifted module: for a homogeneous \(c\), both its shifted source parity and the parity of \(t_1c\) are \(|c|+1\). Conjugation by \(t_1\) fixes \(t_1\) and negates \(t_2\), giving the last line. The induced real generator frame is thus reflected in its second coordinate. Keeping the regular grading together with two positive generators would instead retain the original orientation; it would lose the actual reflected orientation of this inverse transfer.

Grading: 2 points for the volume permutation and eigenvalue; 3 for the module shift and contracted Koszul signs; 3 for the even unitary and both conjugations; 2 for the full orientation conclusion.

Exercise 59 (10 points; the full conjugate line). An oriented rank-two bundle has a prescribed spin-c transition \(zs\) on an overlap, with \(s=\exp(-\theta t_1t_2/2)\). Tensor its prescribed module by an even line whose transition is \(h\in U(1)\). Compute the exact transition of \(\mathcal D_E\), including its grading. Suppose that line is nontrivial but its square is trivial. Explain what a determinant-only comparison would miss. Also give the transferred inverse in rank zero for a full orientation line of parity \(\epsilon\).

Solution. Formula (295) removes the \(a\) spin lift and retains the physical \(b\) spin lift. The finite contraction sends the even physical word \(b_1b_2\) to \(t_1t_2\), since its two contracted generator signs multiply to one. The inverse line phase is conjugated. Thus

\[ \begin{aligned} \mathcal D_{E}^{\,H}&\cong\mathcal D_E\otimes H^*, \qquad g_{\mathcal D_E^{\,H}} =h^{-1}z^{-1}\exp(-\theta t_1t_2/2) \quad\text{on }\Pi C_2,\\ r=0:\quad \mathcal T_0(\alpha_E)&=[H^*,\mathrm{multiplication},0], \qquad |H^*|=\epsilon. \end{aligned} \tag{297} \]

For example, a line transition \(h=i\) contributes \(-i\) on the inverse, while a transition \(h=-1\) remains \(-1\). A spin-c determinant transition squares the line phase. A nontrivial order-two line therefore leaves that determinant unchanged but remains in the full module as the nontrivial dual line. Formula (293) and its evaluations retain it; no determinant argument can remove it. In rank zero the conjugate line has the same parity as the original line. Its zero operator is a cycle because multiplication by every \(C_0(X)\) function is compact on this finite line section module. An odd line remains odd; the canonical even rank-zero unit cannot replace it.

Grading: 4 points for the spin word, full phase and shifted module; 3 for the two-torsion/determinant distinction; 3 for the rank-zero line, parity and compact defect.

Exercise 60 (10 points; the horizontal-double rotation). In one orthonormal horizontal pair take \((t,b_H)=(1,0)\). Compute its image under (301) at \(\theta=0,\pi/4,\pi/2\). Verify the spin unitary and explain why its formula glues when the horizontal bundle is nonorientable. At the endpoint, identify the two horizontal coordinates in \(L\) and the horizontal contribution to the ambient Euclidean vector.

Solution. The exact values and implementing unitary are

\[ \begin{aligned} R_0(1,0)&=(1,0),& R_{\pi/4}(1,0)&=(2^{-1/2},-2^{-1/2}),& R_{\pi/2}(1,0)&=(0,-1),\\ s_\theta&=\exp\bigl((\theta/2)\gamma_t\gamma_b\bigr),& s_\theta\gamma_t s_\theta^* &=\cos\theta\,\gamma_t-\sin\theta\,\gamma_b . \end{aligned} \tag{311} \]

The bivector is skew-adjoint because its two positive self-adjoint generators anticommute. Its commutators with \(\gamma_t,\gamma_b\) are \(-2\gamma_b,2\gamma_t\); the elementary two-dimensional exponential therefore implements both columns of (301), not a rotation with the opposite sign. For several pairs, the bivector sum is invariant under simultaneous orthogonal changes of both copies: the coefficient of the sum is the metric contraction. This includes a frame change of determinant \(-1\); no orientation of \(H\) is needed.

For general input the endpoint sends \((t,b_H)\) to \((b_H,-t)\). Formula (302) consequently gives the horizontal double \((a_H,b_H)\) in \(L\), while the Euclidean coordinate contains \(-du(t)\). With \(\eta\in\nu_u\), this is the normal vector \(\chi(\eta,t)=\eta-du(t)\). The two full \(H\)-double evaluations now cancel; their source and target exterior gradings are interleaved. Moving the two even-dimensional right blocks has the stated even exterior implementer, but flips of individual odd vectors still carry their Koszul signs.

Grading: 3 points for all exact coordinates and the rotation sign; 3 for both spin commutators and the unitary; 2 for orthogonal frame invariance; 2 for the full endpoint double and normal quotient.

Exercise 61 (10 points; odd block volumes and even maps). In Lemma 7.19 compare the cases \((r,q,n)=(3,1,4)\) and \((1,3,4)\). Compute the normal shift and generator factor, the product module and both physical blocks, and the unitary from the ambient inverse. Explain why the second map is even although its Clifford multiplier is odd. Track an arbitrary line transition \(z\).

Solution. Since \(k_1=0,k_3=1,k_4=0\), equations (305)–(308) give

\[ \begin{array}{c|c|c|c|c|c} (r,q)&(a,\kappa)&h&\text{product module}&(c_K,c_N)&U\\ \hline (3,1)&(0,-1)&0&C_4&(L_{e_K},L_{e_N})& L_{\omega_K\omega_N}\\ (1,3)&(0,1)&1&\Pi C_4&(-L_{e_K},L_{e_N})& L_{\omega_K} \end{array} \tag{312} \]

The ambient inverse is \(C_4\) with all physical generators negative. In the first row the multiplier has degree \(3+1=0\bmod2\); it is the unitary four-generator volume, up to its specified scalar, and conjugates every real generator to its negative. It therefore maps the ambient negative physical list to the positive product list. In the second row \(\omega_K\) has degree one. Conjugation fixes the single \(K\) generator and negates every normal generator, so it maps the ambient list to \((-e_K,+e_N)\). Its source has the regular grading and its target has the reversed grading; adding one to the underlying Clifford-word degree therefore preserves the full module parity. The map is even and preserves the right action and inner product.

The right target order is \(K,N\) after the specified graded transport. In both examples the two ranks are odd; the coefficient flip must include its odd-word minus sign. The normal structure retains the line transition \(z\); its inverse contains \(z^{-1}\), while the vertical module contains \(z\). Their exact Hermitian evaluation is \(z^{-1}z=1\). Spin transitions give the ambient lift as in (309). No determinant calculation or grading omission can replace these two evaluations.

Grading: 3 points for both exact rows; 3 for the generator conjugations and complete graded parity of the maps; 2 for the odd target-block transport; 2 for the full phase and spin evaluation.

Exercise 62 (10 points; an even transport in six Clifford generators). In the odd rank-three reduction of Lemma 7.20, label the old generators \(e_1,e_2,e_3\), and the new generators \(e_4,e_5,e_6\). Give a unitary even word implementing the move of the old odd generator past the two new even-block generators. Check all moved generators and the total chirality. Explain how the resulting full reducer identifies the reduced transferred inverse with \(\mathcal T_1(y')\).

Solution. Use the two adjacent unit reflections, in their required order: \[ \begin{aligned} w&=\frac{(e_4-e_5)(e_3-e_4)}2,\qquad ww^*=w^*w=1,\\ we_3w^*&=e_5,\qquad we_4w^*=e_3,\qquad we_5w^*=e_4,\\ we_jw^*&=e_j\quad(j=1,2,6),\qquad w\chi_6w^*=\chi_6 . \end{aligned} \tag{322} \] Each numerator vector has square two, so division by \(\sqrt2\) gives an odd self-adjoint unitary. Its twisted adjoint exchanges its two generators and fixes the others. The composition has even degree, so its ordinary adjoint is the composition of the two reflections. This proves every displayed generator identity. The real permutation is a three-cycle, of positive sign; multiplying the entire ordered generator list proves the last identity for \(\chi_6=(-i)^3e_1\cdots e_6\).

After transport, the old even block occupies positions one and two, the new even block positions three and four, and the pair old odd/new odd positions five and six. The full canonical reducer is the even wedge tensor \(\Sigma_1^{\mathrm{old}}\widehat\otimes\Sigma_1^{\mathrm{new}}\widehat\otimes\Sigma_1^{\mathrm{odd,odd}}\). In the balanced tensor, evaluate the new even dual/pair exactly. What remains is the old even source inverse module and the ordered odd coevaluation, namely \(\mathcal T_1((\mu_3^B)^{-1}y)\). The maps preserve both actions, grading and inner products; the two full Morita evaluations prove onto range. No swap of the final odd pair has occurred.

Grading: 3 points for the correctly ordered normalized unitary; 3 for all generator and chirality checks; 2 for the complete reducer decomposition; 2 for the exact balanced evaluation and retained odd order.

Exercise 63 (10 points; the geometric ambient inverse). Compute (319) in dimensions \(n=2,4,6\).
